items.summary:
Anthropic has published research detailing the implementation of a global workspace architecture in language models. This approach aims to enhance the models' ability to manage and integrate information across different tasks and contexts, potentially improving their overall performance and coherence.

The research explores how a global workspace can serve as a centralized mechanism within language models, facilitating better coordination of internal processes. This development represents a significant step in advancing the architecture of language models to handle complex cognitive functions more effectively.

items.title: Martinalderson.com analyzes GLM 5.2 as a competitive open weights AI model and predicts an upcoming collapse in AI inference margins due to easier migration and cost pressures [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: GLM 5.2 and the coming AI margin collapse
items.summary:
Martinalderson.com presents an analysis of GLM 5.2, highlighting it as a competitive open weights AI model comparable to leading models like Opus and GPT. The article argues that the AI industry is approaching a significant shift in economics, with inference costs—rather than training costs—being the primary driver of profitability. GLM 5.2 offers a viable alternative for inference, with easy migration options that could disrupt existing AI service providers.

The analysis notes some limitations of GLM 5.2, such as slower response times and lack of vision and robust web search capabilities, which affect its suitability for interactive and agentic tasks. However, the model's compatibility with existing APIs makes it a practical drop-in replacement, potentially leading to reduced margins for established AI labs as users shift to more cost-effective open weights models.

This development suggests an impending collapse in AI inference margins due to easier migration and increased competition, challenging the current business models of frontier AI companies. The article emphasizes that while some technical gaps remain, ongoing improvements and third-party integrations are likely to address these issues, accelerating the shift in AI economics.

items.title: AMD launches Ryzen AI Halo mini-PC with Zen 5 Ryzen AI Max+ 395 processor, 128GB LPDDR5x memory, 2TB SSD, and integrated Radeon 8060S GPU for $4,000 [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AMD Ryzen AI Halo – $4k AI Dev Kit
items.summary:
AMD has introduced the Ryzen AI Halo, a compact mini-PC powered by the Zen 5 Ryzen AI Max+ 395 processor featuring 16 cores and 32 threads. The system includes 128 GB of LPDDR5x-8000 unified memory, a 2 TB removable M.2 SSD, and integrated Radeon 8060S graphics, designed to support AI development with ROCm and AMD hardware. Priced at $4,000, it comes preloaded with either Windows 11 Pro or a custom AMD Linux distribution based on Debian 13.4.

The Ryzen AI Halo measures just 15 cm square and under 5 cm tall, weighing 1.2 kg, and offers connectivity options including four USB 3.2 Type-C ports, HDMI 2.1, 10 GbE Ethernet, Wi-Fi 7, and Bluetooth 5.4. It features a cooling system with two blower fans and a distinctive white light ring around the base. The device targets AI developers needing a powerful yet portable platform with substantial memory and storage for local AI models.

items.title: OfficeCLI launches open-source Office suite enabling AI agents to read, create, and edit Microsoft Word, Excel, and PowerPoint files without Office installation [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: OfficeCLI: Office suite for AI agents to read and edit Microsoft Office files
items.summary:
OfficeCLI is an open-source Office suite designed specifically for AI agents, enabling them to read, create, and edit Microsoft Word, Excel, and PowerPoint files without requiring an Office installation. It operates as a single binary with no dependencies and includes a built-in HTML rendering engine that allows AI to interact with documents visually and efficiently. Users can control OfficeCLI through a command-line interface or a GUI app called AionUi, which supports natural language commands for document creation and editing.

The tool simplifies complex document manipulation tasks into single commands, supporting a wide range of features such as text formatting, layout adjustments, formula handling, and content reorganization. It also offers internationalization and right-to-left language support, making it versatile for global use. OfficeCLI integrates with various AI coding agents, allowing seamless automation of Office document workflows without manual intervention.

By providing a streamlined and AI-friendly interface to Office documents, OfficeCLI has the potential to enhance productivity and enable new AI-driven applications in document management and creation. Its open-source nature encourages community involvement and further development, positioning it as a significant advancement in AI-assisted office productivity tools.

items.title: Researchers introduce SALT benchmark for evaluating LLM uncertainty in long-form generation using deterministic ground truth across six tasks and analyze 50+ models' confidence functions and error drivers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Evaluating LLM Uncertainty in Long-Form Generation Using Deterministic Ground Truth
items.summary:
Researchers have developed SALT (Single-answer Atomic Long-form Target), a new benchmark designed to evaluate uncertainty in long-form text generation by large language models (LLMs) using deterministic ground truth across six tasks. SALT enables fine-grained assessment of correctness, calibration, and confidence ranking at the unit level without relying on external judges, addressing challenges posed by label imperfections in existing benchmarks. Analyzing over 50 LLMs with SALT, the study identifies dominant confidence functions for different uncertainty aspects and reveals that confidence ranking deteriorates at atomic resolution despite clearer separability at coarser levels.

The benchmark also allows controlled interventions at the atomic level during generation, uncovering two main drivers of future errors: error propagation from corrupted prefixes influenced by global context correctness, and degradation linked to increasing answer-context length. Additionally, the research finds that reasoning techniques, such as Chain-of-Thought prompting or training-based internalization, improve accuracy but can reduce the reliability of confidence rankings. These insights have important implications for applications where precise error detection and mitigation are critical.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03870v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As LLMs generate increasingly long outputs, effective uncertainty estimation must identify errors at fine-grained levels rather than discard entire responses. While such methods exist, evaluating uncertainty at any resolution (token to an entire generation) is challenging and highly sensitive to label imperfections, making zero-noise benchmarks essential; yet, long-form generation benchmarks tend to rely on fallible labels rather than deterministic ground truth. We introduce Single-answer Atomic Long-form Target (SALT), a benchmark of six procedurally generated tasks with single deterministic long textual ground truths, enabling unit-level evaluation of correctness, calibration, and ranking without external judges. Equipped with SALT, our analysis of 50+ LLMs reveals key insights: We identify which confidence functions dominate each uncertainty aspect and show that confidence ranking largely breaks at atomic resolution, even when clearer separability emerges at coarser line-level units. SALT further enables controlled atom-level interventions throughout generation, revealing two separable drivers of future errors: propagation from corrupted prefixes, dominated by global context correctness, and bounded degradation from increasing answer-context length. Finally, we demonstrate that reasoning, via Chain-of-Thought prompting or internalized through training, introduces a trade-off, improving accuracy while degrading confidence ranking. These findings directly impact risk-critical applications requiring reliable error identification and mitigation.

items.originalTitle: Explainable AI for Screening Abuse-Related Trauma in Bangladeshi Children: A Training-Free Multimodal Framework Evaluated on Noise-Aware Synthetic Data
items.summary:
Researchers have developed ShishuRaksha AI, a training-free multimodal explainable AI framework designed to support early screening of abuse-related psychological trauma in Bangladeshi children. The system integrates four screening methods—validated questionnaires, Bengali narrative text, House-Tree-Person drawing features, and facial affect—using a clinically weighted fusion approach with cross-modal attention. It generates bilingual reports with risk explanations and referral guidance to national child-protection services, addressing the lack of culturally adapted tools and limited mental health resources in Bangladesh.

The study openly discusses limitations such as reliance on synthetic data and subgroup disparities, positioning this work as a feasibility study and a step toward ethically deployable child-protection screening tools in low-resource settings.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04010v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bangladesh has an estimated 1.17 mental-health professionals per 100,000 population and only six child psychiatrists nationwide. No Bengali-language, culturally adapted tool exists for early screening of abuse-related psychological trauma in children. We present ShishuRaksha AI, a decision-support (not diagnostic) framework that fuses four screening modalities: validated questionnaires (SDQ, CPSS), Bengali narrative text, House-Tree-Person (HTP) drawing features, and facial affect. The fusion is training-free and clinically weighted, uses cross-modal attention, and includes a single-modality override rule. Every risk score is explained through clinically weighted, perturbation-based additive attribution and rendered as a bilingual (Bangla/English) report with referral routing to national child-protection services (OCC, DSS, NMHH) under the Children Act 2013. No clinical dataset of abused children can be collected ethically at this stage, so we introduce a noise-aware synthetic benchmark (500 cases, 116 positive [23.2%], four deliberate noise layers, literature-grounded HTP priors) and evaluate tree-ensemble surrogates of the fusion design (facial channel excluded) under 5-fold stratified cross-validation. The fused model reaches an AUC of 0.874 [0.834-0.908], against 0.756 [0.705-0.803] for an SDQ-only baseline, with ablation, operating-point, subgroup, and calibration analyses. We state all limitations openly, including synthetic-only data, no held-out set, text-feature circularity, and an urban-rural subgroup gap. This work is a feasibility study and a design contribution toward ethically deployable child-protection screening in low-resource settings.

items.title: Researchers introduce LLM-as-a-Verifier, a general-purpose framework providing fine-grained, continuous verification scores for agentic tasks, achieving state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: LLM-as-a-Verifier: A General-Purpose Verification Framework
items.summary:
Researchers have developed LLM-as-a-Verifier, a new framework that enhances large language models' ability to verify the correctness of solutions in agentic tasks by providing fine-grained, continuous verification scores without additional training. This approach uses a probabilistic method to generate continuous scores from token logits, allowing for improved score granularity, repeated evaluation, and criteria decomposition, which together increase verification accuracy and calibration. The framework achieves state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks, including Terminal-Bench V2, SWE-Bench Verified, RoboRewardBench, and MedAgentBench.

LLM-as-a-Verifier also introduces a cost-efficient ranking algorithm to select the best solutions based on continuous scores and offers fine-grained feedback that can estimate task progress. An extension for Claude Code enables developers to monitor and improve agentic systems, while the framework's dense feedback supports reinforcement learning, enhancing sample efficiency in robotics and mathematical reasoning tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.05391v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scaling pre-training, post-training, and test-time compute have become the central paradigms for improving the capabilities of LLMs. In this work, we identify verification, the ability to determine the correctness of a solution, as a new scaling axis. To unlock this and demonstrate its effectiveness, we introduce LLM-as-a-Verifier, a general-purpose verification framework that provides fine-grained feedback for agentic tasks without requiring additional training. Unlike standard LM judges that prompt LLMs to produce discrete scores for candidate solutions, LLM-as-a-Verifier computes the expectation over the distribution of scoring token logits to generate continuous scores. This probabilistic formulation enables verification to scale along multiple dimensions: (1) score granularity, (2) repeated evaluation, and (3) criteria decomposition. In particular, we show that scaling the scoring granularity leads to better separation between positive and negative solutions, resulting in more calibrated comparisons. Moreover, scaling repeated evaluation and criteria decomposition consistently lead to additional gains in verification accuracy through variance and complexity reduction. We further introduce a cost-efficient ranking algorithm for selecting the best solution among candidates using the verifier's continuous scores. LLM-as-a-Verifier achieves state-of-the-art performance on Terminal-Bench V2 (86.5%), SWE-Bench Verified (78.2%), RoboRewardBench (87.4%), and MedAgentBench (73.3%). Beyond verification, the fine-grained signals from LLM-as-a-Verifier can also serve as a proxy for estimating task progress. We build an extension for Claude Code, enabling developers to monitor and improve their own agentic systems. Finally, we show that LLM-as-a-Verifier can provide dense feedback for RL, improving the sample efficiency of SAC and GRPO on robotics and mathematical reasoning benchmarks.

items.title: Researchers propose Lagrangian Reward Augmentation to improve safe inference-time alignment in frozen language models under safety constraints, enhancing helpfulness-harmlessness tradeoff [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Safe Inference-Time Alignment via Lagrangian Reward Augmentation
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Lagrangian Reward Augmentation (LARA), a new framework designed to improve inference-time alignment of frozen language models under explicit safety constraints. Unlike existing methods that optimize a single scalar score and often overlook safety constraints or rely on manually tuned penalties, LARA formulates the problem as a constrained optimization using both reward and cost models. This approach transforms the challenge into a one-dimensional convex problem, enabling the use of an augmented reward signal that integrates seamlessly with current inference-time alignment techniques.

LARA has been tested on sequence-level methods like Best-of-N reranking and token-level reward-guided decoding, showing improved balance between helpfulness and harmlessness. The Best-of-N method, in particular, achieved performance close to that of finetuning-based direct alignment approaches, marking a significant advancement in safely steering language model outputs without the need for repeated weight updates.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02781v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Inference-time alignment steers a frozen language model during decoding using auxiliary reward signals, avoiding the cost of repeated weight updates. However, existing inference-time alignment methods typically optimize a single scalar score, so explicit safety constraints must either be ignored or encoded through manually tuned penalties. We propose Lagrangian Reward Augmentation (LARA), a general inference-time alignment framework under safety constraints. Starting from a KL-regularized constrained objective with a reward model and a cost model, LARA dualizes the constraint and reduces the optimization problem to a one-dimensional convex problem over a nonnegative dual variable. Estimated on a small calibration set, this dual variable defines an augmented reward that can be used as a drop-in scoring signal within existing inference-time alignment methods. For sequence-level sampling methods, such as Best-of-N reranking, the calibrated dual variable corresponds to the solution of the expected-cost constrained problem. For token-level reward-guided decoding methods, the same construction yields a principled dual-calibrated heuristic rather than an exact constrained-policy guarantee. We evaluate LARA on both sequence-level and token-level inference-time alignment methods, and find that LARA improves the helpfulness-harmlessness tradeoff, with Best-of-N achieving the best performance among inference-time methods, approaching finetuning-based direct alignment baselines.

items.title: Researchers propose BDLM Mamba-H hybrid model for long-context language generation, achieving up to 19.7x throughput over prior diffusion models at 65K tokens [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Training Hybrid Block Diffusion Language Models with Partial Bidirectionality
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a hybrid model called BDLM Mamba-H that significantly improves long-context language generation by combining efficient attention mechanisms with block-based token generation. This approach addresses memory bandwidth limitations by restricting reverse-direction scans to active blocks, enabling exact caching and enhancing throughput. BDLM Mamba-H achieves up to 19.7 times the throughput of previous diffusion models at 65,000 tokens while maintaining competitive performance on validation tasks.

The model was tested on configurations ranging from 87 million to 350 million parameters, showing superior perplexity scores compared to existing baselines and maintaining efficiency at larger scales. By optimizing the interaction between Mamba mixing and attention, BDLM Mamba-H offers a promising architecture for handling very long sequences in language modeling.

This advancement suggests that hybrid diffusion architectures like BDLM Mamba-H could become a key solution for scaling language models to handle extensive contexts more efficiently, potentially impacting future developments in natural language processing and large-scale model deployment.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02805v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-throughput long-context generation is one of the central challenges for large language models. Generation is typically memory-bandwidth-bound rather than compute-bound: each decoding step must stream the accumulated key/value (KV) cache from memory, so bandwidth demand grows with context length while only one token is emitted. Two parallel approaches have therefore emerged: reducing memory access with efficient attention variants and linear-time mixers such as Mamba, or increasing parallel computation by generating blocks of tokens at once. However, technical challenges arise when combining these two ideas. Earlier hybrid diffusion models such as DiffuMamba use bidirectional Mamba mixing, including a reverse-direction scan relative to causal generation. This reverse scan needs to scan the entire sequence, so its states are not prefix-only and cannot be precisely reused as a cache even when diffusion is performed block by block. We propose a BDLM Mamba--attention hybrid that addresses this challenge by restricting the reverse Mamba scan to the active denoising block, which enables exact caching across blocks. In an 87M-parameter DCLM sweep, BDLM Mamba-H achieves the best C4-en validation perplexity compared to BDLM attention and full-sequence baselines. At 350M parameters, it remains competitive with BDLM attention. For long-context inference, BDLM Mamba-H reaches 19.7x the throughput of full-sequence DiffuMamba-H at 65K tokens and 3.7x the throughput of BDLM attention at 262K, showing that Mamba hybrids are a potential long-context diffusion architecture.

items.title: Researchers find 12 to 31% of weights in sparse transformers are interpretable with consistent functional descriptions across full training data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Individual Parameters in Weight-Sparse Transformers Appear Interpretable
items.summary: Researchers have developed an automated pipeline using large language models to interpret individual weights in sparse transformer neural networks by generating and verifying concise, human-readable descriptions of when each weight influences model predictions. Their study found that between 12% and 31% of weights in sparse transformers can be meaningfully interpreted with consistent functional descriptions across the entire training data, a higher proportion than in dense transformers. This approach advances mechanistic interpretability by providing a global understanding of weight functions rather than focusing on specific behaviors or input subsets.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02964v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A central goal of mechanistic interpretability is to understand how neural networks work and what each individual component does. Dominant circuit-finding approaches focus on a specific behavior and reverse-engineer the role of components on the associated sub-distribution. However, past work has shown that components can have different functions that are active on different subsets of the input distribution. In this work we ask whether a single weight can be understood globally across the full training distribution by characterizing when it matters (the inputs on which ablating it changes the model's predictions). We introduce an automated LLM pipeline that writes a short, human-readable description of when a weight matters and verifies it on held-out text, crediting a weight only if its description generalizes. Across two sparse and two dense transformers, the fraction of weights that are interpretable (in this sense) is higher in sparse transformers than in dense ones, a gap that widens once unreliable descriptions are discarded. Our results show that a meaningful fraction of a sparse transformer model's weights can be interpreted: 12 to 31% of weights have a single short description that identifies what the weight is used for.

items.title: Researchers propose IsoLoCo, a model merging-inspired aggregation method that improves DiLoCo distributed training efficiency and performance across language model pre-training tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Can Model Merging Improve Aggregation in DiLoCo?
items.summary:

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03011v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Model merging techniques, which aggregate independently finetuned models into one to combine their capabilities, have become a topic of significant interest in recent years, with a broad array of methods having been proposed to tackle this problem. Simultaneously, an emerging trend in distributed learning has been the use of methods such as local SGD and DiLoCo, which greatly reduce communication costs by periodically aggregating the independently trained local models. However, these communication-efficient methods have been shown to degrade in performance relative to the FLOP-matched data-parallel gold standard as the number of independent local models grows and as the number of local training steps before global communication is increased. In this work, we draw an explicit analogy between the pseudo-gradient aggregation step in local SGD/DiLoCo and task arithmetic-based model merging, establishing a straightforward way to utilize merging methods in the context of distributed optimization. We then evaluate multiple state-of-the-art model merging methods in this setting and identify one method in particular, Iso-C, as a promising approach for improving DiLoCo. We find that DiLoCo SGD with Iso-C aggregation outperforms not only simple pseudo-gradient averaging but even the momentum-based DiLoCo, despite lacking a momentum mechanism itself. Building on this finding, we propose IsoLoCo, which adapts Iso-C for distributed training by equipping it with Nesterov momentum. Our empirical evaluations on language model pre-training across varying numbers of local workers show that IsoLoCo significantly outperforms DiLoCo, with the gap between them widening as the number of workers increases. This advantage remains present across model sizes and inner step counts, confirming that merging-inspired aggregation is an effective strategy for low-communication distributed training.

items.title: Researchers propose KARMA, a knowledge graph-based method for automated reasoning and slot-aligned contrastive candidate synthesis, outperforming baseline models across biomedical, computer science, and chemistry benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: KARMA: Knowledge graph-based Automated Reasoning Materialization and Alignment
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced KARMA, a novel method that leverages knowledge graphs for automated reasoning and slot-aligned contrastive candidate synthesis. KARMA addresses the Resolution Mismatch Problem by enumerating schema-constrained paths over domain knowledge graphs and converting them into slot-aligned contrastive candidates. This approach, combined with Slot-Parallel Alignment (SPA) that applies a decoupled slot-level objective, enhances preference supervision on discriminative entity slots.

KARMA was evaluated across benchmarks in biomedical, computer science, and chemistry domains, where it outperformed baseline large language models and same-data supervised fine-tuning methods. It also showed competitive results compared to sequence and token-level preference techniques, demonstrating its effectiveness in improving contrastive synthesis and reasoning tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03166v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Template-based contrastive synthesis is scalable, but its candidates often differ only in a few entity-slots while sequence-level optimization spreads supervision over mostly shared templates. We formalize this as the Resolution Mismatch Problem and propose KARMA, which enumerates schema-constrained paths over domain knowledge graphs and verbalizes them into slot-aligned contrastive candidates. Slot-Parallel Alignment (SPA) then applies a decoupled slot-level objective to route preference supervision to discriminative entity-slots, with slot-aware masked attention serving as an optional packed-evaluation implementation. Across biomedical, computer-science, and chemistry benchmarks, KARMA outperforms base LLM and same-data SFT baselines, and compares favorably with sequence and token-level preference methods.

items.title: Researchers introduce Transition Information Density and Positional Identity to capture structured intermediate states in neural training, demonstrating effects in phonetic and semantic representations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Transition Information Density: Morphological Trajectories, Synesthetic Perception, and Structured Interpolation in Neural Training (or: The Synesthetic AI)
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced the concepts of Transition Information Density (TID) and Positional Identity to capture and analyze the structured intermediate states that occur between distinct training endpoints in machine learning. These constructs were tested across multiple empirical contexts, including grapheme-color synesthesia and a four-condition training experiment involving different representational mediums. The study found that probes trained on structured interpolation at defined Positional Identities showed significantly lower intrinsic dimensionality in phonetic and semantic representations compared to controls, while visual and cross-modal mediums did not exhibit this effect.

The research provides a formal definition of TID and Positional Identity, along with a nine-metric shape characterization framework and an experimental design that isolates the effects of trajectory structure, data volume, and Positional Identity. Analysis revealed modality-specific differences in representation consistency, with phonetic space showing globally consistent representations and visual space showing collapsed representations. These findings highlight the importance of considering intermediate state structures in neural training and suggest modality boundaries in how such structures influence learned representations.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03210v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Standard machine learning training presents data as discrete endpoint pairs, omitting the structure of the space between them. This paper introduces Transition Information Density (TID) -- the information content recoverable from structured intermediate states between categorically distinct training endpoints -- and Positional Identity, the defined location of an intermediate state on the A-to-B continuum. Both constructs are grounded in three empirical contexts: grapheme-color synesthesia, the Synesthesia Grid (a boundary-contour morphing algorithm instantiating TID in visual morphological space), and a four-condition training experiment across four representational mediums. Probes trained on structured interpolation at defined Positional Identities (C3) exhibit substantially lower intrinsic dimensionality than volume-matched controls (C2) in Phonetic/Linguistic (C3: 3.33 vs. C2: 10.81) and Semantic Description (C3: 4.59 vs. C2: 8.67) mediums. Visual and cross-modal mediums do not show this effect, establishing a modality boundary condition. A fixed-N=50 comparison confirms that Positional Identity structure, not sample count, drives the effect. Resolution N scales monotonically with representational richness. Pooled TwoNN analysis reveals globally collapsed representations in visual space (0.075) and globally consistent representations in phonetic space (0.977). The paper contributes a formal definition of TID and Positional Identity, a nine-metric shape characterization framework, and a four-condition experimental design isolating trajectory structure, data volume, and Positional Identity as distinct factors.

items.title: Researchers propose DMVM, a decentralized framework for efficient multi-task dataset valuation via model merging without retraining or data sharing, supporting privacy and scalability [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Efficient Decentralized Multi-task Dataset Valuation via Model Merging
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced DMVM, a decentralized framework designed to efficiently value datasets used in training multi-task models without the need for retraining or data sharing. This approach leverages model merging and task arithmetic to assess each dataset's contribution across multiple tasks, addressing limitations of existing methods that focus on single-task settings and require extensive computation or centralized coordination. DMVM supports privacy and scalability by enabling collaborative valuation through a secure aggregation protocol that protects individual model parameters and data.

The framework aligns dataset valuation with multi-task generalization behavior and offers theoretical guarantees on approximation quality. Its effectiveness has been demonstrated through experiments in computer vision and natural language processing, highlighting its potential for fair and transparent data marketplaces where multiple contributors provide data for complex model training scenarios.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03346v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate and efficient dataset valuation is essential for enabling fair and transparent data marketplaces, especially when multiple contributors provide data for training multi-task models. Most existing valuation methods, however, are limited to single-task settings, overlooking scenarios where a buyer aims to optimize performance across multiple downstream tasks. Moreover, traditional valuation approaches, such as Shapley-based or retraining-based methods, are computationally expensive and poorly suited for decentralized environments without a trusted central coordinator and with strict privacy constraints. We propose DMVM (Decentralized Multi-task Valuation via Model Merging), a novel framework that bypasses retraining and data sharing by leveraging task arithmetic to infer dataset contributions directly from model combinations. Instead of retraining or sharing raw data, DMVM quantifies how models trained on different datasets combine in parameter space to infer each dataset's marginal utility across multiple tasks. This formulation yields a valuation process that is scalable, computationally efficient, and explicitly aligned with multi-task generalization behavior. To support decentralized deployment, we introduce a secure aggregation protocol that enables collaborative valuation without revealing individual model parameters or private data. We also provide theoretical error bounds characterizing the approximation quality of DMVM and validate our framework through comprehensive experiments on computer vision and natural language processing tasks.

items.title: CaresAI presents TNM stage prediction models using classical and deep learning approaches on TCGA pathology reports for SMM4H-HeaRD 2026, showing varied performance and generalizability challenges [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: CaresAI at SMM4H-HeaRD 2026: Predicting TNM Staging
items.summary:
CaresAI developed models to independently predict Tumor, Node, and Metastasis (TNM) stages using pathology reports from the Cancer Genome Atlas as part of the SMM4H-HeaRD 2026 shared task. The study framed the problem as three multi-label classification tasks and applied both classical and deep learning methods, including TF-IDF features and embeddings from ClinicalBERT, BioBERT, and PubMedBERT, combined with classifiers like Logistic Regression, LightGBM, Feed-Forward Neural Networks, and Wide Residual Networks. Results showed that combining embeddings improved prediction, with LightGBM using TF-IDF achieving the highest AUROC and F1 scores during training.

Evaluation on test sets revealed a decline in performance, indicating challenges in model generalizability, sensitivity to class imbalance, and handling lengthy clinical documents. Despite providing an efficient baseline and reproducible pipeline, the study highlights the need for further optimization and validation before these models can be reliably applied in clinical settings.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03466v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study aims to predict Tumor, Node, and Metastasis (TNM) stage labels independently, with the Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) pathology report as the sixth shared task of SMM4H-HeaRD 2026. The problem is framed as three multi-label classification tasks. We explore both classical and deep learning approaches using Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) features and embeddings from ClinicalBERT, BioBERT, and PubMedBERT. These representations are used with Logistic Regression (LR), Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), Feed-Forward Neural Networks (FFNN), and Wide Residual Networks (WRN). Our results show that individual embeddings perform similarly to the TNM label classification, while their combination improves its predictive ability. WRN achieves AUROC scores of 0.839 (T), 0.8502 (N), and 0.803 (M) with F1-scores of 0.622, 0.702, and 0.9337, respectively, for the training phase. LightGBM with TF-IDF performs best with AUROC scores of 0.9368 (T), 0.9524 (N), and 0.8311 (M) and F1-scores of 0.7559 (T), 0.7384 (N), and 0.7017 (M) during the training phase. Furthermore, the result of the Codabench for the test sets indicates a Macro-F1 score of 0.978, 0.957, and 0.879 for the T, N, and M categories respectively for test set 1; while test set 2 records a Macro-F1 score for T, N, and M is 0.807, 0.767, 1.0 respectively. However, performance declined during the evaluation phase of the test sets, a drop from 0.938 to 0.858 of test set 1 to 2, for the Macro-F1 score across all stages; suggesting limitations in model generalizability, sensitivity to class imbalance, and challenges in processing lengthy clinical documents. Although this study provides an efficient baseline model and a reproducible pipeline, further optimization and validation are required before it can be considered suitable for use in a real-world clinical setting.

items.title: Researchers decode hidden multi-step reasoning in frontier LLMs over filler tokens using unsupervised methods with 80-95% accuracy across four task families [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Reading Between the Dots: Decoding Hidden Computation across Filler Tokens
items.summary:
Researchers have developed an unsupervised decoding method that reveals how advanced large language models (LLMs) perform multi-step reasoning over content-free filler tokens, such as dots or counting sequences, achieving 80-95% accuracy across four task families including fact retrieval and numeric composition. Using two open-weight models, DeepSeek V3 and Kimi K2, the study shows that these LLMs process filler tokens in a structured manner, with attention mechanisms routing questions through filler regions and intermediate computations becoming visible in the models' hidden states.

The approach relies solely on analyzing hidden states without ground-truth labels or training, demonstrating that hidden computations—previously undetectable through surface outputs—can be decoded directly from the models' internal residual streams. This finding suggests that the monitorability of LLM reasoning depends on access to the full computational trace rather than just observable token outputs, offering new insights into understanding and interpreting complex model behaviors.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03502v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Frontier LLMs can perform multi-step reasoning over content-free filler tokens like dots or counting sequences, producing correct answers with no visible chain-of-thought (CoT). This is a limit case for behavioral oversight, where surface tokens carry no information about the underlying reasoning. But hidden from the output is not the same as hidden from us. On four task families (fact retrieval, parallel numeric composition, string manipulation, and in-context computation), two open-weights frontier models (DeepSeek V3, Kimi K2) compute over filler tokens in a structured, legible way: attention routes the question through the filler region to the answer, logit-lens readouts show retrieved facts emerging early and their composition crystallizing in late layers, and KV-cache transplants at filler positions causally swap outputs between examples. We introduce an unsupervised decoding pipeline that takes only hidden states as input and recovers intermediate values with 80-95% accuracy (best LLM judge) across both models and all four tasks, without ground-truth labels or training. Hidden computation that defeats behavioral CoT monitoring is, on these tasks, directly readable from the residual stream, suggesting monitorability is a property of the model's full computational trace, not just its surface tokens.

items.title: Researchers propose Reinforcement Learning for Selection Reward to align large language models with selective prediction metrics, improving risk-coverage trade-off in decision-critical AI tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Aligning Language Models with Selective Prediction
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced a new method called Reinforcement Learning for Selection Reward (RLSR) to improve the reliability of large language models (LLMs) in critical decision-making tasks. This approach focuses on selective prediction, enabling LLMs to make predictions only when confident, thereby balancing the trade-off between risk and coverage and allowing uncertain cases to be handled by humans. RLSR aligns LLMs with selective prediction performance metrics, specifically targeting the area under the risk-coverage curve (AURC), which leads to better risk-coverage outcomes compared to existing alignment techniques.

The study emphasizes post-training alignment of LLMs using reinforcement learning to optimize selective prediction metrics rather than traditional correctness or calibration measures. Experiments demonstrate that RLSR achieves superior performance on both in-domain and out-of-domain tasks, enhancing the practical reliability of LLMs in high-stakes applications where decision accuracy and human-AI collaboration are crucial.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03528v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as critical decision-making components in high-stakes real-world AI systems, rendering LLM reliability a foremost practical concern. In this paper, we focus on enhancing LLM reliability through selective prediction (SP), a strategy that allows an LLM to only predict for inputs where it is likely to be correct (i.e., coverage) and hence reduce the error rate (i.e., risk) on that portion of inputs -- flagging the remaining inputs for future human discretion. In other words, SP improves LLM reliability by balancing the risk-coverage trade-off and enabling seamless human-AI collaboration. To integrate SP into LLMs, we focus on the LLM post-training alignment stage and propose to align LLMs with SP performance metrics, in contrast with existing LLM alignment methods that focus primarily on correctness or calibration metrics. Specifically, we propose a novel alignment framework, Reinforcement Learning for Selection Reward (RLSR), which targets the area under the risk-coverage curve (AURC) -- a popular SP performance metric -- as its alignment objective. RLSR achieves substantially better risk-coverage trade-off compared to multiple alignment baselines on both in-domain and out-of-domain tasks.

items.title: Researchers find language models represent communicative intent reliably across six models but often fail to act on it by default, with intent decodable before output generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: They Infer What You Meant: Models Represent Communicative Intent More Reliably Than They Act On It
items.summary:
Researchers have found that large language models reliably represent the communicative intent behind user inputs across six different models, but often fail to act on this intent by default. By applying a linear probe to the models' hidden states, the study decoded whether users intended their input to be recognized or evaluated, demonstrating that intent is encoded well before it influences the model's output. This finding holds across multiple model families and extends to more nuanced intents such as support versus help.

The study highlights a gap between the internal representation of intent and the model's behavior, with some models not acting on the decoded intent without intervention. By identifying a specific direction in the model's internal layers linked to intent, researchers showed that steering this direction can recover the intended behavior without explicit prompts. This approach distinguishes between routing the represented intent and generic feedback, offering a causal handle to improve model responsiveness to user intent.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03598v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When a person shares something with a language model, the model often answers the surface of the message rather than what the sender was doing by sending it: share a finished project and it critiques the code; share a raw late-night line and it runs a wellness check. We treat the sender's communicative intent, the Gricean what-was-meant, as a first-class interpretability object, and show the failure is one of readout on top of a robust representation. A linear probe decodes the sender's intent, whether they want a thing recognized or evaluated, from a model's default-pass hidden states, cleanly and surface-independently, across six models and four families and in the base checkpoints. The representation generalizes further, to intent that is only pragmatically inferred, and to a second, lexically clean intent (support versus help). The behavioral half of the story, and every causal test, is established on the recognize/evaluate contrast, where what varies is whether the default output acts on the intent. The readout lags the representation in depth within a model (the intent is decodable several layers before it drives the output); across models, which ones act on it by default is model-specific, an observed stratification (three of six show the failure) that we do not read as a scaling law. Where the gap is open, a direction closely tied to the representation, the discriminative direction at a searched-for layer, is a causal handle: steering it recovers the intended behavior, as well as an explicit instruction does and with no prompt at all. This direction is near-orthogonal to the feedback-offering axis, so it routes a represented intent rather than a generic feedback knob, though at the recovery dose the routed intent can override an explicit request. We support each link with controls against obvious deflations and report the nulls as plainly as the confirmations.

items.title: Researchers introduce Stabilized Adapter for self-Report (SAR) to detect hidden behaviors in fine-tuned language models, outperforming existing introspection methods across seven implanted behaviors [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Revealing Hidden Model Behaviors with Task-Specific Self-Reports
items.summary:
Researchers have developed the Stabilized Adapter for self-Report (SAR), a lightweight LoRA adapter designed to help fine-tuned language models reveal their hidden behaviors in plain language. SAR effectively detects subtle or harmful behaviors implanted during fine-tuning across seven tested cases, outperforming existing introspection methods by identifying all hidden behaviors and reducing hallucinations in its reports. This advancement enables more reliable auditing of language models to understand what they have actually learned during training.

SAR was tested against Introspection Adapters (IA), the closest existing baseline, which failed to detect some behaviors and often produced incorrect reports. In contrast, SAR maintained positive detection signals in all scenarios where IA failed and halved the rate of hallucinations, even when models exhibited broad misalignment beyond the training data. This improvement offers practitioners a more accurate and practical tool for evaluating model behavior and safety.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03640v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fine-tuning can give a language model a hidden behavior--it may give false answers under a narrow condition, or give harmful advice only when a prompt touches a particular topic. We introduce the Stabilized Adapter for self-Report (SAR), a lightweight LoRA adapter that makes a fine-tuned model describe its own hidden behavior in plain language, using only the model and the dataset it was trained on. Across seven implanted behaviors (plus a no-behavior control), SAR detects the hidden behavior in every one--even when the model has generalized into broad misalignment that the training data alone does not predict. Introspection Adapters (IA), the closest existing baseline, detects some behaviors from our suite but misses others entirely--and where it misses, it hallucinates, consistently reporting wrong behaviors. SAR retains positive signal on every setting where IA fails and halves the rate of hallucinations. This makes it much easier for practitioners to audit their models and obtain reliable answers to "what did my model actually learn?" type of questions.

items.title: Researchers show classification-head fine-tuning improves performance of Tiny Language Models under 3B parameters on multiple-choice benchmarks, achieving state-of-the-art results on Qwen3-0.6B and 1.7B [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Punching Above Their Weight: Classification-Head Fine-Tuning of Tiny Language Models (TLMs) for Verifiable Multiple-Choice Tasks
items.summary:
Researchers have demonstrated that classification-head fine-tuning significantly improves the performance of Tiny Language Models (TLMs) with fewer than 3 billion parameters on multiple-choice benchmarks. Their study compared three LoRA-based fine-tuning methods across various Qwen3 models ranging from 0.6B to 8B parameters on five benchmarks, including HellaSwag, WinoGrande, and PIQA. The classification-head approach consistently outperformed label generation fine-tuning by 2-3% at the 0.6B and 1.7B scales, achieving state-of-the-art results for Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B on several tasks.

The fine-tuned TLMs using this discriminative method showed competitive performance compared to much larger models such as GPT-3 (175B), PaLM (540B), and GPT-4, highlighting the effectiveness of this approach for adapting smaller models to verifiable multiple-choice tasks. This advancement suggests that efficient fine-tuning strategies can enable smaller, consumer-device-compatible models to perform at levels comparable to leading large-scale language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03801v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We define Tiny Language Models (TLMs) as models below roughly 3B parameters that fit on mainstream consumer devices. We study how to adapt them for and use them on verifiable multiple-choice tasks. We compare three LoRA-based fine-tuning paradigms (label generation, gold only, and our discriminative classification head) on a unified setup across several Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 8B and five benchmarks: HellaSwag, WinoGrande, PIQA, SciQ and ARC-C. Classification-head fine-tuning reliably outperforms label generation (+2-3%) at the 0.6B and 1.7B scales. Further, TLMs fine-tuned using the discriminative method are competitive to zero-/few-shot GPT-3 (175B), PaLM (540B) and GPT-4. The performance we report for Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B are SOTA on HellaSwag, WinoGrande, and PIQA.

items.title: Researchers develop a local hidden-state probe to replace GPT-3.5-turbo prompting for metadata filtering in Multi-Meta-RAG, achieving 90.9% accuracy on 2556 multi-hop queries [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Probe, Don't Prompt: A Hidden-State Probe for Metadata Filtering in Multi-Meta-RAG
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a local, deterministic hidden-state probe to replace the GPT-3.5-turbo prompting method used for metadata filtering in Multi-Meta-RAG, a system designed to improve retrieval for multi-hop question answering. This probe, trained on the hidden states of a small open-source language model, achieves 90.9% set-exact accuracy on 2,556 MultiHop-RAG queries, outperforming both a model-free substring baseline and GPT-3.5. The probe's fixed output vocabulary prevents it from drifting outside the allowed metadata sources, addressing a limitation of the prompted model.

The probe's effectiveness relies on three key design choices: selecting a shallow model layer, applying mean pooling, and using class-imbalance-aware multi-label training to handle the long tail of sources. A 135-million-parameter model performs nearly as well as a 1.5-billion-parameter one, making the filter computationally efficient since it requires only a partial forward pass through the initial layers plus a linear classification head, without needing an external API. The code for this approach is publicly available on GitHub.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03929v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-Meta-RAG improves retrieval for multi-hop question answering by filtering a vector store on metadata (the news source) that it extracts from each query by prompting gpt-3.5-turbo. We show this proprietary, free-form extractor can be replaced by a local, deterministic probe trained on the hidden states of a small open-source language model. On all 2556 MultiHop-RAG queries the probe reaches 90.9% set-exact accuracy against 88.0% for a model-free substring baseline and 80.9% for GPT-3.5, a margin that comes entirely from null queries, on which GPT-3.5 never abstains; on non-null queries all three stay within about a point. Because the probe's output space is exactly the fixed 49-source vocabulary, it cannot drift outside the allow-list as the prompted model does. Three design choices make it work: selecting a shallow layer, mean pooling, and class-imbalance-aware multi-label training over the long tail of sources. A 135M-parameter model lands within ~1.5 points of a 1.5B one, so the filter is cheap to output: a partial forward pass through the first few layers plus one linear head, with no API. The code is available at https://github.com/mxpoliakov/Multi-Meta-RAG.

outputCleanup.description:
Researchers have developed a local, deterministic hidden-state probe to replace the GPT-3.5-turbo prompting method used for metadata filtering in Multi-Meta-RAG, a system designed to improve retrieval for multi-hop question answering. This probe, trained on the hidden states of a small open-source language model, achieves 90.9% set-exact accuracy on 2,556 MultiHop-RAG queries, outperforming both a model-free substring baseline and GPT-3.5. The probe's fixed output vocabulary prevents it from drifting outside the allowed metadata sources, addressing a limitation of the prompted model.

The probe's effectiveness relies on three key design choices: selecting a shallow model layer, applying mean pooling, and using class-imbalance-aware multi-label training to handle the long tail of sources. A 135-million-parameter model performs nearly as well as a 1.5-billion-parameter one, making the filter computationally efficient since it requires only a partial forward pass through the initial layers plus a linear classification head, without needing an external API. The code for this approach is publicly available on GitHub.

items.title: Researchers introduce Telescope Perplexity metric to improve zero-shot detection of LLM-generated text by measuring token repetition probability, showing state-of-the-art performance across datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Telescope: Improving Zero Shot Detection of LLM Generated Content By Measuring Token Repetition Probability
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a new metric called Telescope Perplexity to improve the zero-shot detection of text generated by Large Language Models (LLMs). This metric measures the probability of token repetition, revealing a persistent bias in LLMs against repeating tokens that emerges early in their training. By leveraging this "Vestigial Heuristic," Telescope Perplexity effectively distinguishes LLM-generated text from human writing with state-of-the-art performance across various datasets and models.

The study shows that this token repetition signature appears early in the pre-training phase of LLMs and can be used efficiently to detect AI-generated content without prior examples. The researchers also introduced new evaluation sets and tested their method against different perturbation schemes, demonstrating competitive or superior results compared to existing detection techniques.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04061v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Distinguishing Large Language Model (LLM) generated text from human writing is a critical and difficult challenge. While LLMs are trained to write like humans, we hypothesize that this training leaves an indelible mark. LLMs develop a particularly strong aversion to token repetition very early in training. This bias persists as a ''Vestigial Heuristic'' (a developmental artifact) that is activated in LLM-generated text, separating LLM from human writing. To probe this phenomenon, we introduce Telescope Perplexity, a metric that evaluates the token repetition of the model, $P(s_i | s_{1:i})$ . Our empirical investigation reveals that the Telescope Perplexity signature emerges early in pre-training, and Telescope Perplexity empirically enables highly effective zero-shot LLM detection. We show state-of-the-art or competitive performance across diverse datasets (including modern evaluation sets we introduce), reference models, and perturbation schemes with greater efficiency than other methods.

items.title: Researchers release MTEB-PT, a Portuguese sentence encoder benchmark evaluating 17 models across 14 datasets, showing task-dependent performance and benefits of language-specific fine-tuning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Beyond Multilingual Averages: MTEB-PT, a Benchmark for Portuguese Sentence Encoders
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced MTEB-PT, a new benchmark designed to evaluate Portuguese sentence embedding models across 14 datasets covering tasks such as Semantic Textual Similarity, classification, retrieval, and reranking. The benchmark assesses 17 open- and closed-source models, revealing that performance in Portuguese varies significantly by task and that multilingual model rankings do not reliably predict effectiveness for Portuguese-specific tasks. No single model excels across all tasks, and models with strong long-context capabilities perform better on tasks involving longer inputs.

The study also demonstrates that language-specific fine-tuning enhances model performance in Portuguese, particularly when the fine-tuning data closely matches the target task. To explore this, the researchers fine-tuned three backbone models using Portuguese contrastive supervision and Matryoshka Representation Learning, achieving notable improvements in Semantic Textual Similarity and retrieval tasks. The team has released the MTEB-PT benchmark, the fine-tuned models, and the associated training and evaluation code to support further research in Portuguese language processing.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04071v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Portuguese remains underrepresented in text embedding evaluation, despite being one of the most widely spoken languages in the world. As a result, embedding models are often selected based on English or multilingual metrics, while their effectiveness in Portuguese remains unclear. We present MTEB-PT, a Portuguese benchmark constructed from a subset of MMTEB, comprising 14 existing datasets across Semantic Textual Similarity (STS), classification, retrieval, and reranking. We use this benchmark to evaluate 17 open- and closed-source embedding models under a unified protocol. Our results show that Portuguese performance is strongly task-dependent: multilingual rankings do not reliably predict Portuguese-specific performance across task families, no single model dominates all settings, and models with stronger long-context capacity are particularly advantageous on longer-input tasks such as retrieval and reranking. The benchmark also shows that language-specific fine-tuning still improves model performance in Portuguese, especially on task types that match the adaptation data most closely. To examine this effect, we fine-tune three representative backbone models with Portuguese contrastive supervision and Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL). These benchmark-informed baselines yield their strongest gains on STS, consistent with the predominantly symmetric supervision used during training, while also improving retrieval and remaining competitive under dimensional truncation. We release the MTEB-PT benchmark, the fine-tuned models, and the training and evaluation code.

items.title: Researchers propose DynaVieW, a schema-guided world model for hierarchical visual dynamics prediction and simulation, improving visual narrative creation and world simulation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: DynaVieW: Schema-Guided World Modeling for Understanding Hierarchical Visual Dynamics
items.summary:
Researchers have developed DynaVieW, a dynamic schema-guided world model designed to improve the prediction and simulation of hierarchical visual dynamics in videos and multi-image sequences. This model addresses the challenge of capturing multiple levels of dynamic elements, such as actions and environmental changes, by learning interleaved state-transition sequences that represent broad visual scenes and detailed dynamic constituents within a hierarchical framework. DynaVieW employs a mixture-of-experts architecture with selective attention and a specialized loss function to enhance learning effectiveness and robustness.

By jointly modeling transition prediction and state simulation, DynaVieW achieves a deeper understanding of visual dynamics, which enhances its performance in tasks like visual narrative creation and world simulation. The model demonstrates improved consistency, controllability, and adherence to instructions, marking a significant advancement in the systematic modeling of temporal visual scene evolution.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04112v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal LLMs struggle to systematically model the temporal evolution of visual scenes in videos or multi-image sequences. Such inputs require models to predict or simulate multiple levels of dynamic constituents, such as actions taken in the visual sequence, and the associated changes to the visual environment that result. To address this challenge, we propose a dynamic schema-guided world model, DynaVieW, optimized for visual dynamic prediction and simulation. DynaVieW achieves an in-depth understanding of visual dynamics by learning interleaved state-transition sequences, where states cover broad visual scenes from video keyframes, and transitions capture comprehensive dynamic constituents within a hierarchical schema. DynaVieW jointly models transition prediction and state simulation under a mixture-of-experts architecture, with a cross-expert selective attention and a schema token re-weighted loss, to ensure effective and robust learning. DynaVieW's understanding of visual dynamics boosts its downstream performance in visual narrative creation and world simulation, showing improved consistency, controllability, and instruction-following.

items.title: Researchers demonstrate practical trigger-word data poisoning attacks on smolVLA vision-language robotics model causing complete task denial on LeRobot platform with minimal poisoned samples [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: !Imperio, smolVLA: The Implications of Data Poisoning on Open Source Robotics
items.summary:
Researchers have demonstrated that trigger-word data poisoning attacks on vision-language action models, specifically the smolVLA model, are practical and effective in disabling robotic tasks. By introducing just a few poisoned samples into the training data, they were able to embed a backdoor that causes the robot to lock into a fixed position and fail to complete tasks on the LeRobot platform. The attack remains stealthy under normal conditions, as clean prompts still yield about a 50% success rate, but even a single poisoned episode drastically reduces task success.

The study tested various poison ratios and trigger placements, finding that only three poisoned episodes among 320 clean ones were enough to cause complete denial of service. The attack generalized across different trigger positions despite training only on front-placed triggers. These findings highlight the vulnerability of open-source robotics ecosystems to low-cost, stealthy data poisoning attacks and emphasize the importance of carefully managing dataset provenance to maintain trust and security.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04146v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This work establishes that trigger-word data poisoning of vision language action models is practical, while at the same time the open-source robotics ecosystem holds trust assumptions about community contributions. A few poisoned samples can silently embed a backdoor that disables a robot on command. We evaluate this threat against smolVLA on a real-world pick-and-place task, training on three poison ratios and evaluating across different prompts on the LeRobot platform. Three poisoned episodes in 320 clean episodes suffice for a complete denial of service. Success rate drops to 0.0 plus minus 0.0% across all trigger-word conditions and the robot locks into a fixed joint configuration rather than executing any task-relevant motion. Clean-prompt behaviour holds at approx. 50% success rate across all poison ratios, confirming the attack is stealthy under normal operation. A single poisoned episode already reduces success rate to 6.7 plus minus 6.7%. The robot still moves, but no longer completes the task. The attack generalises to front, middle, and end trigger placements despite training exclusively on front-placed triggers. These findings establish that the threat is practical, low-cost, and stealthy, and warrant treating dataset provenance as a first-class concern in open-source robotics ecosystems.

items.title: Researchers introduce GASP, a span-level detector for hallucinations in retrieval-augmented generation, achieving up to 0.73 AUC on RAGTruth and outperforming existing baselines without labeled data [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Detecting Hallucinations in Retrieval-Augmented Generation through Grounding-Aware Sensitivity by Perturbation (GASP)
items.summary:
Researchers have developed GASP (Grounding-Aware Sensitivity by Perturbation), a novel span-level detector designed to identify hallucinations in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems. Unlike existing detectors that provide only an overall answer-level score, GASP evaluates each sentence's dependence on retrieved evidence by measuring changes in likelihood when context is altered. This method achieves up to 0.73 area under the ROC curve (AUC) on the RAGTruth benchmark, outperforming traditional baselines without requiring labeled data.

GASP operates by rescoring answers under varying contexts—full, none, and with individual chunks removed—and analyzing the resulting likelihood drops and divergences. Grounded sentences show significant likelihood decreases when their supporting passages are removed, whereas hallucinated sentences remain largely unaffected. The approach was tested across multiple benchmarks and model families, demonstrating strong performance especially for outputs constructed from retrieved context rather than those relying solely on parametric knowledge.

The study highlights GASP's advantage over other methods, including perplexity measures and natural language inference baselines, and notes that a training-free threshold on grounding features can effectively detect hallucinations without additional labeled data. While effective on certain benchmarks, GASP's signal was less pronounced in short-answer question answering tasks, indicating its suitability primarily for context-dependent generation scenarios.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04223v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) reduces but does not eliminate hallucination, and existing detectors return a single answer-level score that does not indicate which sentence is unsupported, or why. To close this gap, we introduce Grounding-Aware Sensitivity by Perturbation (GASP), a span-level detector that scores each answer sentence by how strongly its likelihood depends on the retrieved evidence, a quantity we term grounding sensitivity. GASP holds the answer fixed and re-scores it under the full context, under no context, and with each chunk removed, then measures the log-likelihood drops and Jensen-Shannon divergences (JSD). The likelihood of a grounded sentence collapses once its supporting passage is removed, whereas a hallucinated sentence is almost unaffected, a contrast we interpret by casting decoding as a random nonlinear iterated function system (RNIFS). We evaluate GASP on three benchmarks (RAGTruth, TofuEval, RAGBench) with three instruction-tuned scorers from two model families (Qwen2.5-0.5B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, and SmolLM2-1.7B) under a leakage-clean protocol. On RAGTruth it reaches a response-level area under the ROC curve (AUC) of about 0.73 and a span-level AUC of about 0.67, improving significantly over perplexity and by clear margins over length, whole-context natural language inference (NLI), and self-consistency baselines. The only baseline competitive at the span level is a well-configured chunk-level entailment verifier, which requires a separate model, whereas a training-free threshold on the grounding features matches the trained classifier without labeled data and serves as the default detector. Beyond RAGTruth, the signal transfers to TofuEval but not to short-answer question answering in RAGBench, showing GASP is best suited to outputs constructed from the retrieved context rather than answers recoverable from parametric knowledge.

outputCleanup.description:
Researchers have developed GASP (Grounding-Aware Sensitivity by Perturbation), a novel span-level detector designed to identify hallucinations in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems. Unlike existing detectors that provide only an overall answer-level score, GASP evaluates each sentence's dependence on retrieved evidence by measuring changes in likelihood when context is altered. This method achieves up to 0.73 area under the ROC curve (AUC) on the RAGTruth benchmark, outperforming traditional baselines without requiring labeled data.

GASP operates by rescoring answers under varying contexts—full, none, and with individual chunks removed—and analyzing the resulting likelihood drops and divergences. Grounded sentences show significant likelihood decreases when their supporting passages are removed, whereas hallucinated sentences remain largely unaffected. The approach was tested across multiple benchmarks and model families, demonstrating strong performance especially for outputs constructed from retrieved context rather than those relying solely on parametric knowledge.

The study highlights GASP's advantage over other methods, including perplexity measures and natural language inference baselines, and notes that a training-free threshold on grounding features can effectively detect hallucinations without additional labeled data. While effective on certain benchmarks, GASP's signal was less pronounced in short-answer question answering tasks, indicating its suitability primarily for context-dependent generation scenarios.

items.title: Researchers present CausalGame benchmark to evaluate causal thinking of 30 LLM agents in 14 scientific discovery scenarios with selection bias and hidden confounders [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: CausalGame: Benchmarking Causal Thinking of LLM Agents in Games
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced CausalGame, a new benchmark designed to assess the causal reasoning abilities of 30 large language model (LLM) agents across 14 scientific discovery scenarios that include challenges such as selection bias, measurement error, and hidden confounders. The benchmark requires LLM agents to design experiments, gather data, and provide explanations, simulating realistic scientific investigation conditions. Despite these efforts, none of the tested models demonstrated robust causal thinking, with the best achieving only 68% effectiveness compared to analytical optima of 78-85%, and only a small fraction of sessions meeting causal reasoning criteria.

CausalGame aims to fill a gap in existing AI Scientist benchmarks by explicitly incorporating common real-world scientific challenges that affect causal inference. By providing a controlled and scalable environment, it offers a valuable tool for evaluating and improving the causal reasoning capabilities of AI agents engaged in scientific discovery.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04293v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Building AI Scientist agents with Large Language Models (LLMs) has recently attracted growing attention. Since scientific discovery fundamentally relies on uncovering causal relationships from observations, the capability of causal thinking, i.e., distinguishing causation from correlation and recognizing hidden biases, is essential to LLM agents. Although a number of benchmarks exist for AI Scientists, none explicitly incorporate challenges from selection bias, measurement error, and hidden confounders that widely exist in real-world scientific discovery. To this end, we present CausalGame, a benchmark that evaluates the causal thinking capabilities of LLM agents through interactive games. CausalGame asks LLM agents to actively design experimental protocols, collect observation data, and derive a final solution with an explanation report. To emulate realistic scientific discovery challenges, we design 14 scenarios that incorporate selection bias, measurement error, and hidden confounders. Across 30 LLM agents, none demonstrates reliable causal thinking: the best model reaches only 68.0% survival against analytical optima of 78-85%, and merely 5-7% of sessions receive credits on the causal-reasoning rubrics. CausalGame provides a scalable and controlled testbed for evaluating the causal thinking of AI Scientist agents.

items.title: HiFA4 introduces training-free 4-bit FlashAttention for LLM inference on Ascend HIF4 NPUs, reducing quantization errors and improving accuracy across five models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: HiFA4: Training-Free 4-bit FlashAttention on Ascend HIF4 NPUs for LLM Inference
items.summary:
HiFA4 is a new post-training operator-level design that enables training-free 4-bit FlashAttention for large language model (LLM) inference on Ascend HIF4 NPUs. It executes key matrix operations in low precision while maintaining the softmax state in higher precision, aiming to reduce quantization errors and improve accuracy. HiFA4 introduces two mechanisms—Smooth-QK and P-Reordering—that recalibrate attention computations and fuse normalization steps to enhance performance and reduce output scaling errors.

Evaluated across five LLMs, HiFA4 significantly reduces accuracy loss caused by quantization. For example, on the Qwen3-8B model, it recovers over a third of the accuracy gap introduced by direct quantization and cuts prediction inconsistencies and accuracy regressions substantially. The design also projects a notable latency reduction by integrating normalization into core computations, although hardware validation remains future work.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04302v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present HiFA4, a post-training operator-level design that executes both QK^T and PV in FlashAttention as 4-bit HIF4 Cube GEMMs for LLM inference on Ascend NPUs, while maintaining the online softmax state in FP16. To our knowledge, HiFA4 is the first Ascend-HIF4-targeted design of this kind evaluated on standard NLP benchmarks. HiFA4 combines two mechanisms. Smooth-QK applies a calibration-static per-channel equivalent rescaling to Q and K after RoPE, transferring quantization difficulty from K to Q without per-tile online reduction at inference. P-Reordering accumulates the softmax normalizer from the same quantized attention weights P_hat used in the PV GEMM, rather than from a higher-precision reconstruction. We show that this inconsistent formulation introduces a coherent output-scaling error, and validate the effect on a Qwen3-8B Layer-0 MMLU trace, where all 3.6M measured attention tiles exhibit net probability-mass loss with median epsilon_bar = -0.064. P-Reordering also allows the normalizer to be fused into the PV Cube GEMM. Across five LLMs, HiFA4 reduces quantization-induced decision drift. On Qwen3-8B, it recovers 37.5% of the accuracy gap introduced by direct HIF4 quantization, narrows the sample-weighted accuracy loss from 1.12 pp to 0.70 pp, reduces BF16-inconsistent MMLU predictions from 16.3% to 8.2%, and cuts MMLU accuracy regressions by 57% (1071 to 465). On Gemma2-9B, mild smoothing keeps HiFA4 within 0.7 pp of BF16 while reducing MMLU regressions by 27%. On LLaMA3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, and Phi-4B, where Smooth-QK is disabled, P-Reordering with the adopted Q-Mean auxiliary still reduces full-set MMLU regressions by 41-52%. A preliminary instruction-scheduling analysis projects a 35.4% critical-path latency reduction relative to BF16 by fusing the softmax normalizer into the PV Cube GEMM; on-hardware validation is left to future work.

items.title: Researchers propose UI-MOPD, a multi-teacher on-policy distillation method for continual learning of cross-platform GUI agents using the Uni-GUI dataset, achieving up to 38.2% task success [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: UI-MOPD: Multi-Platform On-Policy Distillation for Continual GUI Agent Learning
items.summary:
Researchers have developed UI-MOPD, a novel multi-teacher on-policy distillation method designed for continual learning of GUI agents across multiple platforms. Utilizing the newly created Uni-GUI dataset, UI-MOPD dynamically selects platform-specific teachers to transfer behavioral knowledge to a shared policy, enabling agents to adapt to new platforms while retaining existing capabilities. This approach addresses challenges such as limited cross-platform interaction data and the risk of catastrophic forgetting during training.

Experiments conducted on OSWorld and MobileWorld platforms demonstrate that UI-MOPD achieves task success rates of 38.2% and 12.0%, respectively. These results highlight the method's effectiveness in balancing the retention of cross-platform skills with the adaptation to new environments, marking a significant advancement in the development of versatile GUI agents capable of operating across diverse platforms.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04425v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in multimodal foundation models and agent systems have driven GUI agents from single-platform task execution toward cross-platform interaction. However, building multi-platform GUI agents remains challenging. On one hand, high-quality and executable cross-platform interaction trajectories are still scarce, and existing data often suffer from limited platform coverage. On the other hand, different platforms exhibit distinct interaction conventions, making joint or continual training prone to behavioral pattern mixing, platform-specific capability degradation, and catastrophic forgetting. To address these challenges, we construct Uni-GUI, a high-quality cross-platform GUI interaction dataset, and propose UI-MOPD, the first method that incorporates multi-teacher on-policy distillation into continual learning for GUI agents. UI-MOPD dynamically selects a platform-specific teacher according to the current environment and transfers platform-specific behavioral priors to a shared policy through platform-conditioned distillation, enabling adaptation to new platforms while preserving capabilities on existing ones. Experiments on OSWorld and MobileWorld show that UI-MOPD achieves task success rates of 38.2% and 12.0%, respectively, demonstrating its effectiveness in balancing cross-platform capability retention and new-platform adaptation. Project page: https://elispectre.github.io/UI-MOPD/.
