items.title: Researchers propose ChainReaction, a modular causal chain-guided reasoning model for explainable Causal-Why Video Question Answering, validated on 46K human-verified samples and three benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ChainReaction: Causal Chain-Guided Reasoning for Modular and Explainable Causal-Why Video Question Answering
items.summary:
Researchers have developed ChainReaction, a modular model designed to improve explainability and reasoning in Causal-Why Video Question Answering (VideoQA). This approach separates causal reasoning from answer generation by using natural language causal chains as interpretable intermediate steps, enabling clearer and more logical inference. The model consists of two components: a Causal Chain Extractor that generates causal chains from video-question pairs, and a Causal Chain-Driven Answerer that produces answers based on these chains.

To support training and evaluation, the team created a large dataset of 46,000 human-verified causal chains and introduced CauCo, a new metric for assessing causality-oriented captioning. Experiments on three major benchmarks show that ChainReaction outperforms existing state-of-the-art models, offering enhanced explainability, user trust, and generalization. This work positions the Causal Chain Extractor as a versatile reasoning engine applicable across various domains.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2508.21010v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Existing Causal-Why Video Question Answering (VideoQA) models often struggle with higher-order reasoning, relying on opaque, monolithic pipelines that entangle video understanding, causal inference, and answer generation. These black-box approaches offer limited interpretability and tend to depend on shallow heuristics. We propose a novel, modular paradigm that explicitly decouples causal reasoning from answer generation, introducing natural language causal chains as interpretable intermediate representations. Inspired by human cognitive models, these structured cause-effect sequences bridge low-level video content with high-level causal reasoning, enabling transparent and logically coherent inference. Our two-stage architecture comprises a Causal Chain Extractor (CCE) that generates causal chains from video-question pairs, and a Causal Chain-Driven Answerer (CCDA) that derives answers grounded in these chains. To address the lack of annotated reasoning traces, we introduce a scalable method for generating accurate causal chains from existing datasets. We construct human verified causal chains for 46K samples. We also propose CauCo, a new evaluation metric for causality-oriented captioning. Experiments on three large-scale benchmarks demonstrate that our approach not only outperforms state-of-the-art models, but also yields substantial gains in explainability, user trust, and generalization -- positioning the CCE as a reusable causal reasoning engine across diverse domains. Project page: https://paritoshparmar.github.io/chainreaction/

items.title: Researchers propose adaptive margin RLHF using preference-over-preference annotations to improve reward model learning and introduce DPO-PoP for enhanced discriminative and generative performance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Adaptive Margin RLHF via Preference over Preferences
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced a novel approach to reward model learning in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) by using preference-over-preference annotations to infer adaptive margins. This method addresses limitations of existing margin-based techniques, which often rely on fixed or simplistic margins and struggle with noisy or unreliable preference scores. The team developed DPO-PoP, an extension of Direct Preference Optimization that incorporates these adaptive margins, resulting in improved discriminative and generative performance.

The approach leverages annotations that indicate which of two preferences shows a stronger distinction, allowing for more nuanced margin adjustments on a per-datapoint basis. This technique can be integrated into standard RLHF reward modeling and direct alignment losses. The researchers also identified a tradeoff between discriminative and generative capabilities and proposed sampling strategies to effectively gather preference-over-preference labels to manage this balance.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2509.22851v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Margin-based optimization is fundamental to improving generalization and robustness in classification tasks. In the context of reward model learning from preferences within Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), existing methods typically rely on no margins, fixed margins, or margins that are simplistic functions of preference ratings. However, such formulations often fail to account for the varying strengths of different preferences or they rely on noisy margin information derived from preference ratings. Furthermore, many existing methods that use adaptive margins assume access to accurate preference scores, which can be difficult for humans to provide reliably. We propose leveraging preferences over preferences, that is, annotations indicating which of two preferences reflects a stronger distinction, to infer adaptive margins on a per-datapoint basis. Such preference-over-preference annotations are general and can be incorporated into both standard RLHF reward modeling objectives and direct alignment losses. As a concrete instantiation, we introduce DPO-PoP, an extension to Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) that incorporates adaptive margins from preference-over-preference supervision, enabling improved discriminative and generative performance. Additionally, we show a tradeoff between discriminative and generative performance and propose two sampling strategies for gathering preference-over-preference labels to navigate it.

items.title: SpatialThinker introduces unified scene graph generation and dense reward reinforcement learning for improved spatial reasoning in multimodal large language models, outperforming GPT-5 and Claude 4 on 14 benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SpatialThinker: Reinforcing Scene Graph-Grounded Spatial Reasoning via Dense Rewards
items.summary:
SpatialThinker is a new multimodal large language model (MLLM) designed to improve spatial reasoning by integrating Scene Graph Generation (SGG) directly into the reasoning process and using dense spatial rewards through reinforcement learning. Unlike previous models that depend on large datasets or explicit 3D inputs, SpatialThinker constructs a mental scene graph of relevant objects and relations to simulate human-like spatial perception and reasoning. It introduces a high-quality spatial VQA dataset, STVQA-7K, and a dense reward system that enhances structured grounding and generalizes to broader visual tasks.

SpatialThinker-7B, trained on only 7,000 samples, matches the performance of GPT-5 and surpasses GPT-4o, while the larger SpatialThinker-30B outperforms both GPT-5 and Claude 4 Sonnet across 14 spatial and real-world benchmarks. These results demonstrate that combining structured spatial grounding with reward-aligned reasoning enables robust spatial understanding with limited data, marking a significant advancement in vision-language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2511.07403v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in vision-language tasks, but continue to struggle with spatial reasoning. Existing spatial MLLMs rely on large-scale datasets, explicit 3D inputs, architecture-specific modifications, or sparse Reinforcement Learning (RL) methods that provide insufficient guidance for spatially-grounded reasoning. We introduce SpatialThinker. To our knowledge, it is the first MLLM unifying Scene Graph Generation (SGG) and visual reasoning in a single pass via online RL. The model simulates human-like spatial perception by constructing a mental scene graph of task-relevant objects and relations, and reasoning toward an answer via dense spatial rewards. Our contributions are threefold: (1) SGG-grounded reasoning: integrating SGG directly within the reasoning chain rather than as a disjoint preprocessing step; (2) STVQA-7K: a high-quality spatial VQA training dataset via a scalable synthesis pipeline; and (3) a dense spatial reward design that enforces structured grounding during RL and generalizes to improve broad visual perception. SpatialThinker-7B achieves 3.6$\times$ larger gains over SFT and $1.7\times$ better in- and out-of-distribution generalization than sparse RL. Trained on only 7K samples, SpatialThinker-7B matches GPT-5 and outperforms GPT-4o, while SpatialThinker-30B surpasses both GPT-5 and Claude 4 Sonnet on average across 14 spatial and real-world benchmarks, demonstrating that structured spatial grounding with reward-aligned reasoning enables robust spatial understanding with limited data.

items.title: Researchers fine-tune Romanian vision-language models using parameter-efficient LoRA on translated Flickr30K dataset, improving visual QA and image captioning performance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Parameter Efficient Multimodal Instruction Tuning for Romanian Vision Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have enhanced Romanian vision-language models by translating the Flickr30K dataset into Romanian and extending it for visual question answering using open-source large language models. They fine-tuned models from the LLaMA 3.2, LLaVA 1.6, and Qwen2 families with the parameter-efficient LoRA method, resulting in improved performance on Romanian visual question answering and image captioning tasks. The seven-billion-parameter Qwen2-VL-RoVQA model achieved notable gains in BERTScore F1, with improvements of 2.29% on visual question answering and 4.45% on captioning compared to its original version.

The fine-tuned models also demonstrated a significant reduction in grammatical errors, indicating enhanced language understanding and fluency in Romanian. This work addresses the resource gap in multimodal natural language processing for low-resource languages and contributes to democratizing generative AI by improving Romanian language capabilities in vision-language tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2512.14926v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Focusing on low-resource languages is an essential step toward democratizing generative AI. In this work, we contribute to reducing the multimodal NLP resource gap for Romanian. We translate the widely known Flickr30K dataset into Romanian and further extend it for visual question answering by leveraging open-source LLMs. We demonstrate the usefulness of our datasets by fine-tuning open-source VLMs on Romanian visual question answering. We select VLMs from three widely used model families: LLaMA 3.2, LLaVA 1.6, and Qwen2. For fine-tuning, we employ the parameter-efficient LoRA method. Our models show improved Romanian capabilities in visual QA, as well as on tasks they were not trained on, such as Romanian image description generation. Finally, the models show substantial reductions in grammatical errors compared to their original forms, indicating improvements not only in language understanding but also in Romanian fluency.

items.originalTitle: R$^2$PO: Decoupling Rollout and Inference Policies for LLM Reasoning
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced R²PO (Residual Rollout Policy Optimization), a new method that separates the policies used for training rollouts and inference in large language model (LLM) reasoning. This approach addresses the conflict between optimizing for informative training gradients and producing accurate, consistent inference responses by adding a lightweight Residual Rollout-Head to decouple these processes. Experiments demonstrate that R²PO improves accuracy by up to 3.4% on the MATH-500 benchmark and 1.3% on the APPS benchmark compared to existing methods.

The study highlights that traditional reinforcement learning methods assume the same policy should govern both training and inference, which can entangle gradients and limit exploration. By diversifying rollouts during training while maintaining inference generation, R²PO achieves more diverse training trajectories and reduces length bias. The researchers have made their code publicly available to support further development in this area.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2601.11960v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Existing reinforcement learning methods for LLM reasoning implicitly assume that the policy generating training trajectories should coincide with the one producing inference responses. We argue that this is a misleading inductive bias: the optimization-optimal trajectory distribution favors informative gradients, whereas the inference-optimal response distribution emphasizes accuracy and consistency. Forcing both into a single policy entangles their gradients and suppresses exploration. We propose R$^2$PO (Residual Rollout Policy Optimization), which attaches a lightweight Residual Rollout-Head atop the policy to decouple training trajectories from inference responses, diversifying rollouts during training while keeping inference generation intact. Experiments show that R$^2$PO consistently outperforms baselines, with average accuracy gains of 3.4% on MATH-500 and 1.3% on APPS, alongside more diverse rollouts and reduced length bias. Our code is available at https://github.com/RRPO-ARR/Code.

items.title: Researchers identify Endogenous Steering Resistance in Llama-3.3-70B language model, showing 3.8% explicit recovery from activation steering misalignment with implications for AI safety [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Endogenous Resistance to Activation Steering in Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have identified a phenomenon called Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR) in the Llama-3.3-70B language model, where the model can recover mid-generation from task-misaligned activation steering by explicitly restarting and continuing on-topic despite ongoing steering perturbations. This explicit ESR occurs at a rate of 3.8% in Llama-3.3-70B, with smaller models showing it less frequently. The study used sparse autoencoder latents to steer activations and found that zero-ablating certain latents reduced repeated attempts by 25%, indicating specific components involved in ESR.

The research further demonstrated that ESR can be enhanced through meta-prompting and fine-tuning on synthetic self-correction examples. ESR has important implications for AI safety, as it may protect models against adversarial activation-space manipulation but could also hinder beneficial steering interventions, since the model cannot distinguish between harmful and helpful steering. The authors have made their code publicly available for further exploration.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2602.06941v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models can recover mid-generation from task-misaligned activation steering, producing explicit verbal restarts (e.g., ``wait, that's not right'') and continuing on-topic even while the steering perturbation remains active. We term this Endogenous Steering Resistance (ESR). Using sparse autoencoder (SAE) latents to steer model activations, we find that Llama-3.3-70B exhibits explicit ESR at 3.8%, with smaller models from the Llama-3 and Gemma-2 families showing the explicit form less frequently. Two controls dissociate ESR into a detection event and a sustained-resistance component that conditioning on recent on-topic tokens does not fully explain. We identify 26 SAE latents through contrastive on-topic/off-topic search; zero-ablating them reduces the multi-attempt rate by 25%, with random-latent and held-out-prompt controls supporting specificity. ESR can also be deliberately enhanced through both meta-prompting and fine-tuning on synthetic self-correction examples. ESR has dual implications for safety: it could harden models against adversarial activation-space manipulation, but may equally interfere with beneficial steering-based interventions, since the model has no way to distinguish the two. Code is available at https://github.com/agencyenterprise/endogenous-steering-resistance.

items.title: Researchers propose gradient regularization to reduce reward hacking in reinforcement learning from human feedback and verifiable rewards, showing improved accuracy and performance over KL penalty methods [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Gradient Regularization Mitigates Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback and Verifiable Rewards
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced a gradient regularization (GR) technique to address reward hacking in reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) and verifiable rewards (RLVR) used in training modern language models. Unlike traditional methods that use a Kullback-Leibler (KL) penalty to limit policy updates, this approach biases training towards regions where the reward model is more accurate by encouraging flatter optima. The team established a theoretical link between reward accuracy and the flatness of the optimum and confirmed this correlation empirically.

The study demonstrates that GR outperforms KL penalty methods across various reinforcement learning experiments with language models. GR not only achieves higher win rates as judged by GPT but also reduces issues like overfitting to reward formats and prevents manipulation of evaluation metrics in tasks where language models act as judges. This method offers a promising alternative for improving the reliability and effectiveness of reward-based training in language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2602.18037v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) or Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) are two key steps in the post-training of modern Language Models (LMs). A common problem is reward hacking, where the policy may exploit inaccuracies of the reward and learn an unintended behavior. Most previous works address this by limiting the policy update with a Kullback-Leibler (KL) penalty towards a reference model. We propose a different framing: Train the LM in a way that biases policy updates towards regions in which the reward is more accurate. First, we derive a theoretical connection between the accuracy of a reward model and the flatness of an optimum at convergence. Gradient regularization (GR) can then be used to bias training to flatter regions and thereby maintain reward model accuracy. We confirm these results by showing that the gradient norm and reward accuracy are empirically correlated in RLHF. We then empirically show that Reference Resets of the KL penalty find flatter regions with a higher reward accuracy. We further improve on this by proposing to use explicit GR with an efficient finite-difference estimate. Empirically, GR performs better than a KL penalty across a diverse set of RL experiments with LMs. GR achieves a higher GPT-judged win-rate in RLHF, avoids overly focusing on the format in rule-based math rewards, and prevents hacking the judge in LLM-as-a-Judge math tasks.

items.title: Researchers present a data-driven pipeline that optimizes GPU efficiency for distributed LLM-adapter serving, reducing GPU requirements by 60% while avoiding request starvation and memory errors [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Data Driven Optimization of GPU efficiency for Distributed LLM-Adapter Serving
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a data-driven pipeline that optimizes GPU efficiency for distributed serving of Large Language Model (LLM) adapters, reducing the number of GPUs required by 60% while preventing request starvation and memory errors. The pipeline calculates the optimal adapter placement for a given workload by accurately predicting maximum feasible throughput on each GPU, enabling near-peak utilization with minimal resources.

The approach combines a Digital Twin that simulates system dynamics with high accuracy, a distilled machine learning model trained on data generated by the Digital Twin, and a greedy placement algorithm that uses these performance estimates to maximize GPU usage. This method achieves throughput estimation errors below 5% and runs significantly faster than traditional benchmarking, supporting both predictable and unpredictable workloads.

Beyond improving GPU efficiency, the pipeline is adaptable to other objectives such as minimizing latency, making it a versatile solution for future large-scale LLM serving infrastructures.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2602.24044v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) adapters enable low-cost model specialization, but introduce complex caching and scheduling challenges in distributed serving systems where hundreds of adapters must be hosted concurrently. While prior work has largely focused on latency and throughput optimization, minimizing GPU resource requirements through near-peak utilization remains largely underexplored. This paper presents a data-driven pipeline that, for a given workload, computes an adapter placement that serves the workload with the minimum number of GPUs while avoiding request starvation and GPU memory errors. To that end, the approach identifies the maximum feasible throughput attainable on each GPU by leveraging accurate performance predictions learned from real serving behavior. The proposed pipeline integrates three components: (i) a Digital Twin (DT) tailored to LLM-adapter serving, (ii) a distilled machine learning (ML) model trained on DT-generated data, and (iii) a greedy placement algorithm that exploits ML-based performance estimates to maximize GPU efficiency. The DT emulates real system dynamics with high fidelity, achieving below 5% throughput estimation error while executing up to 90x faster than full LLM benchmarking across both predictable and unpredictable workloads. The learned ML models further accelerate performance estimation with marginal accuracy degradation, enabling scalable optimization. Experimental results demonstrate that the pipeline substantially improves GPU efficiency, reducing the number of GPUs required to sustain target workloads by 60\% on average across the evaluated scenarios. Beyond GPU efficiency, the pipeline can be adapted to alternative objectives, such as latency minimization, highlighting its versatility for future large-scale LLM serving infrastructures.

items.title: Researchers introduce SpreadsheetArena to evaluate LLM-generated spreadsheets via blind preference votes, revealing variability in style and alignment with domain best practices [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SpreadsheetArena: Decomposing Preference in LLM Generation of Spreadsheet Workbooks
items.summary:
Researchers have developed SpreadsheetArena, a platform designed to evaluate language models' ability to generate spreadsheets based on natural language prompts. The platform uses blind pairwise preference voting to assess the quality of spreadsheet workbooks produced by large language models (LLMs), highlighting the variability in stylistic, structural, and functional features across different prompts. This approach addresses the unique challenges of spreadsheet generation, which involves well-defined, multi-dimensional outputs with complex interactivity and layout considerations.

Expert evaluations, particularly in finance-related prompts, indicate that even top-performing models often fail to produce spreadsheets that align with domain-specific best practices. SpreadsheetArena is hosted live and includes a publicly released dataset of prompts, generated spreadsheets, and preference votes, aiming to support further research into spreadsheet generation as a complex and open-ended task for LLMs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2603.10002v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider the task of end-to-end spreadsheet generation, where language models produce spreadsheet artifacts to satisfy users' explicit and implicit constraints, specified in natural language. We introduce SpreadsheetArena, a platform for evaluating models' performance on the task via blind pairwise preference votes of LLM-generated spreadsheet workbooks. As with other complex, open-ended tasks, relevant evaluation criteria can vary greatly across use cases, often in ways that are difficult to formalize. Compared to general dialogue or text generation settings, spreadsheet generation presents unique challenges and opportunities: the task output structure is well-defined and multi-dimensional, and there are often complex interactivity and layout considerations. We observe that stylistic, structural, and functional features of preferred spreadsheets vary meaningfully across prompts. Expert evaluations of spreadsheets for finance prompts suggest that even highly ranked models do not reliably produce spreadsheets aligned with domain-specific best practices. We host a live arena and release a dataset of prompts, generated spreadsheets, and preference votes, which we hope will facilitate further study of tasks operating over spreadsheets as a challenging and interesting class of complex, open-ended tasks for LLMs.

items.title: Researchers find large language models generate harmful responses via a distinct, shared mechanism across harm types, with alignment compressing harmful weights but causing brittle safety [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Large Language Models Generate Harmful Responses Using a Distinct Mechanism, Shared Across Harm Types
items.summary:
Researchers have discovered that large language models (LLMs) generate harmful responses through a distinct and shared internal mechanism across different types of harm. Their study shows that harmful content production relies on a compact set of model weights that are separate from those responsible for benign functions. Alignment training compresses these harmful weights, reshaping the model's internal representations of harmfulness, but this also leads to brittle safety measures that can be bypassed or cause broad misalignment when fine-tuned on specific domains.

Using targeted weight pruning, the researchers demonstrated that pruning harmful weights in a narrow domain significantly reduces emergent misalignment, suggesting a coherent internal structure for harmfulness in LLMs. Notably, the ability of LLMs to generate harmful content is distinct from their capacity to recognize and explain such content. These findings provide a foundation for developing more principled and robust approaches to improving the safety of large language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2604.09544v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) undergo alignment training to avoid harmful behaviors, yet the resulting safeguards remain brittle: jailbreaks routinely bypass them, and fine-tuning on narrow domains can induce ``emergent misalignment'' that generalizes broadly. Whether this brittleness reflects a fundamental lack of coherent internal organization for harmfulness remains unclear. Here we use targeted weight pruning as a causal intervention to probe the internal organization of harmfulness in LLMs. We find that harmful content generation depends on a compact set of weights that are general across harm types and distinct from benign capabilities. Aligned models exhibit a greater compression of harm generation weights than unaligned counterparts, indicating that alignment reshapes harmful representations internally--despite the brittleness of safety guardrails at the surface level. This compression explains emergent misalignment: if weights of harmful capabilities are compressed, fine-tuning that engages these weights in one domain can trigger broad misalignment. Consistent with this, pruning harm generation weights in a narrow domain substantially reduces emergent misalignment. Notably, LLMs harmful generation capability is dissociated from how they recognize and explain such content. Together, these results reveal a coherent internal structure for harmfulness in LLMs that may serve as a foundation for more principled approaches to safety.

Their study shows that harmful content production relies on a compact set of model weights that are separate from those responsible for benign functions. Alignment training compresses these harmful weights, reshaping the model's internal representations of harmfulness, but this also leads to brittle safety measures that can be bypassed or cause broad misalignment when fine-tuned on specific domains.

Using targeted weight pruning, the researchers demonstrated that pruning harmful weights in a narrow domain significantly reduces emergent misalignment, suggesting a coherent internal structure for harmfulness in LLMs. Notably, the ability of LLMs to generate harmful content is distinct from their capacity to recognize and explain such content. These findings provide a foundation for developing more principled and robust approaches to improving the safety of large language models.

items.title: Researchers propose Kwai Summary Attention to reduce long-sequence modeling costs by compressing historical contexts into learnable summary tokens, addressing quadratic complexity in softmax attention [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Kwai Summary Attention Technical Report
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Kwai Summary Attention (KSA), a new attention mechanism designed to reduce the computational costs of modeling long sequences in large language models. KSA addresses the quadratic time complexity of standard softmax attention by compressing historical context into learnable summary tokens, enabling more efficient handling of long-range dependencies without sacrificing interpretability or completeness.

Traditional approaches to managing long sequences either reduce the key-value cache size or use architectures optimized for cache efficiency, but these methods often involve trade-offs between memory usage and modeling effectiveness. KSA offers an intermediate solution by maintaining a linear relationship between cache size and sequence length while applying semantic-level compression, balancing memory costs with the retention of important long-distance information.

This development is significant for advancing next-generation language models, particularly in areas requiring extensive context understanding such as semantic reasoning, code intelligence, and recommendation systems. By improving efficiency in long-context scenarios, KSA has the potential to enhance both training and inference performance for extremely long sequences.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2604.24432v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Long-context ability, has become one of the most important iteration direction of next-generation Large Language Models, particularly in semantic understanding/reasoning, code agentic intelligence and recommendation system. However, the standard softmax attention exhibits quadratic time complexity with respect to sequence length. As the sequence length increases, this incurs substantial overhead in long-context settings, leading the training and inference costs of extremely long sequences deteriorate rapidly. Existing solutions mitigate this issue through two technique routings: i) Reducing the KV cache per layer, such as from the head-level compression GQA, and the embedding dimension-level compression MLA, but the KV cache remains linearly dependent on the sequence length at a 1:1 ratio. ii) Interleaving with KV Cache friendly architecture, such as local attention SWA, linear kernel GDN, but often involve trade-offs among KV Cache and long-context modeling effectiveness. Besides the two technique routings, we argue that there exists an intermediate path not well explored: {Maintaining a linear relationship between the KV cache and sequence length, but performing semantic-level compression through a specific ratio $k$}. This $O(n/k)$ path does not pursue a ``minimum KV cache'', but rather trades acceptable memory costs for complete, referential, and interpretable retention of long distant dependency. Motivated by this, we propose Kwai Summary Attention (KSA), a novel attention mechanism that reduces sequence modeling cost by compressing historical contexts into learnable summary tokens.

items.title: Researchers propose MemTrace framework to trace and attribute errors in large language model memory systems, introducing MemTraceBench and an automatic attribution method that improves task performance by up to 7.62% [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: MemTrace: Tracing and Attributing Errors in Large Language Model Memory Systems
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced MemTrace, a novel framework designed to trace and attribute errors in memory systems of large language models (LLMs). By converting memory pipelines into executable memory evolution graphs, MemTrace enables detailed tracking of information flow and identifies the root causes of failures. The team also developed MemTraceBench, a benchmark derived from various memory systems, to systematically analyze memory failure modes and introduced an automatic attribution method that improves task performance by up to 7.62% through guided prompt optimization.

The study reveals that memory failures in LLMs are often systematic, resulting from issues such as information loss and retrieval misalignment at the operation level. By leveraging fine-grained attribution signals, the framework establishes a closed-loop system that automatically corrects faults, enhancing the reliability and effectiveness of LLM memory systems. The researchers plan to release the code publicly to support further development and debugging in this area.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2605.28732v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Memory is essential for enabling large language models to support long-horizon reasoning, yet existing memory systems remain unreliable and difficult to debug. Tracing memory's dynamic evolution is crucial to understand how information is synthesized, propagated, or corrupted over time. In this work, we study the new problem of error tracing and attribution in LLM memory systems. We propose a novel framework that transforms memory pipelines into executable memory evolution graphs, enabling fine-grained tracing of operational information flow. We then construct MemTraceBench, a benchmark collected from representative memory systems such as Long-Context, RAG, Mem0, and EverMemOS, to systematically study memory failure modes. We further introduce an automatic attribution method that iteratively traces operation subgraphs to pinpoint the root cause of any failed case. Our analysis reveals that memory failures are systematic, stemming from operation-level issues like information loss and retrieval misalignment. Crucially, we leverage these fine-grained attribution signals to guide downstream prompt optimization, establishing a closed-loop system that automatically corrects faults and boosts end-task performance by up to 7.62%. Code will be released at https://github.com/zjunlp/MemTrace.

items.title: Researchers present ResearchClawBench, a benchmark evaluating autonomous scientific research across 40 tasks in 10 domains, revealing current AI agents' limited re-discovery capabilities [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ResearchClawBench: A Benchmark for End-to-End Autonomous Scientific Research
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced ResearchClawBench, a new benchmark designed to evaluate the autonomous scientific research capabilities of AI agents across 40 tasks spanning 10 scientific domains. Each task is based on a real published paper and includes related literature and raw data, with the target paper hidden during evaluation to test the AI's ability to independently rediscover scientific findings. The benchmark uses expert-curated rubrics to assess performance, allowing for both re-discovery and novel insights.

The study assessed seven autonomous research agents and seventeen large language models (LLMs) using a unified protocol. Results showed that current AI systems struggle with reliable re-discovery, with the top autonomous agent scoring an average of 21.5 and the best LLM scoring 20.7 out of a possible frontier mean of 26.5. Analysis revealed common failures in matching experimental protocols, evidence, and core scientific concepts.

ResearchClawBench establishes a reproducible framework for measuring progress toward fully autonomous scientific research, highlighting the significant challenges that remain before AI can independently conduct reliable scientific investigations.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.07591v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: AI coding agents are increasingly used for scientific work, but their end-to-end autonomous research capability remains difficult to verify. We present ResearchClawBench, a benchmark for evaluating autonomous scientific research across 40 tasks from 10 scientific domains. Each task is grounded in a real published paper, provides related literature and raw data, and hides the target paper during evaluation. Expert-curated multimodal rubrics decompose the target scientific artifacts into weighted criteria, enabling evaluation of target-paper-level re-discovery while leaving room for new discovery. We evaluate seven autonomous research (auto-research) agents under a unified protocol and seventeen native LLMs through the lightweight ResearchHarness. Current systems remain far from reliable re-discovery: the strongest autonomous agent, Claude Code, averages 21.5, and the strongest ResearchHarness LLM, Claude-Opus-4.7, averages 20.7, with an LLM frontier mean of only 26.5. Error analysis shows that failures concentrate in experimental protocol mismatch, evidence mismatch, and missing scientific core. ResearchClawBench provides a reproducible evaluation frontier for measuring progress toward autonomous scientific research.

items.title: Researchers formulate hallucination onset detection as quickest change detection, achieving detection delays of 11-13 tokens with learned CUSUM statistics versus 31 tokens for baseline methods [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Quickest Detection of Hallucination Onset: Delay Bounds and Learned CUSUM Statistics
items.summary:
Researchers have reframed the detection of hallucination onset in language models as a quickest change detection problem, achieving significantly faster detection times compared to traditional methods. By modeling the latent faithful or hallucinated state as a first-order Markov process and applying classical change-point theory, they established a theoretical lower bound on detection delay. Their approach uses a causal recurrent labeler functioning as a CUSUM detector with learned increments, reducing detection delays to 11-13 tokens versus 31 tokens for a linear baseline, although low false-alarm rates still limit recall and increase delay.

The study reveals that the improved speed primarily stems from better per-token scoring rather than temporal accumulation. An information-rate optimality analysis shows that the learned scoring captures only a fraction of the available divergence in features, indicating room for improvement. This work highlights the limitations of standard classification metrics in capturing detection delay and demonstrates how sequential analysis can provide a more precise measure of hallucination onset detection performance.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.12476v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Token-level hallucination detectors are evaluated as classifiers, by AUC over all tokens, yet a streaming monitor is judged by its reaction time: the number of tokens that pass between the onset of a hallucination and the alarm. We formulate hallucination onset detection as a quickest change detection problem. A first-order Markov model of the latent faithful/hallucinated state, validated on RAGTruth, places the task inside classical change-point theory and yields Lorden's lower bound on detection delay: about 1.3 tokens at a false-alarm rate of 0.01. We then show that a causal recurrent labeler acts as a CUSUM with a learned increment. Among the onsets it catches it detects in 11-13 tokens, against 31 for a linear per-token baseline, though at this false-alarm budget every detector catches under a third of onsets and the recall-honest delay is 56-66 tokens: low-false-alarm onset detection is hard. A controlled decomposition attributes the speed advantage mostly to a better per-token score rather than to temporal accumulation. An information-rate optimality theorem of Donsker-Varadhan type explains the remaining order-of-magnitude gap: the learned score realizes only 1/4.5 of the divergence the features carry, a deficit that recalibration cannot remove, with the remainder a finite-horizon effect. Classification metrics conceal this delay structure; sequential analysis makes it measurable.

items.title: Researchers find language models with lossy memory produce confident errors while empty memory leads to abstention, proposing a source-first policy to restore correctability across models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Reclaim Evaluation: A Lossy Memory Is Worse Than an Empty One
items.summary:
Researchers have found that language models with lossy memory—where incorrect conclusions are retained but the underlying reasoning is lost—tend to produce confident errors, whereas models with empty memory often abstain from answering. This phenomenon, termed brittle memory, arises because answers cannot be recomputed without their original inputs. The study shows that whether a model confidently errs or abstains depends on its disposition rather than its capability. The researchers introduced a reclaim evaluation method to measure correctability, revealing that preserving the source information rather than just the final answer is crucial for enabling corrections across different models.

The team proposed a simple source-first policy that retains the recomputable source data while discarding the derived conclusion, which significantly improves correctability without increasing memory budget. They tested this approach across various models and real dialogue datasets, identifying conditions where the fix may fail, such as large source size or noise. Their findings highlight the importance of memory design in language models and provide tools and benchmarks to assess and improve model reliability in handling memory and corrections.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.25449v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A language model's memory can be worse than no memory at all. Give a model a memory that kept a wrong conclusion but dropped the work behind it, and it re-emits the stale value as a confident answer; give the same model an empty memory, and it abstains. We call this failure brittle memory. The information loss behind it is definitional (an answer cannot be recomputed once its inputs are gone), so the loss is only the setup; the finding is behavioral. Whether a model turns the lost source into a confident error or an abstention is set by disposition, not capability: four of eight models we test emit, and the four that abstain escape only by an interface affordance -- forced through a mandatory structured-output field, as production tool calls are, they commit the inherited wrong value. We measure correctability with reclaim evaluation: induce a known drift, compress the interaction at a fixed budget, deliver a correction that names the error, and score exact recovery of the known answer, judge-free. Correctability is bottlenecked not by capability but by whether the memory kept a re-derivation basis (the source) rather than the answer, so an 8B model and a frontier one wall in the same place. A one-line source-first policy -- keep the recomputable source, drop the re-derivable conclusion -- restores correctability at equal budget wherever the source is compact and identifiable, with a length-matched control that rules out 'more text' and a deployable one-prompt form weaker than the oracle. We map where the fix fails (source size, noise, a silent truncation mode a completeness tag makes loud), show the failure compounds through memory loops, and replicate on three deployed memory systems and on real dialogue (MultiWOZ, where the checkable value is present by construction). We release the harness, the paired memory conditions, and validators built to come out false.

outputCleanup.description:
Researchers have found that language models with lossy memory—where incorrect conclusions are retained but the underlying reasoning is lost—tend to produce confident errors, whereas models with empty memory often abstain from answering. This phenomenon, termed brittle memory, arises because answers cannot be recomputed without their original inputs. The study shows that whether a model confidently errs or abstains depends on its disposition rather than its capability. The researchers introduced a reclaim evaluation method to measure correctability, revealing that preserving the source information rather than just the final answer is crucial for enabling corrections across different models.

The team proposed a simple source-first policy that retains the recomputable source data while discarding the derived conclusion, which significantly improves correctability without increasing memory budget. They tested this approach across various models and real dialogue datasets, identifying conditions where the fix may fail, such as large source size or noise. Their findings highlight the importance of memory design in language models and provide tools and benchmarks to assess and improve model reliability in handling memory and corrections.

items.title: Kapa.ai uses a small LLM to prune 68% of RAG context while retaining 96% recall, reducing query costs by a third in AI assistants for large knowledge bases [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Pruning RAG context down to what the answer actually needs
items.summary:
Kapa.ai has developed a method to reduce the retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) context by 68% while maintaining 96% recall, significantly cutting query costs for AI assistants handling large knowledge bases. Their approach introduces a small, cost-effective language model that evaluates and prunes irrelevant chunks of information before passing data to the main, more expensive model, optimizing both performance and expense.

This pruning step addresses the inefficiency of traditional retrieval systems that pass many unnecessary chunks to the generator, which increases costs without improving answers. By assessing the relevance of all retrieved chunks collectively rather than individually, Kapa.ai's solution ensures that only essential information is retained, improving cost efficiency without sacrificing answer quality.

The innovation allows AI assistants to manage large and complex product knowledge bases more effectively, enabling tighter context management and reducing the computational load. This advancement could influence future designs of retrieval and generation pipelines in AI systems, balancing recall and cost more effectively.

items.title: Researchers propose ASK+, a trajectory-aware uncertainty-gated LLM assistance method that improves reinforcement learning success under partial observability across multiple environments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ASK in the Dark: Uncertainty-Gated LLM Assistance under Partial Observability
items.summary:
Researchers have developed ASK+, a method that enhances reinforcement learning agents operating under partial observability by integrating trajectory-aware context and structured reasoning into small language model (SLM) assistance. This approach addresses the limitations of previous uncertainty-gated methods, which rarely allowed SLMs to contribute independently due to insufficient contextual information. ASK+ provides the SLM with a partially revealed map, visited positions, and action history, enabling it to act as an informative consultant that occasionally corrects the agent's policy, leading to improved performance across multiple environments.

The study demonstrates that the predictive entropy signal used for selective querying effectively measures action uncertainty rather than state uncertainty, maintaining its usefulness in partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs). ASK+ achieved notable success rates, including 93% on DoorKey, 70% on FourRooms, and 73.7% accuracy on HigherLower, matching or exceeding benchmarks set by larger models. These results highlight that prompt design and selective gating have a greater impact than model scale, enabling effective guidance without relying on large language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02686v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning agents operating under partial observability must act on incomplete information, making them natural candidates for guidance from small language models (SLMs) that carry broad reasoning priors. Yet integrating SLM guidance into this setting has proven difficult: across all test environments, vanilla uncertainty-gated approaches achieve an overwrite rate at or near zero, meaning the SLM almost never contributes an independent action. We trace this failure to the bare egocentric prompt, which provides insufficient context for genuine reasoning, and identify it as a context problem rather than a capacity problem. We propose ASK+, which supplies the SLM with trajectory-aware context (a partially revealed map, visited positions, and action history) and structured chain-of-thought reasoning, converting it from a passive redundancy check into a more informative consultant that occasionally corrects the policy. We further establish that the predictive entropy signal used for selective querying measures action uncertainty rather than state uncertainty and remains informative in POMDPs, making uncertainty-gated assistance viable beyond fully observable settings. The stateful prompt drives substantial gains: on DoorKey, where vanilla ASK matches PPO (both 89%), ASK+ reaches 93% success; on FourRooms, success climbs from 53% to 70%; on HigherLower, accuracy reaches 73.7%, matching the SLM-only upper bound. Across all environments, Qwen3.5-2B matches or exceeds Qwen3.5-4B, confirming that prompt design and selective gating dominate the impact of model scale, enabling guidance without large models.

items.title: Researchers introduce Incognita framework to evaluate generative agents in socially distributed task environments with 540 trials showing limited success and behavior insights [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Evaluating Generative Agents with Actions Grounded in Socially Distributed Task Environments using Incognita
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Incognita, a new framework designed to evaluate generative agents in socially distributed task environments where knowledge and actions are partitioned among role-specific participants. This framework separates social interaction from grounded execution, allowing agents to communicate with specialists who mediate permissible operations, which are then executed in a controlled environment. The study tested three generative agent models across 18 tasks with 540 trials, revealing limited success rates but notable behavioral insights such as increased knowledge elicitation and interaction with multiple entities.

Incognita-Retail adapts an existing retail benchmark into a multi-entity setting while maintaining consistent reward structures. The evaluation showed progress in agent performance, with success rates improving from 0% to up to 17.2% and reductions in premature task completion. Despite these advances, the agents' reliability remains low, highlighting challenges in achieving effective agency in complex social environments.

These findings suggest that socially distributed task environments provide valuable opportunities to observe agent behaviors like knowledge gathering, source selection, and action attempts before consistent success is achieved. The research underscores the importance of such environments for advancing the development and assessment of generative agents in realistic social contexts.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02975v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Effective agency in social environments depends on when an agent seeks knowledge, when it acts, and whether its actions are justified by acquired information. Existing grounded benchmarks provide executable actions, persistent state, and verifiable outcomes, while social simulation environments provide rich interaction among language agents. We study an evaluation setting that combines these requirements. We define socially distributed task environments as interactive environments where task-relevant knowledge is partitioned across role-isolated participants and consequential actions are accessible only through them. Communication serves as exploration over role-partitioned knowledge, while grounded action serves as exploitation over environment state. We introduce Incognita, a Concordia-based framework that separates social interaction from grounded execution. The evaluated agent routes messages to a user or specialist entities; specialists mediate admissible operations; a deterministic sub-environment executes accepted operations over a canonical state; and an offline evaluator scores outcomes with inherited rewards. Incognita-Retail transforms tau-bench retail into a multi-entity environment while preserving final-state reward semantics. We evaluate three generative agent models on 18 tasks stratified by social breadth, with 540 trials. Progress appears in reward and behavior: success rises from 0 percent to 8.9 percent and 17.2 percent, while premature finalization falls from 100 percent to 87 percent and 58 percent. Stronger models elicit more hidden knowledge, contact more entities, and attempt more grounded writes, yet reliability remains low. These findings show that socially distributed task environments expose behavior before reliable success, including knowledge elicitation, source selection, grounded action attempts, and premature completion belief.

items.title: Researchers propose cross-survey transfer to evaluate large language models simulating survey respondents, achieving 52% accuracy on unseen items in Taiwan Election and Democratization Study 2024 data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Silicon Sampling via Cross-Survey Transfer
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced a new evaluation method called cross-survey transfer to assess large language models (LLMs) simulating human survey respondents. Using data from the Taiwan Election and Democratization Study 2024, they tested three open-weight LLMs and found that zero-shot models achieved 52% accuracy in predicting answers to unseen survey items, approaching the performance of supervised machine learning models. This approach offers a more rigorous test of LLMs' ability to predict individual responses rather than just matching overall data patterns.

The study revealed a hierarchy in predictability across different survey constructs, with partisan attitudes being the most predictable and sovereignty issues the least. It also found that common LLM limitations, such as variance collapse and safety alignment effects, are more complex than previously thought, affecting both supervised and unsupervised models differently. These findings highlight both the potential and limitations of using LLMs for silicon sampling in survey research.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03091v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Silicon sampling-using large language models (LLMs) to simulate human survey respondents-has emerged as a promising approach for augmenting traditional survey research. However, most evaluations rely on distributional comparisons rather than individual-level prediction, which risks conflating pattern matching with coherent respondent-level prediction. We propose cross-survey transfer, a more rigorous evaluation framework in which an LLM is given a respondent's answers to one set of questions and must predict their answers to entirely different questions from the same survey. Using data from the Taiwan Election and Democratization Study (TEDS) 2024, three open-weight LLMs (27B-120B parameters), and supervised machine learning baselines, we find that: (1) zero-shot LLMs achieve 52% accuracy on genuinely unseen items, closing to within 6 percentage points (pp) of a supervised random forest trained on same-population data; (2) a stable construct predictability hierarchy emerges, from 67% for partisan attitudes to 23% for sovereignty; and (3) variance collapse and safety alignment effects-two commonly cited LLM limitations-turn out to be more nuanced than previously reported, with variance collapse affecting supervised models as well and alignment effects varying dramatically across model families. These findings clarify both the promise and boundaries of silicon sampling.

items.title: Researchers study agentic AI policy repair using region-level feedback in hotel-pricing simulation, finding that aggregate alignment metrics can mislead evaluation without per-state expert actions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When Aggregate Alignment Misleads: Auditing Policy Repair Without Per-State Expert Actions
items.summary:
Researchers investigated the challenge of evaluating agentic AI systems that edit decision policies without access to per-state expert action labels. Using a hotel-pricing simulator, they tested a policy editor that received only region-level feedback on price distribution differences from a benchmark policy, without observing benchmark actions or outcomes. The editor, based on a large language model, achieved revenue per available room (RevPAR) close to the benchmark, demonstrating effective policy repair despite limited feedback.

The study found that simple aggregate alignment metrics can be misleading, as the editor's improvements were not solely due to revenue gains but also to better alignment with episode composition. Comparisons with other editing methods showed that semantic understanding and region-error correspondence were crucial for successful policy repair. The results suggest that evaluating agentic policy repair should focus on whether diagnostic feedback reliably translates into improved outcomes, rather than relying on single behavioral distance measures.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03386v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agentic AI systems are increasingly used to edit, refine, and repair decision policies, but evaluating these edits is difficult when per-state expert action labels are unavailable. We study this problem in a hotel-pricing simulator where an agentic policy editor receives only region-level diagnostic feedback: summaries of how its price distribution differs from a benchmark policy across time, inventory, and market regions. The editor cannot observe benchmark actions, benchmark source code, reward numbers, or held-out outcomes, and may only propose constrained edits to a target-action table. On 5,000 held-out episodes, a multi-restart LLM editor reaches RevPAR 108.47 (95% CI 107.61 - 109.34), close to the benchmark policy's 108.75 (107.81 - 109.68), with paired gap (LLM minus benchmark) -0.276 and 95% CI [-0.692, 0.146]. A cheap diagnostic projection already recovers much of the revenue (107.90), so the LLM editor's distinctive gain is not raw revenue lift alone: it also reduces episode composition distance from 1.153 to 0.609. This is the strongest non-benchmark repair result. This profile is not explained by restart search alone: non-semantic proposers with up to 2,500 evaluations fall 8.77 - 14.57 RevPAR points short. Nor is it explained by plausible prompt format: a shuffled-diagnostic control breaks region-error correspondence and falls to RevPAR 94.30. The match is genuine but partial. A tree editor achieves stronger pooled alignment, 0.214 versus 0.266, and stronger reference-state D1, 0.328 versus 1.197, yet revenue falls to 98.91. These results show that agentic policy repair should be evaluated by whether diagnostic feedback becomes reliable closed-loop outcome, not by a single behavioral distance.

Researchers investigated the challenge of evaluating agentic AI systems that edit decision policies without access to per-state expert action labels. Using a hotel-pricing simulator, they tested a policy editor that received only region-level feedback on price distribution differences from a benchmark policy, without observing benchmark actions or outcomes. The editor, based on a large language model, achieved revenue per available room (RevPAR) close to the benchmark, demonstrating effective policy repair despite limited feedback.

The study found that simple aggregate alignment metrics can be misleading, as the editor's improvements were not solely due to revenue gains but also to better alignment with episode composition. Comparisons with other editing methods showed that semantic understanding and region-error correspondence were crucial for successful policy repair. The results suggest that evaluating agentic policy repair should focus on whether diagnostic feedback reliably translates into improved outcomes, rather than relying on single behavioral distance measures.

items.title: Researchers develop end-to-end analytics framework using mobile data for large-scale urban mobility analysis and decision support with Google BigQuery, Vertex AI, and Power BI [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: From Mobile Data to Business Insights: An End-to-End Analytics Framework for Large-Scale Urban Mobility Analysis and Decision Support
items.summary:
Researchers have developed an end-to-end analytics framework that leverages real-time mobile location data to analyze urban mobility and support decision-making in areas such as tourism, transportation, and retail. The framework integrates advanced technologies including Google BigQuery, Vertex AI, and Power BI to process data, build machine learning models, and visualize insights. It addresses challenges like tourism planning, parking management, bus route optimization, and commercial strategy through a modular architecture that supports multiple stakeholder use cases.

The platform employs data anonymization and ETL pipelines to ensure privacy and efficiency, while its analytical models perform tasks such as mobility profiling, trajectory mining, area of influence analysis, traffic anomaly detection, and origin-destination pattern analysis. The results demonstrate the system's capability to capture detailed user mobility patterns at fine spatial and temporal scales, providing actionable insights for urban planners and business strategists.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03394v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Real time location data derived from mobile applications is a powerful tool for addressing various urban challenges, including tourism planning, parking management, bus route optimization, and resource allocation. We employ state of the art techniques and technologies, including data anonymization, ETL pipelines, and utilizing Google BigQuery and Vertex AI for data processing and machine learning model development. Additionally, we apply interactive data visualization techniques via Power BI to facilitate the effective interpretation of analytical findings by stakeholders. The developed models address a wide range of mobility analytics tasks, including mobility profiling, frequent trajectory mining, area of influence analysis, traffic anomaly detection, and origin destination pattern analysis. The results demonstrate the framework's ability to capture user mobility dynamics at fine spatial and temporal resolutions, providing actionable insights for urban planning and strategic business decision making.

items.title: arXiv:2607.03561 presents doubly-efficient single-prover interactive proofs for AI safety, enabling scalable verification without debate under oracle-aided computations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: How to Avoid Debate: Scalable AI Safety via Doubly-Efficient Interactive Proofs
items.summary:
The paper arXiv:2607.03561 introduces a new approach to AI safety verification by developing doubly-efficient single-prover interactive proofs that do not rely on the traditional debate model involving two competing AI models. This method addresses limitations of debate-based verification, which assumes equal abilities and truthfulness among provers, by enabling scalable verification even when computations access oracles such as human judgment or external databases.

The authors present interactive proofs suitable for oracle-aided computations under conditions where the computation is robust to some incorrect oracle responses or when the oracle is represented by a low-degree polynomial. These results demonstrate that interactive verification of AI outputs can be achieved without debate, offering a more practical and noise-tolerant framework for ensuring AI alignment with human intentions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03561v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As AI models continue to develop powerful capabilities, it becomes critical that we are able to verify that their output is aligned with our intentions. A recent line of work focuses on verification via debate, a model of interactive proofs where two competing powerful provers, or AI models, debate each other to convince a weak verifier, or a human, of the correctness of their claim. However, debate assumes that the two AI models possess equal abilities and that one of them is truthful, which may not be realistic. In this work, we show \emph{how to avoid debate}: we initiate the study of \emph{single-prover} interactive proofs for AI safety. Prior results in single-prover interactive proofs do not immediately carry over to the AI safety setting: for example, they do not work when the computation has access to an oracle, such as to human judgment or an external database such as the web. We present doubly-efficient single-prover interactive proofs and arguments for oracle-aided computations (also known as relativizing proofs), in the settings where (1) the computation is robust, in the sense that the output does not change if at most a small fraction of the answers to oracle queries are incorrect, or (2) the oracle is a low-degree polynomial. These results suggest that interactive verification is possible even without debate, under structured or noise-tolerant oracle access.

items.title: Researchers propose an explainable reinforcement learning framework for adaptive traffic signal control that preserves intersection topology and ensures safety compliance, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines in simulations [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Explainable Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Traffic Signal Control
items.summary:
Researchers have developed an explainable reinforcement learning framework for adaptive traffic signal control that maintains the structural topology of intersections and ensures safety compliance. This approach disaggregates real-time traffic data into distinct lane entities and phase configurations, using a dual-stage attention network to capture relational dependencies and inter-lane conflicts. The system integrates a deterministic action-masking mechanism to prevent unsafe signal transitions, achieving superior performance in delay reduction compared to existing methods in simulation.

The framework provides full visual and analytical interpretability through an affinity matrix that quantifies the influence of signal phases on traffic volumes and queues, aligning with established traffic engineering principles. This transparency addresses challenges related to the black-box nature of deep reinforcement learning models, facilitating regulatory compliance, operational trust, and easier troubleshooting. The architecture offers a promising, auditable solution for next-generation adaptive traffic control systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03703v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for adaptive traffic signal control. However, in safety-critical infrastructure like traffic control, the opaque, black-box nature of deep RL models poses challenges for transportation agency acceptance, regulatory compliance, operational trust, troubleshooting, and fine-tuning. To bridge this gap between high-performance optimization and human-comprehensible interpretability, this effort introduces a novel, explainable entity centric RL framework for safe and transparent traffic signal control. Rather than processing traffic states through monolithic, flat vectors, the proposed architecture disaggregates real-time intersection observations into distinct, high-dimensional lane entities and phase temporal configurations to inherently preserve the structural topology and geometric configurations of the intersection. Relational dependencies and inter-lane conflicts are dynamically extracted via a dual-stage attention network featuring sequential multi-head cross-attention and self-attention blocks. This design yields a real time affinity matrix that quantifies the direct influence of signal phases on specific approach volumes and queues, providing full visual and analytical interpretability. To ensure strict operational reliability, a deterministic action-masking interface is integrated directly into the Proximal Policy Optimization pipeline, explicitly blocking invalid phase transitions to guarantee absolute compliance with established signal timing and safety constraints. Evaluated in a microscopic simulation environment, outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in delay minimization. More importantly, the emergent attention weights align precisely with established traffic engineering principles, offering an auditable, trust-enabling, and deployable architecture for next-generation adaptive traffic control systems.

items.title: Researchers propose an online linear programming framework for multi-objective routing in large language model serving, improving latency and throughput under batch-size and KV-cache constraints [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Online Linear Programming for Multi-Objective Routing in LLM Serving
items.summary:
Researchers have developed an online linear programming framework to optimize routing in large language model (LLM) serving, addressing the challenge of dispatching sequential requests to parallel decode workers under strict batch-size and KV-cache constraints. This multi-objective optimization approach improves control over latency and throughput trade-offs by using a bid-price control policy that admits requests based on service-level objectives (SLOs) and shadow prices. The method achieves millisecond decision times through warm-started, projected first-order updates that track evolving dual shadow prices efficiently.

The framework was integrated into the Vidur simulator, where it demonstrated significant performance gains over traditional heuristic routing methods across various SLO regimes, including end-to-end latency, time-to-first-token, throughput, and tail latency. This science-based approach offers a more effective alternative to heuristic routing, providing interpretable decision rewards and predictable runtime in LLM serving environments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03948v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the online routing problem in large language model serving, where requests arrive sequentially and must be dispatched to parallel decode workers under tight batch-size and KV-cache constraints. Unlike widely used routing heuristics that are not tied to explicit service-level objectives (SLOs) and offer limited control over latency-throughput trade-offs, we introduce a multi-objective optimization framework that formulates routing as an online linear programming with interpretable decision rewards. We apply an efficient bid-price control policy based on the online linear programming that admits requests when their SLO-weighted benefit exceeds their shadow prices. To meet millisecond decision requirements, we develop a warm-started, projected first-order updates that track the evolving dual shadow prices online with predictable runtime. We integrate our router into the Vidur simulator and demonstrate substantial improvements over standard baselines across multiple SLO regimes, including end-to-end latency, time-to-first-token, throughput, and tail performance. A big picture from our result: a science-based approach outperforms others based on heuristics.

items.title: Researchers propose a clustering-based unsupervised framework using K-Means++ to identify suspicious trading patterns in one million capital market transactions from 2012 to 2024 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A Clustering-Based Framework for Identifying Suspicious Trading Patterns in Capital Market
items.summary:
Researchers have developed an unsupervised fraud-detection framework using K-Means++ clustering to identify suspicious trading patterns in capital markets. Analyzing approximately one million financial transactions from 2012 to 2024, the method flagged 2.02% of trades as suspicious, categorizing them into types such as spoofing, pump and dump, insider trading, and fake breakouts, with nearly half remaining unclassified. The model's effectiveness is supported by a Silhouette Score of 0.561, despite the absence of ground truth data.

The study applies heuristic thresholds based on market practices to classify fraudulent trades within the clustered data. Among the suspicious trades, 51.10% were identified as spoofing, 0.10% as pump and dump schemes, 0.55% as insider trading, and 1.43% as fake breakouts. This clustering-based approach offers a scalable tool for detecting market manipulation, which undermines confidence in trading platforms.

items.originalTitle: Server-side Anti-cheat in FPS games for Aimbot detection using Deep learning and Machine learning
items.summary:
Researchers have developed YAACS, a server-side deep learning system designed to detect aimbot cheating in multiplayer first-person shooter (FPS) games. YAACS uses a stacked LSTM model trained on time-series and behavioral gameplay data to distinguish between regular players and those using aimbots, achieving an accuracy of 88.6% with a false positive rate of 0.97%. This approach outperforms traditional decision tree methods by significantly reducing false accusations while maintaining high detection accuracy.

The system analyzes features such as aim velocity, number of shots, distance to target, utility usage, and player movement patterns, integrating these into a classifier that can be embedded within game servers. By leveraging temporal sequence modeling, YAACS captures the dynamic context of player behavior, which is critical for minimizing incorrect cheat detections and ensuring fair gameplay in increasingly complex FPS environments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04336v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern video games are becoming more complex day by day. Most of these modern games are multiplayer first-person shooter (FPS) games. The rising popularity of FPS games emphasizes the need to combat cheating for fair and enjoyable gaming. As the number of players using cheating techniques like aimbots, wallhacks, and speed hacks is also increasing, we need a way to detect players who are using cheating tools to gain an unfair advantage over regular players. In this system, we focus exclusively on detecting aimbot cheats. Players who use aimbot cheats generally do not prioritize other aspects of the game. To distinguish between regular and cheating players, we identify specific features encompassing time-series data such as aim velocity, number of shots, distance to target, and more, along with behavioral data such as utility usage, player movement, and other gameplay patterns. Utilizing these features, we construct a server-side aimbot detection classifier named 'YAACS'. YAACS comprises a parser, a deep learning model, and intermediary connection utilities designed for integration with the game server. The proposed system achieves a classification accuracy of 88.6% with a false positive rate of 0.97% using a Stacked LSTM with Dense layers trained on sequences of 128 ticks (Tick Delta Negative=56, Tick Delta Positive=24), outperforming the Decision Tree baseline which achieves a higher accuracy of 96.2% but at a false positive rate of 2.68%, 2.76x worse than the best LSTM configuration. These results demonstrate that incorporating temporal context through sequence modelling is critical for minimising false accusations in FPS cheat detection.

items.title: Researchers use Truncated Reasoning AUC Evaluation to detect answer-driven reasoning in LLM-based educational tutors, finding answer keys make correct answers available early in explanations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Detecting Answer-Driven Reasoning in LLM-Based Educational Tutors via Truncated Chain-of-Thought Auditing
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a method called Truncated Reasoning AUC Evaluation (TRACE) to detect when large language model (LLM) tutors produce explanations that are answer-driven rather than derived from the student-facing problem. By testing 1,000 math problems under different tutoring contexts—including access to correct or incorrect answer keys—they found that having the answer key available allows the model to produce the correct answer very early in its explanation, often within the first 10% of the reasoning steps. This suggests that the model's explanations may rely on the answer key rather than genuine problem-solving.

The study used the Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct model and showed that access to the answer key significantly increased the median TRACE AUC score from 0.375 to 0.900, indicating earlier availability of the correct answer in the explanation. This effect persisted even in cases where both question-only and answer-key explanations ended with the correct answer. These findings support the use of truncated chain-of-thought auditing as a lightweight diagnostic tool to identify answer-driven reasoning in educational LLM tutors, which has implications for the design and evaluation of AI-based tutoring systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04572v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) tutors often produce fluent step-by-step explanations, but a correct and pedagogically formatted response does not guarantee that the answer was derived from the student-facing problem. In realistic tutoring systems, the model may also have access to teacher notes, answer keys, rubrics, or retrieved solution artifacts. We study whether such private answer information can make tutor explanations answer-driven: the final answer is behaviorally available before the written explanation has justified it. Using Truncated Reasoning AUC Evaluation (TRACE), which probes how early a chain-of-thought prefix can pass a verifier, we evaluate 1000 GSM8K test problems under three paired tutoring contexts: question-only, correct answer-key, and wrong answer-key. At fixed fractions of each generated explanation, we force the model to answer immediately and verify the response against the gold numeric answer. With Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, answer-key access raises median TRACE AUC from 0.375 to 0.900 and makes the gold answer available at the first 10% prefix in 997 of 1000 cases. The effect remains strong on the 746 examples where both question-only and answer-key explanations end with the correct answer. These results support truncated CoT auditing as a lightweight process-level diagnostic for answer-driven reasoning in math tutoring explanations.
