items.title: DSpark introduces confidence-scheduled speculative decoding with semi-autoregressive generation to accelerate large language model inference and improve throughput by up to 85% in live serving systems [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: DSpark: Confidence-Scheduled Speculative Decoding with Semi-Autoregressive Generation
items.summary:
DSpark is a new speculative decoding framework designed to accelerate large language model (LLM) inference by combining high-throughput parallel generation with adaptive, load-aware verification. It uses a semi-autoregressive architecture to maintain draft quality by modeling dependencies within token blocks and employs confidence-scheduled verification to dynamically adjust verification length based on predicted token acceptance, improving efficiency in high-concurrency serving systems.

In offline benchmarks, DSpark outperforms state-of-the-art autoregressive and parallel drafters by significantly increasing the accepted token length. When integrated into the DeepSeek-V4 serving system under live traffic, it reduces verification waste and boosts per-user generation speeds by 60 to 85 percent compared to the existing production baseline, enabling higher performance tiers and improving overall system throughput without sacrificing interactivity.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.05147v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates Large Language Model (LLM) inference by decoupling draft generation from target verification. While recent parallel drafters efficiently propose long token sequences in a single forward pass, they suffer from rapid acceptance decay due to a lack of inter-token dependencies. Furthermore, indiscriminately verifying these extended blocks wastes critical batch capacity on tokens with high rejection risks, severely degrading throughput in high-concurrency serving systems. We introduce DSpark, a speculative decoding framework that unifies high-throughput parallel generation with adaptive, load-aware verification. To maintain draft quality, DSpark utilizes a semi-autoregressive architecture, coupling a parallel backbone with a lightweight sequential module, to introduce intra-block dependency modeling and mitigate suffix decay. To optimize system efficiency, DSpark employs confidence-scheduled verification, dynamically tailoring the verification length for each request based on estimated prefix survival probabilities and engine-specific throughput profiles. On offline benchmarks across diverse domains, DSpark substantially improves the accepted length over state-of-the-art autoregressive and parallel drafters. When deployed within the DeepSeek-V4 serving system under live user traffic, DSpark successfully mitigates verification waste. Compared to the established production baseline (MTP-1), DSpark accelerates per-user generation speeds by 60 to 85 percent at matched throughput levels. More importantly, by preventing severe throughput degradation under strict interactivity constraints, it enables performance tiers that were previously unattainable, shifting the Pareto frontier of our serving system.

items.title: Researchers find privileged on-policy self-distillation reduces accuracy by up to 17% in thinking models on long reasoning tasks across multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Rethinking On-Policy Self-Distillation for Thinking Models
items.summary:
Researchers have found that using privileged on-policy self-distillation, where a language model teaches itself using additional information like problem solutions, can reduce accuracy by up to 17% in advanced thinking models during long reasoning tasks. This effect was observed across multiple models and benchmarks, including Qwen3 and OLMo models tested on AIME24, AIME25, and HMMT25 datasets. The accuracy drop is linked to how the privileged context influences learning at decision points with multiple possible reasoning paths, particularly affecting models during extended reasoning sequences where they typically perform best.

The study highlights that while on-policy distillation generally improves thinking models, adding privileged information reverses these gains by lowering the diversity of reasoning paths and penalizing reconsideration steps. This contrasts with instruction-tuned models, which benefit from privileged context. The findings suggest that self-distillation methods for strong reasoning models need careful attention to token-level signals, especially around correction and verification steps, to avoid impairing their problem-solving abilities.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.05184v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-distillation is a promising recipe for self-improvement in language models. In this setting, a model can serve as its own teacher when given privileged information, such as a solution to a math problem. This seems especially appealing for thinking models, which can use test-time reasoning to absorb the privileged information. Surprisingly, we show that privileged self-distillation degrades thinking models on long reasoning traces: across five Qwen3 and OLMo thinking models evaluated on AIME24, AIME25, and HMMT25, privileged-context distillation causes a relative drop of up to 17% in avg@16 accuracy. The degradation scales with the amount of privileged context withheld from the student and is most pronounced at long rollout budgets, where thinking models otherwise obtain their largest gains. This failure mode is not specific to self-distillation: on-policy distillation (OPD) improves thinking models, but privileged OPD reverses these gains. Our diagnostics link this failure mode to how privileged teacher context reshapes learning at high-entropy forking positions, where multiple continuations remain plausible and may lead to different reasoning paths. Privileged context lowers fork rates in thinking-model rollouts but not in instruction-model rollouts. This leads to an interesting dichotomy, where privileged context can help instruction-tuned models but hurts stronger thinking models. The effect is visible when the student begins a self-correction branch, where privileged OPD penalizes sampled reconsideration tokens that vanilla OPD supports. Thinking models trained with a privileged teacher produce fewer verification, backtracking, and hedging markers, even after length normalization. These findings indicate that self-distillation for strong thinking models requires attention to token-level signal, especially around correction and reasoning steps.

items.title: Researchers propose SiamixFormer, a fully-transformer Siamese network with temporal fusion for improved building and change detection in bi-temporal remote sensing images [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SiamixFormer: a fully-transformer Siamese network with temporal Fusion for accurate building detection and change detection in bi-temporal remote sensing images
items.summary:
Researchers have developed SiamixFormer, a fully-transformer Siamese network designed to improve building detection and change detection in bi-temporal remote sensing images. Unlike traditional models that rely solely on pre-disaster images, SiamixFormer processes both pre- and post-disaster images using two encoders and a hierarchical transformer architecture. This approach incorporates temporal transformers for feature fusion, enhancing the model's ability to maintain large receptive fields and effectively analyze changes over time.

The model generates queries from pre-disaster images and keys and values from post-disaster images, allowing temporal features to be integrated during fusion. Outputs from the temporal transformer are decoded by a simple MLP at each stage. Evaluations on datasets such as xBD, WHU, LEVIR-CD, and CDD demonstrate that SiamixFormer outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in both building detection and change detection tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2208.00657v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Building detection and change detection using remote sensing images can help urban and rescue planning. Moreover, they can be used for building damage assessment after natural disasters. Currently, most of the existing models for building detection use only one image (pre-disaster image) to detect buildings. This is based on the idea that post-disaster images reduce the model's performance because of presence of destroyed buildings. In this paper, we propose a siamese model, called SiamixFormer, which uses pre- and post-disaster images as input. Our model has two encoders and has a hierarchical transformer architecture. The output of each stage in both encoders is given to a temporal transformer for feature fusion in a way that query is generated from pre-disaster images and (key, value) is generated from post-disaster images. To this end, temporal features are also considered in feature fusion. Another advantage of using temporal transformers in feature fusion is that they can better maintain large receptive fields generated by transformer encoders compared with CNNs. Finally, the output of the temporal transformer is given to a simple MLP decoder at each stage. The SiamixFormer model is evaluated on xBD, and WHU datasets, for building detection and on LEVIR-CD and CDD datasets for change detection and could outperform the state-of-the-art.

items.originalTitle: From Tensor Buffer to Distributed Memory Hierarchy: A Survey of KV Cache Management for LLM Serving
items.summary:
A recent survey examines over thirty key-value (KV) cache management systems used in large language model (LLM) serving, categorizing them along four dimensions: locality, lifetime, ownership, and substrate. This classification reveals five main architectural archetypes—local-paged, disaggregated-pipeline, shared-store, memory-pool, and hybrid-tier—and highlights how ownership significantly influences design differences in distributed systems once workload and hardware are fixed. The study also reviews current evaluation methods and identifies seven missing KV-specific metrics, connecting these gaps to unresolved challenges in areas such as fault tolerance, isolation, tiered eviction, speculative decoding, mixture-of-experts serving, and shared-cache semantics.

By providing a comprehensive framework for understanding KV cache architectures and pinpointing evaluation shortcomings, the survey offers valuable insights for advancing distributed memory hierarchies in LLM serving. It underscores the importance of addressing these open problems to improve system robustness and efficiency in managing KV caches across diverse hardware and workload scenarios.

items.title: Researchers present Homer, a hierarchical memory and agentic reasoning framework that improves understanding of long-form videos by enabling multi-scale memory retrieval and causal reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Homer: Understanding Long-form Videos with Hierarchical Memory and Agentic Reasoning
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Homer, a hierarchical memory and agentic reasoning framework designed to improve the understanding of long-form videos by enabling multi-scale memory retrieval and causal reasoning. Unlike existing methods that either use compact visual representations lacking semantic depth or organize memory based on temporal proximity without explicit causal links, Homer structures memory to reflect the multi-scale nature of long videos, from raw perception to events connected by temporal and causal relations. Its agentic reasoner mimics human exploration by locating relevant scenes, retrieving details, and composing answers through iterative memory retrieval with verification and correction at each step.

Homer demonstrated significant performance improvements over previous methods, achieving higher scores on benchmarks such as M3-Bench-robot, M3-Bench-web, and Video-MME-Long. It also consistently enhanced the capabilities of various large language model backbones, indicating its model-agnostic potential for grounded retrieval and multi-hop narrative reasoning in processing hour-long videos under limited memory constraints.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02588v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multimodal large language models excel on short clips but struggle on hour-long videos in an online setting, where frames are processed incrementally under limited memory. Existing online methods either retain compact visual representations that lack semantic structure, or build higher-level memory stores organized around temporal proximity rather than explicit causal links, leaving multi-hop narrative reasoning to be reconstructed by the LLM at every query. We bridge this gap with \textsc{Homer}, a Hierarchical Online Memory Exploration and Reasoning framework. \textsc{Homer}'s memory mirrors the multi-scale structure of long videos, ranging from raw perception, to recurring entities, to events connected by explicit temporal and causal relations. Its agentic reasoner then explores this memory the way humans do, locating the relevant scene, looking up details, and composing the answer through multi-round memory retrieval, with a harness that verifies and corrects each step. \textsc{Homer} outperforms the previous best agent method by $+5.5$, $+10.8$, and $+4.4$ points on M3-Bench-robot, M3-Bench-web, and Video-MME-Long, and consistently lifts three various LLM backbones, indicating a model-agnostic structural capability for grounded retrieval over long videos.

items.title: Researchers introduce Fusion, a unified adaptive inference framework for Vision Transformers that coordinates token merging, early exiting, and pruning to reduce energy use by 48% and improve calibration on ImageNet-1k [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Fusion: A Framework for Unified Sequential Token AdaptatIon in VisiOn TraNsformers
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Fusion, a unified adaptive inference framework for Vision Transformers that integrates token merging, early exiting, and token pruning to enhance efficiency and accuracy. Fusion processes tokens in a staged manner—merging tokens first, then evaluating confidence, and finally pruning tokens only for samples continuing inference—allowing these mechanisms to work cooperatively. This approach reduces inference energy consumption by 48% and improves calibration error by up to four times on ImageNet-1k, while maintaining or surpassing the performance of existing adaptive Vision Transformer methods.

Fusion includes lightweight routing modules that adjust compression strength based on each input and enable real-time tuning of the accuracy-latency trade-off without retraining. The framework demonstrates consistent transferability across multiple datasets and Vision Transformer backbones without requiring dataset-specific tuning, highlighting its versatility and potential for broader application in efficient image classification tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02612v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision Transformers achieve strong image classification accuracy but process all image regions with nearly the same computation, even when many regions are redundant or uninformative. Recent adaptive inference methods reduce this cost by selectively compressing tokens or terminating inference early, but combining these mechanisms often causes unstable intermediate representations and accuracy degradation. We introduce Fusion, a unified adaptive inference framework that coordinates token merging, early exiting, and token pruning through a simple staged design: tokens are merged first, confidence is evaluated next, and pruning is applied only to samples that continue inference. This ordering allows the three mechanisms to operate cooperatively rather than competitively. Fusion further includes lightweight routing modules that adapt compression strength to each input and support inference-time adjustment of the accuracy--latency trade-off without retraining. On ImageNet-1k with DeiT-S, Fusion matches or surpasses state-of-the-art adaptive ViT methods at comparable compute budgets while reducing calibration error by up to $4\times$ and inference energy by $48\%$. Experiments across ImageNet-100, CIFAR-100, and ImageNette with multiple ViT backbones demonstrate consistent transferability without dataset-specific tuning.

items.title: Researchers present QuantFlow, a federated Mamba-based foundation model for time-series forecasting that supports privacy and uncertainty across diverse datasets including cryptocurrency and weather [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: QuantFlow: A Federated Mamba-Based Post-Transformer Foundation Model for Time-Series Forecasting
items.summary:
Researchers have developed QuantFlow, a federated foundation model designed for time-series forecasting that emphasizes privacy and uncertainty management. This model integrates inverted sequence embedding, bidirectional Mamba state-space decoders, quantile regression, and federated learning to handle diverse datasets such as cryptocurrency, traffic, electricity, influenza, and weather data without centralizing sensitive information. QuantFlow processes each variable across the entire observation window in both forward and reverse directions, projecting results to multiple conditional quantiles to improve forecasting accuracy.

QuantFlow employs TSMixup, a technique that enhances temporal diversity while maintaining sequence structure, and demonstrates strong performance with mean squared errors of 0.2834 on the ETTm1 dataset and 0.2218 on weather data. In a federated setting with 20 clients and non-identically distributed data, the model maintained useful accuracy after only three communication rounds, highlighting its potential for scalable and privacy-conscious applications. However, the study also notes challenges in handling irregular epidemiological signals and long-horizon forecasting, indicating areas for future improvement.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02632v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Time-series forecasting supports decisions in finance, en-ergy, transportation, public health, and industrial monitoring. Recent foundation models improve transfer across forecast-ing tasks, but many depend on centralized data and Trans-former attention, which restricts their use for long, high-di-mensional, and privacy-sensitive signals. This paper presents QuantFlow, a probabilistic forecasting framework that com-bines inverted sequence embedding, bidirectional Mamba state-space decoders, quantile regression, and federated learning. Each variable is embedded over the complete ob-servation window, processed in forward and reverse direc-tions, and projected to five conditional quantiles. TSMixup expands temporal diversity through Dirichlet-weighted inter-polation while preserving sequence structure. Experiments cover cryptocurrency, traffic, electricity, Electricity Trans-former Temperature, influenza, and weather data. QuantFlow obtains mean squared errors of 0.2834 on ETTm1 and 0.2218 on Weather, and a 20-client non-IID deployment retains use-ful accuracy after three communication rounds without cen-tralizing raw records. The results indicate that selective state-space modelling is a promising basis for scalable, uncer-tainty-aware, and privacy-conscious time-series prediction, while also revealing limitations on irregular epidemiological signals and long-horizon generalization.

items.title: Researchers apply federated learning to drone object detection, achieving up to 67.8% mAP improvement without centralizing data on KIIT-MiTA dataset [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Federated Learning for Object Detection: Enabling Collaborative Drone Learning Without Centralizing Data
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a federated learning approach for object detection in drone systems, allowing drones to collaboratively improve a shared model without centralizing sensitive image data. Using the KIIT-MiTA dataset and the Sherpa.ai federated learning platform, their method achieved significant improvements in mean Average Precision (mAP), with the lightweight YOLO26 nano model showing up to 67.8% relative gain compared to single-drone training. This approach addresses privacy, regulatory, and bandwidth challenges inherent in centralized data collection for distributed drone deployments.

The study compared federated learning with single-drone and centralized training baselines, demonstrating that federated learning closely matches centralized performance while preserving data privacy. The results highlight the potential for scalable, high-performing, and privacy-preserving object detection across distributed drone fleets, even on limited edge infrastructure, without the need to transfer large volumes of aerial imagery to a central server.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02636v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Object detection is a fundamental capability for AI-driven perception in safety-critical drone and edge-vision systems, including disaster response, operational security environments, infrastructure monitoring and defense applications. Robust model performance in such environments depends on large, continuously updated datasets. However, training high-performing detectors typically requires centralizing aerial imagery, which raises privacy, regulatory, storage, and bandwidth challenges. This is especially problematic in distributed drone deployments, where visual data is generated onboard and is often impractical or undesirable to transfer to a centralized infrastructure. In this work, we apply Federated Learning (FL) for object detection, enabling drones to improve a shared model while keeping image data local and private. We implement a federated object detection pipeline using the Sherpa.ai FL platform on the KIIT-MiTA dataset, and compare it with Single-drone and Centralized baselines using mean Average Precision (mAP) at IoU thresholds of 0.50 and 0.50-0.95. In our experiments, the proposed FL approach remains close to Centralized training while dramatically improving over Single-drone training, with the best lightweight model (YOLO26 nano), suitable for deployment even on very limited edge infrastructure, achieving relative gains of 52.89% and 67.80% in mAP@0.50 and mAP@0.50:0.95, respectively. These results show that FL enables scalable, high-performing, and privacy-preserving object detection across distributed drone fleets without data centralization.

items.title: Researchers propose generator-agnostic method to improve synthetic image utility by selecting diverse subsets, reducing samples by up to 40% without retraining [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Post-Generation Curation of Synthetic Images via Homogeneous-Heterogeneous Splitting
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a generator-agnostic method to enhance the utility of synthetic images by selecting diverse subsets from a fixed pool of generated data. This approach addresses a common bias in modern generative models, which tend to overproduce typical class modes while underrepresenting intra-class variation. By dividing each real class into homogeneous and heterogeneous subsets and applying a fidelity-diversity scoring criterion, the method improves downstream performance without requiring retraining or generator-specific adjustments.

The technique consistently outperforms existing data selection baselines across multiple benchmarks, achieving comparable results to real data with up to 40% fewer synthetic samples. It remains effective even when applied to stronger, task-tuned generators, benefiting both classification and segmentation tasks. This post-generation selection strategy complements advances in generative models by enhancing the quality and efficiency of synthetic training data.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02637v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent generative models can produce high-quality synthetic images, offering scalable training training data for data-hungry models. Existing approaches to exploiting this potential typically involve 1) training or fine-tuning generators, or 2) using lightweight post-hoc adaptation like prompt engineering or inference-time guidance, making them generator-specific and expertise-intensive. We study a complementary question: given a fixed pool of generated images, can downstream utility be improved purely by selecting an informative subset? The answer is yes. We show that effective selection must counter a structural bias of modern generators: they tend to over-produce canonical modes of each class while underrepresenting intra-class variation. Building on this insight, we split each real class into a canonical Homogeneous (HO) subset and a non-redundant Heterogeneous (HE) subset, then score synthetic images by a fidelity-diversity criterion that rewards semantic alignment while penalizing canonical redundancy. The method is generator-agnostic and requires no retraining. Across multiple benchmarks, it consistently outperforms state-of-the-art data selection baselines and matches the real-data performance with up to 40% fewer synthetic samples. The same criterion remains effective when applied on top of stronger task-tuned generators, with gains on both classification and segmentation tasks. Post-generation selection is therefore not a substitute for better generators, but a complementary mechanism for improving the utility of synthetic data.

items.title: Researchers introduce a synthetic diagnostic framework using image generative models to evaluate and improve aerial-view vehicle detectors, achieving up to 13% AP50 gains with targeted real data supplementation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Diagnosing Aerial-View Object Detectors with Foundational Image Generative Models
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a synthetic diagnostic framework that uses large-scale image generative models to evaluate and improve aerial-view vehicle detectors. This framework combines text-guided image generation, attribute-controlled editing, and automated verification to create a controllable synthetic testbed, enabling detailed assessment of pretrained detectors across diverse scenes and conditions that are hard to isolate in real datasets. Testing across multiple detection architectures and real aerial datasets showed that synthetic performance trends closely match real-world weaknesses, allowing targeted data supplementation that improved detection accuracy by up to 13% AP50 with fewer additional samples than traditional augmentation methods.

The approach leverages controlled synthetic probing to identify performance gaps and guide efficient data collection, demonstrating its potential as a diagnostic tool beyond conventional data augmentation. The modular framework can integrate alternative generative or vision-language models as technology advances, offering a flexible platform for ongoing improvements in aerial object detection. The researchers have made their code and datasets publicly available to support further development in this area.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02718v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent advances in large-scale image generative models enable photorealistic scene synthesis with controllable attributes. Beyond data augmentation, their potential as diagnostic tools for trained vision systems remains unexplored in the aerial and remote sensing domains. We introduce a synthetic diagnostic framework for aerial-view vehicle detection that combines text-guided generation, attribute-controlled editing, and automated attribute verification to construct a controllable synthetic testbed. This enables fine-grained evaluation of pretrained detectors under diverse scene types and environmental conditions that are difficult to isolate in real datasets. Across three detection architectures and three real aerial datasets, synthetic scene-wise performance trends closely match real-world weaknesses. Guided by these diagnostics, targeted supplementation with small real datasets from the identified weak categories yields improvements of up to 13% AP50 while requiring substantially fewer additional samples than non-targeted augmentation. Our results show that controlled synthetic probing can predict real-domain performance gaps and guide efficient data collection. The proposed diagnostic framework is modular and can incorporate alternative generative or vision-language models as capabilities evolve. Our code and datasets are available here: https://humansensinglab.github.io/AVODDiag/

items.title: Researchers present a multimodal NLP framework using XLM-RoBERTa and CLIP for early detection of fake news and violence-prone mob activity with 98% accuracy on Bangla and English datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Echoes of Unrest: A Multimodal NLP Framework for Early Warning of Fake News and Violence-Driven Mob Activity
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a multilingual, multimodal Natural Language Processing (NLP) framework that combines XLM-RoBERTa for text analysis and CLIP for visual embedding to detect fake news and violence-prone mob activity with 98% accuracy. The system was tested on a fused dataset of over 138,000 Bangla and English samples, integrating additional features like sarcasm detection and geospatial metadata to enhance early warning capabilities. This approach addresses the rapid spread of misinformation on social media platforms, which has been linked to real-world unrest and violence, particularly in South Asia.

The framework uses a multi-head attention mechanism to fuse textual and visual data, improving detection performance beyond traditional methods. Experiments on a stratified subset of the dataset demonstrated strong precision and recall, highlighting the effectiveness of combining multiple data modalities and auxiliary signals. The inclusion of geospatial information is particularly valuable for anticipating potential escalation of misinformation into physical conflict.

This research underscores the potential of advanced multimodal NLP techniques to provide timely alerts about misinformation and related social risks, offering a tool to help mitigate the impact of false information before it leads to harm. The findings suggest that integrating diverse data sources can significantly improve early detection systems, which is critical given the speed at which misinformation can spread compared to fact-checking efforts.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02734v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rapid growth in social media has transformed global communication by enabling fast information exchange, but it has also accelerated the spread of misinformation. Fake news, manipulated content, and provocative narratives are increasingly linked to social unrest, political instability, and mob violence. Incidents in South Asia and elsewhere demonstrate how false information disseminated via platforms such as Facebook and WhatsApp can trigger real-world harm, often spreading faster than fact-checking efforts can respond. To address this challenge, this chapter presents a multilingual, multimodal Natural Language Processing (NLP) framework for early detection of misinformation and violence-prone dynamics. A fused dataset of 138,256 Bangla and English samples was created by combining multiple benchmark datasets. The framework integrates XLM-RoBERTa for multilingual text representation, CLIP for visual embedding, and a multi-head attention mechanism for multimodal fusion, enhanced with auxiliary features such as sarcasm and geospatial metadata. Experiments on a stratified 30% subset achieved 98% test accuracy with strong precision and recall. The outcomes show the efficacy of multimodal approaches in early misinformation detection and highlight the added value of geospatial signals for anticipating real-world escalation.

items.title: Researchers introduce RiskAverseOOD benchmark showing risk aversion learned by Qwen3-8B language model at low stakes generalizes partially to astronomically high stakes across multiple model scales and families [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Out-of-Distribution Generalization of Risk Aversion in Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced RiskAverseOOD, a benchmark designed to evaluate how well risk aversion learned by AI language models generalizes from low-stakes to extremely high-stakes scenarios. Their study focused on the Qwen3-8B model, demonstrating that risk-averse behavior trained on low-risk situations can partially extend to decisions involving astronomically higher stakes, with significant increases in choosing safer options compared to baseline rates. This effect was observed across different model sizes and families, including Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-14B, Gemma-3-12B-IT, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct.

The researchers applied various training methods such as supervised fine-tuning, direct preference optimization, and activation steering to induce risk aversion. Their fine-tuned reward model also showed high accuracy in distinguishing risk-averse reasoning from risk-neutral or overly risk-averse alternatives. Despite these promising results, the generalization of risk aversion is not yet consistent enough to serve as a reliable safety mechanism, highlighting the need for further research to achieve dependable risk-averse AI behavior at all stakes.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02755v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Training AIs to be risk-averse in resources could offer a failsafe in the event that AIs turn out misaligned. Misaligned but risk-averse AIs would tend to prefer low-risk, low-reward strategies like cooperation over high-risk, high-reward strategies like rebellion, limiting the downsides of any misalignment. But we can only feasibly train AIs to be risk-averse on low-stakes gambles, and we will only be safe if their risk aversion generalizes to astronomically-high-stakes gambles. Will it? To shed light on this question, we introduce RiskAverseOOD: a benchmark for measuring how well risk aversion generalizes out of distribution. We then offer some initial results. Using a variety of methods to make Qwen3-8B choose risk-aversely when the stakes are low, we find that we can induce substantial risk aversion when the stakes are astronomically high. Our models' learned risk aversion generalizes at least partially across 98 orders of magnitude. From a baseline 2% rate of choosing a safe `Cooperate' option, we see rates around 70% (SFT and tie training), 52% (DPO), and 39% (activation steering). In another experiment, our fine-tuned reward model reliably scores risk-averse reasoning above risk-neutral or excessively risk-averse alternatives (99.6% pairwise accuracy). We replicate these effects at different scales (Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-14B) and across model families (Gemma-3-12B-IT and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct). Overall, we find that risk aversion learned at low stakes can generalize OOD to astronomically high stakes, though not yet consistently enough to serve as a reliable failsafe. Achieving that level of consistency is an open problem.

items.title: Researchers introduce Gemma 4, a new generation of open-weight multimodal language models with 2.3B to 31B parameters, featuring improved encoders, unified architecture, and reasoning capabilities [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Gemma 4 Technical Report
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Gemma 4, a new generation of open-weight, multimodal language models ranging from 2.3 billion to 31 billion parameters. The Gemma 4 suite features both dense and Mixture-of-Experts architectures, improved vision and audio encoders, and a unified, encoder-free design for the 12 billion parameter model that processes raw audio and image patches. It also includes a thinking mode that allows the models to generate reasoning traces before responding, enhancing their reasoning capabilities.

The design improvements in Gemma 4 focus on increasing compute efficiency, inference speed, memory usage, and long-context understanding. These advancements result in significant performance gains across STEM, multimodal, and long-context benchmarks, positioning Gemma 4 to rival larger, state-of-the-art open models in human-rated tasks.

items.title: Researchers present CoC-Seduce benchmark assessing rule adherence and vulnerability to rhetorical injection attacks in LLMs acting as adjudicators in semi-open textual game environments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Seduced by the Narrative: Assessing Rule Adherence in Semi-Open Textual Sandboxes
items.summary: Researchers have introduced CoC-Seduce, a benchmark designed to evaluate how well large language models (LLMs) adhere to rules and resist rhetorical injection attacks when acting as adjudicators in semi-open textual game environments. These environments, based on Tabletop Role-Playing Game mechanics, require models to enforce explicit rules while interacting entirely through natural language. The study tested 20 adjudicator models against adversarial inputs generated by leading models like GPT-5.4, revealing that neither larger model size nor explicit reasoning guarantees robustness, with pseudo-logical reasoning identified as the primary attack method.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02802v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As LLMs are increasingly deployed as autonomous adjudicators in semi-open textual game environments, robust rule adherence becomes critical when user intent conflicts with system rules. items.title: Researchers find large language models struggle to apply Cognitive Behavioral Therapy effectively despite high theoretical knowledge, showing bias toward validation and reflection strategies [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Where do LLMs Fall Short in CBT-Guided Affective Reasoning?
items.summary:
Researchers have found that large language models (LLMs), despite demonstrating strong theoretical knowledge of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) with up to 96% accuracy on licensing exam questions, struggle to apply CBT effectively in practice. These models tend to default to validation and reflection responses regardless of the user's actual needs, indicating a gap between knowledge and practical application. The study introduces a knowledge-guided framework that decomposes user narratives into structured cognitive concepts and employs a Multiple Chain-of-Thought strategy to guide response selection among validation, Socratic questioning, or alternative perspectives.

The researchers developed a behavior-level metric called Protocol Leverage Force (F) to measure how much an intervention shifts an LLM's default response. Testing across three open-weight LLMs and 14 case studies derived from real CBT sessions showed that simple prompting with protocol definitions did not significantly change model behavior. While the Multiple Chain-of-Thought approach improved strategy selection slightly, the effect remained minimal, with all models still biased toward validation and reflection. These findings highlight that possessing CBT knowledge alone does not ensure effective therapeutic application, providing tools for the affective computing community to better assess and address these limitations in LLMs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02885v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) provides a structured framework for understanding a user's mental state by examining the interaction between cognitive and behavioral factors. However, out-of-the-box LLMs respond fluently and empathetically, yet collapse into validation & reflection, regardless of what the user actually needs. They know theoretical CBT (scoring up to 96% accuracy on licensing exam questions) but fail to apply it effectively. We explore this gap with a knowledge-guided framework that treats CBT dialogue as controlled affective reasoning: user narratives are decomposed into Beck's Cognitive Conceptualization structure, grounded in clinical SNOMED CT concepts validated via Natural Language Inference, and a Multiple Chain-of-Thought (MCoT) strategy selection between Validation & Reflection, Socratic Questioning, or Alternative Perspectives. To measure whether such guidance actually changes behavior, we introduce the Protocol Leverage Force (F), a behavior-level metric that captures how far an intervention shifts a model away from its default response. Across three open-weight LLMs and 14 RealCBT-derived case studies, evaluated with human experts, valence-arousal trajectories, and linguistic entrainment, F shows that simply introducing protocol definitions via single chain-of-thought prompting fails to change LLM behavior, while MCoT on these definitions guides strategy selection better. Still, the effect stays within 1% (approx. 1.2-1.3%), and all models remain biased toward Validation & Reflection. These results show CBT knowledge alone does not ensure effective application, giving the affective-computing community instrumentation to measure where LLMs fall short.

items.title: Researchers introduce SPLIT, a training-free AI-generated and partially edited video detector using spatial patch-level incoherence and temporal roughness, achieving top performance at 0.1% false positive rate across three benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SPLIT: Training-Free AI-Generated and Partially Edited Video Detection via Spatial Patch-Level Incoherence and Temporal Roughness
items.summary:
Researchers have developed SPLIT, a training-free detector designed to identify AI-generated and partially edited videos with an ultra-low false positive rate, crucial for real-world applications to avoid misclassifying authentic content. SPLIT analyzes spatial patch-level incoherence and temporal roughness using patch tokens from a frozen vision encoder, combining two complementary signals—Two-step Temporal Roughness and Local Spatial Motion Incoherence—to effectively distinguish real from fake videos.

The method employs a multiplicative fusion with gamma correction to enhance detection accuracy at strict thresholds and introduces a service-aligned evaluation protocol focusing on Fake Recall at a fixed false positive rate. Tested across three benchmarks—FakeParts, GenVideo, and ViF-Bench—SPLIT outperforms both supervised and other training-free detectors, maintaining robustness against post-processing while requiring minimal computational overhead. The code for SPLIT is publicly available for further research and application.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02886v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Deploying AI-generated video detectors in real-world services demands an ultra-low false positive rate (FPR) on real videos to avoid falsely rejecting authentic content, a regime where standard metrics such as AUROC fail to reflect actual operating behavior. We introduce Spatial Patch-Level Incoherence and Temporal Roughness (SPLIT), a training-free detector that operates on patch tokens from a frozen vision encoder to detect both fully generated and partially edited videos. SPLIT computes two complementary signals: Two-step Temporal Roughness (TTR), capturing non-smooth patch trajectories via one-step and two-step feature variation contrast, and Local Spatial Motion Incoherence (LSMI), measuring spatially inconsistent temporal changes through gradients of a feature-space motion field. The two are fused multiplicatively with gamma correction to sharpen real-fake separation at strict thresholds. We further propose a service-aligned evaluation protocol based on Fake Recall at fixed FPR with real-only threshold calibration and cross-real threshold transfer. Across three benchmarks (FakeParts, GenVideo, and ViF-Bench), SPLIT achieves the highest Fake Recall at FPR = $0.1\%$, substantially outperforming supervised and training-free baselines while remaining robust to post-processing with negligible overhead. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/mldljyh/SPLIT .

items.title: Researchers introduce Bootstrap Flow-Map-Tree sampling framework for efficient online feedback-driven global search and alignment under sampling budget constraints [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Bootstrap Flow-Map Tree Sampling Enables Online Feedback Driven Search
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Bootstrap Flow-Map-Tree (BFMT), a new sampling framework designed to optimize global search and alignment under limited sampling budgets by leveraging sequential feedback. BFMT enables efficient, history-aware exploration by constructing full tree paths from any depth with a single function evaluation, reducing computational costs while guiding sampling decisions. This approach allows a smooth transition from broad exploration to focused refinement of promising regions, addressing challenges faced by existing methods that typically perform local searches and struggle when preferences are unknown in advance.

Extensive experiments across various search and alignment tasks demonstrate that BFMT significantly outperforms baseline methods. Its dynamic scheduling of transition time steps ensures efficient allocation of sampling resources, making it a promising tool for scientific and engineering domains where maximizing discovery within constrained budgets is critical.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02915v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In many scientific and engineering domains, maximizing discovery within a limited sampling budget demands strategic, observation-guided exploration. While generative models have enabled training-free reward alignment, current methods typically excel in local searches within narrow regions of the underlying distribution. These approaches struggle when preferences are unknown a priori and only revealed through sequential feedback-a scenario demanding broad exploration to uncover high-utility regions. To address this, we introduce Bootstrap Flow-Map-Tree (a.k.a BFMT), a novel computationally efficient sampling framework designed for history-aware global search and alignment under sampling budget constraints. BFMT enables full tree-path construction from any tree depth using a single function evaluation, drastically reducing computational overhead while providing critical foresight for sequential sampling. By enabling dynamic transition time steps scheduling, BFMT efficiently allocates its sampling budget, smoothly transitioning from broad global exploration to fine-grained local refinement of high-utility modes discovered through exploration. Extensive experiments and ablations across diverse search and alignment tasks demonstrate that BFMT substantially outperforms baseline approaches.

items.title: Researchers propose PROMPTPET, an LLM-based agent that optimizes prompt obfuscation to balance privacy and utility in AI chatbot interactions using reinforcement learning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: PromptPET: Privacy-Utility Optimized Prompt Obfuscation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed PROMPTPET, an AI agent that enhances privacy in chatbot interactions by optimizing how sensitive information in user prompts is obfuscated. This system balances the tradeoff between protecting user privacy and maintaining the utility of chatbot responses by selecting from four obfuscation methods—redaction, abstraction, replacement, and a novel noising/denoising technique—using a reinforcement learning-based approach. PROMPTPET evaluates each sensitive part of a prompt to apply the most effective obfuscation, ensuring useful and personalized chatbot replies while minimizing the risk of user profiling.

The approach incorporates a data type taxonomy to identify sensitive information and explicitly considers the quality of chatbot responses when deciding how to obfuscate. Tested on real-world chat data, PROMPTPET matches or exceeds the privacy-utility tradeoffs achieved by any single obfuscation method and outperforms previous state-of-the-art techniques, marking a significant advancement in user-side privacy protection for AI chatbots.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02932v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Privacy is an important challenge when users interact with AI chatbots, since users may share sensitive information, explicitly or implicitly, and AI chatbots can use this information for user profiling. In this paper, we aim to protect user privacy via a user-side mechanism that transforms sensitive information in a user prompt, while preserving enough information to elicit a useful response from the chatbot. This approach faces an inherent tradeoff between protecting privacy (i.e., avoiding profiling) and preserving utility (i.e., getting personalized and task-specific responses). To that end, we consider, evaluate, and compare four different obfuscation actions, namely redaction, abstraction, replacement, and a novel noising/denoising scheme that we introduce. Additional novel insights include: utilizing a data type taxonomy to both identify and obfuscate sensitive information and explicitly taking into account the utility of chat responses in making the obfuscation decision. First, we systematically optimize and evaluate each obfuscation action independently in terms of the privacy-utility tradeoff it achieves. Second, we propose PROMPTPET, an LLM-based agent that selects the best obfuscation action for each sensitive part of the prompt, using a reinforcement-learning inspired rule optimizer, applied for the first time in this context. Using a real-world chat dataset, we show that PROMPTPET matches the best privacy-utility tradeoff attainable by any single obfuscation action and significantly outperforms prior state-of-the-art approaches.

items.title: Researchers propose PRECEDE, a precedent-guided AI co-scientist for side-effect-aware drug redesign using biomedical knowledge graphs and human review checkpoints [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A Precedent-Guided Co-Scientist for Side-Effect-Aware Drug Redesign
items.summary:
Researchers have developed PRECEDE, an AI system designed to assist in drug redesign by reducing specific side effects while maintaining therapeutic effectiveness. Unlike traditional methods that generate molecules in isolation, PRECEDE uses evidence-based reasoning over drug-side-effect relationships, biomedical knowledge graphs, and prior examples of safety-focused optimization. The process is guided by a large language model orchestrator and includes human review checkpoints to ensure transparency and scientific rigor.

PRECEDE operates as a human-supervised AI workflow where hypotheses are auditable and grounded in established pharmacological knowledge. This approach aims to enhance drug safety by integrating computational reasoning with expert oversight, potentially improving the drug development process by making it more precise and accountable.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02944v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose PRECEDE, a precedent-guided co-scientist for side-effect-aware drug redesign that revises a parent compound to mitigate a specified side effect while preserving therapeutic function. Rather than isolated molecular generation, PRECEDE frames redesign as evidence-grounded reasoning over drug--side-effect associations, biomedical knowledge graphs, and precedents of safety-driven optimization, coordinated by an LLM orchestrator with explicit policies and human-review checkpoints. items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Hierarchical Landmark Sparse (HiLS) Attention, a new chunk-wise sparse attention mechanism designed to scale large language models (LLMs) to much longer contexts efficiently. HiLS Attention learns chunk selection end-to-end using the language-modeling loss, enabling it to factorize attention hierarchically and fuse outputs based on retrieval scores. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02980v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scaling modern large language models (LLMs) to long contexts is limited by the quadratic computation cost, and poor length extrapolation of dense attention. Chunk-wise sparse attention offers a promising alternative, but all existing methods fall short of full attention because of their inaccurate chunk selection. We propose Hierarchical Landmark Sparse (HiLS) Attention, a chunk-wise sparse attention mechanism that learns chunk selection end-to-end under the language-modeling (LM) loss. HiLS factorizes attention hierarchically: each query performs attention independently with each retrieved chunk to extract chunk-specific information, and the resulting outputs are fused according to chunk retrieval scores. By incorporating retrieval scores into the forward attention computation, HiLS optimizes them directly with the LM loss, enabling end-to-end retrieval learning and native sparse training. Experimental results show that HiLS-Attention achieves performance comparable to, and in some cases better than, full attention at in-domain context lengths. Meanwhile, HiLS-Attention extrapolates more than $64\times$ the training context length with 90% retrieval accuracy, far beyond full attention. Moreover, existing full-attention models can be converted to HiLS-Attention with lightweight continued pretraining, preserving in-domain performance while acquiring ultra-long-context extrapolation. Together with its sparse KV access and computation, HiLS-Attention breaks the usual efficiency-performance trade-off, enabling long-context LLMs that are both more efficient and more effective on general long-context tasks than their full-attention counterparts.

items.title: Researchers present CONFLUX, a latent diffusion model with reinforcement learning post-training for 3D chest CT synthesis, releasing a 200k synthetic dataset with clinical conditioning metadata [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: CONFLUX: A Latent Diusion Model for 3D Chest-CT Synthesis with RL Post-Training
items.summary:
Researchers have developed CONFLUX, a latent diffusion model designed to generate high-quality 3D chest CT images conditioned on clinical metadata such as abnormality findings, sex, age, and reconstruction kernel. The model uses a 3D variational autoencoder to compress volumes and a rectified-flow transformer to generate images in latent space, achieving superior performance compared to existing methods. An additional reinforcement learning post-training phase enhances the model's ability to produce clinically accurate images, reducing the gap in reliability compared to real scans by 47% according to an independent classifier.

Alongside the model, the researchers have released a synthetic dataset of approximately 200,000 chest CT volumes with detailed clinical conditioning metadata. This dataset supports a wide range of clinical findings and offers a valuable resource for further research and development in medical image synthesis and analysis.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02998v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Controllable generative models of 3D medical images can synthesize volumes with specified clinical attributes, but this demands samples that are simultaneously high-fidelity, natively 3D, and faithful to the requested conditioning. We present CONFLUX, a latent diffusion model for chest computed tomography (CT): a 3D variational autoencoder compresses each volume, and a rectified-flow transformer generates in the latent space. Generation is conditioned on structured radiological metadata (18 abnormality findings, sex, age, and reconstruction kernel) through adaptive layer normalization. The model leads strong volumetric baselines on tri-planar Frechet distance (FID 32.3 vs. 74.6 for MAISI) while exposing direct control over clinical attributes. To strengthen that control we add an online reinforcement-learning post-training stage (group-relative policy optimization) that rewards how reliably a classifier recovers the requested findings from each generated volume. Judged by a separate, independent classifier, post-training removes 47% of the shortfall relative to real-scan reliability. We release the model and a ~200k synthetic chest-CT dataset with conditioning metadata spanning a wide variety of clinical findings.

items.title: Researchers propose MolBasic framework to improve molecular large language models' structural understanding via bidirectional SMILES-Graph translation and progressive learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Back to Basics: Improving Molecular Understanding in LLMs via SMILES-Graph Translation
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced MolBasic, a new framework designed to enhance molecular large language models' understanding of molecular structures by focusing on bidirectional translation between SMILES strings and molecular graphs. This approach addresses the limitation of current models that, despite strong performance in molecular tasks, struggle with basic structure recognition, which is crucial since molecular function is determined by structure. MolBasic uses a multi-level structure perception benchmark and a progressive learning scheme to improve alignment between sequential and topological molecular representations.

The framework incorporates a standardized Chain-of-Thought method to guide models from learning structural details to performing higher-level molecular reasoning. Experimental results demonstrate that MolBasic significantly improves structural comprehension and leads to better outcomes in downstream applications such as property prediction and molecular optimization, supporting the effectiveness of a structure-first approach in molecular language modeling.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03007v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in molecular large language models have led to strong performance on molecular understanding and generation tasks, yet these gains often come without reliable structural grounding. In particular, existing approaches conflict with the chemistry principle that structure determines function: despite their downstream success, current molecular LLMs perform poorly on basic structure recognition, suggesting that they fail to capture molecular graphs from canonical SMILES. To remedy this, we propose MolBasic, a structure-first framework that strengthens structural comprehension via SMILES-Graph translation. MolBasic is built around a multi-level structure perception benchmark, where bidirectional SMILES-Graph conversion serves as the core task to align sequential and topological representations. On top of this foundation, we employ a progressive learning scheme with a standardized Chain-of-Thought (CoT) to steer models from structure acquisition toward higher-level molecular reasoning. Experiments show that MolBasic substantially improves structural understanding and yields robust gains on downstream tasks, including property prediction and objective optimization, supporting our structure-first paradigm.

items.title: Researchers propose HyperVAttention, a training-free sparse attention framework using spatio-temporal clustering to improve efficiency and fidelity in video diffusion transformers, reducing latency by up to 2.13× [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: HyperVAttention: Efficient Sparse Attention with Spatio-Temporal Clustering for Video Diffusion
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced HyperVAttention (HVA), a training-free sparse attention framework designed to enhance efficiency and fidelity in Video Diffusion Transformers (VDiTs) used for high-quality video generation. HVA addresses the limitations of existing clustering-based sparse attention methods by reducing clustering overhead and improving GPU execution efficiency, resulting in up to a 2.13× reduction in latency while maintaining or improving video fidelity.

The framework employs 3D local-window clustering to leverage spatio-temporal locality, restricting centroid searches to fixed neighborhoods and implementing this with a custom Triton kernel for speed. It also uses a hybrid clustering strategy that updates only subsets of tokens at intermediate steps, capitalizing on temporal stability. Additionally, hardware-aware cluster merging optimizes GPU block utilization by aligning clusters with execution tiles, enhancing both computational efficiency and approximation accuracy.

Experiments on text-to-video generation demonstrate that HVA sets a new standard for training-free sparse attention in video diffusion models, effectively balancing speed and quality. This advancement could enable more practical generation of longer-duration, high-fidelity videos using diffusion transformers.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03012v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Video Diffusion Transformers (VDiTs) have demonstrated significant capabilities in high-fidelity video generation. However, their ability to produce long-duration videos is fundamentally constrained by the quadratic complexity of the self-attention mechanism. Recent clustering-based sparse attention methods improve the quality-speed trade-off by grouping semantically similar tokens, but their practical efficiency remains limited by two bottlenecks: substantial clustering overhead and low CTA utilization caused by irregular cluster-induced blocks. We propose HyperVAttention (HVA), a training-free sparse attention framework that addresses both bottlenecks jointly. To reduce clustering overhead, we introduce 3D local-window clustering, which exploits the spatio-temporal locality of video tokens to restrict centroid search to fixed local neighborhoods, and implement it with a custom Triton kernel for efficient execution. We further propose a hybrid clustering strategy that performs full clustering only at anchor steps and updates only subset tokens at intermediate steps, leveraging the temporal stability of cluster assignments across denoising steps. To improve CTA utilization, we present hardware-aware cluster merging that minimizes CTA-aligned execution cost through parallel agglomerative merging, improving block density and approximation fidelity by utilizing idle tile capacity. Together, these components reduce clustering overhead, avoid redundant updates, and better align sparse attention with the fixed tile structure of modern GPU kernels. Experiments on Text-to-Video generation show that HVA establishes a new Pareto frontier for training-free sparse attention in video diffusion, reducing end-to-end latency by up to $2.13\times$ while improving fidelity over existing training-free sparse attention baselines.

items.title: Researchers propose OmniFocus, a training-free query-guided token compression method for audio-visual large language models that improves efficiency and maintains accuracy at 25% token retention [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: OmniFocus: Query-Guided Modality-Balanced Token Compression for Omni-Modal Large Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced OmniFocus, a training-free, query-guided token compression method designed for omni-modal large language models (OmniLLMs) that process both audio and video inputs. OmniFocus independently estimates the importance of tokens in each modality, enabling balanced compression that preserves key information from both audio and video while maintaining their alignment. This approach addresses limitations of previous methods that relied on unimodal guidance and assumed temporal alignment of information density across modalities.

Tests on the Qwen2.5-Omni model family across multiple audio-visual benchmarks demonstrate that OmniFocus achieves strong performance even when retaining only 25% of tokens. For instance, on the DailyOmni benchmark with Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, it maintains 59.40% accuracy and offers up to a 1.38 times speedup in inference compared to using all tokens, highlighting an effective balance between accuracy and computational efficiency.

Existing audio-visual token compression methods often rely on unimodal guidance, overlooking the temporal locality of query-relevant evidence in audio-visual inputs and implicitly assuming that the two modalities share a temporally aligned information density distribution. We propose \textbf{OmniFocus}, a training-free query-guided token compression method for OmniLLMs that performs independent importance estimation for video and audio, enabling a modality-symmetric compression design that preserves modality-specific salient evidence while maintaining audio-visual alignment, thereby mitigating the modality bias issue that can arise from unimodal-guided compression. Experiments on the Qwen2.5-Omni model family across four audio-visual benchmarks show that OmniFocus maintains strong compressed performance at low token retention ratios and outperforms existing baselines on several major benchmark scores at 25\% token retention. On DailyOmni with Qwen2.5-Omni-7B at 25\% token retention, OmniFocus maintains 59.40 accuracy while delivering up to 1.38$\times$ prefill speedup relative to the full-token baseline, highlighting a favorable practical accuracy-efficiency trade-off.

items.title: Researchers propose LACE-SVD, a loss-aware SVD method with cumulative error correction for LLM compression, improving LLaMA-7B performance at high compression ratios [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: LACE-SVD: Loss-Aware SVD with Cumulative Error Correction for LLM Compression
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced LACE-SVD, a novel loss-aware singular value decomposition (SVD) method designed to improve compression of large language models (LLMs) like LLaMA-7B. This approach addresses key limitations of existing SVD-based compression techniques by considering layer-wise loss sensitivity and correcting cumulative errors that propagate through the model's residual stream. LACE-SVD optimizes rank allocation under compression constraints and applies local updates alongside propagation-aware corrections to reduce discrepancies in layer outputs.

Experimental results demonstrate that LACE-SVD significantly outperforms previous methods such as Dobi-SVD, achieving a lower perplexity on the WikiText-2 benchmark at a high compression ratio of 0.6. This advancement offers a more effective way to reduce memory and computational demands of large models without sacrificing performance, supporting more efficient deployment of LLMs across diverse hardware platforms.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03057v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid growth in the parameter scale of large language models (LLMs) has created a strong demand for efficient compression techniques. As a hardware-agnostic and highly compatible approach, low-rank compression has been widely adopted to reduce both memory footprint and computational cost. However, existing SVD-based methods are still largely driven by local reconstruction objectives, overlooking two critical limitations: rank budgets are often allocated without explicitly considering layer-wise loss sensitivity, and local approximation errors can propagate and accumulate through the residual stream, leading to amplified global deviations from the original model. To address these issues, we propose LACE-SVD, a Loss-Aware SVD framework with Cumulative Error correction for LLM compression. LACE-SVD first estimates the calibration negative-log-likelihood increase induced by candidate layer-wise compression ratios and solves a budget-constrained allocation problem to assign rank budgets. It then refines the compressed model with closed-form local updates and introduces a propagation-aware correction for residual-stream output modules, reducing layer-output discrepancy as a proxy for cumulative error propagation. Experimental results demonstrate that at a high compression ratio (0.6), the WikiText-2 PPL of our method on LLaMA-7B (32.57) is significantly better than that of Dobi-SVD (46.18).

items.title: Researchers propose Subspace-Aligned Rewiring (SAR) to extract reasoning-effective updates from large language models' spectral space, improving reasoning, multi-domain training, and model merging with under 1% of parameters [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Spectral Rewiring for Exploration, Purification, and Model Merging
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Subspace-Aligned Rewiring (SAR), a method that improves large language models by extracting reasoning-effective updates concentrated in the model's spectral space. SAR retains these core updates while removing orthogonal components that can suppress reasoning performance or cause interference during multi-domain training and model merging. This approach uses less than 1% of the model's parameters to preserve over 99% of post-training performance and enhances capabilities in mathematical reasoning and coding tasks.

SAR has demonstrated effectiveness across various model families and scales, improving exploration in mathematical reasoning and generalizing to agentic coding benchmarks. It also purifies mixed-domain training updates by restoring suppressed coding abilities without compromising other skills. Additionally, SAR facilitates model merging across different expert domains, achieving better cross-domain generalization than previous methods and outperforming single-domain experts.

Overall, SAR offers a training-free technique to enhance reasoning and multi-domain performance by leveraging the geometry of parameter updates, addressing key deployment challenges in large language models such as performance saturation and capability interference.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03065v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning has become a standard post-training recipe for large language models, but dense full-parameter updates create two deployment-relevant bottlenecks: suppressed reasoning performance, often reflected by premature saturation of test-time scaling, and interference when consolidating multiple capabilities through multi-domain training or model merging. We show that the reasoning-effective component of these updates is largely concentrated in the base model's spectral space, motivating Subspace-Aligned Rewiring (SAR), a post-hoc editing method that retains this spectral core while removing orthogonal components. SAR therefore preserves reasoning gains and filters residual update directions that suppress performance or amplify cross-domain interference. Across several model families and scales, SAR extracts compact reasoning cores using as little as approximately 0.58% of total parameters: it preserves over 99% of post-training performance and improves high-k exploration in mathematical reasoning, and generalizes to agentic coding by improving six of seven open benchmarks on an in-house model. SAR also purifies mixed-domain training updates by releasing suppressed coding capability while maintaining math reasoning and instruction following. It further enables model merging across experts, yielding cross-domain generalization that surpasses previous merging baselines and even the best single-domain experts. Overall, SAR shows that extracting reasoning-effective updates from parameter geometry can serve as a training-free mechanism to improve reasoning and multi-domain performance.

items.title: Researchers propose PixCon, a clean-positive pixel-contrastive learning framework for foundation-model semi-supervised segmentation that guarantees contamination-free positive sets and improves accuracy on Pascal VOC, Cityscapes, and ADE20K [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: PixCon: Clean-Positive Contrastive Learning for Foundation-Model Semi-Supervised Segmentation
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced PixCon, a clean-positive pixel-contrastive learning framework designed for semi-supervised semantic segmentation using foundation models. PixCon ensures contamination-free positive sets by maintaining a per-class memory bank that only includes correctly classified labeled pixels, improving accuracy without adding inference-time parameters or requiring threshold tuning. This approach outperforms or matches strong baselines on datasets like Pascal VOC, Cityscapes, and ADE20K.

The framework leverages a DINOv2 teacher model to generate highly clean pseudo-labels and addresses the issue of contamination in contrastive learning by eliminating false positives in the positive set. Analysis shows that contamination negatively impacts learning, and PixCon's design guarantees zero contamination, enhancing robustness especially as teacher model quality varies. The method achieves consistent improvements in mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) scores, demonstrating its effectiveness as a low-cost, reliable solution for foundation-model semi-supervised segmentation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03068v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Semi-supervised semantic segmentation (SSSS) has long turned on one question, which pseudo-labels to trust, and answered it with ever more careful confidence filtering. Foundation backbones change the regime: with a DINOv2 teacher a strict threshold already retains a measured 98%-clean pseudo-label set, so the accuracy that remains lives not in the filter but in how the embedding space is structured by class. We propose PixCon, a clean-positive pixel-contrastive framework. PixCon maintains a per-class memory bank that admits only labeled pixels the student already classifies correctly, guaranteeing a contamination-free positive set ($\rho_F=0$) by construction, unlike prior contrastive SSSS banks (ReCo, U$^2$PL) built from confidence-filtered pseudo-labels. It is a single branch over a consistency backbone, adds no inference-time parameters, and needs no bank-specific threshold. A first-order analysis of the supervised-InfoNCE gradient explains why contamination hurts: its false-positive term scales as $\rho_F/(1-\rho_F)$, which we measure (0.018 on Pascal, 0.106 on ADE20K) rather than assume. Across Pascal VOC, Cityscapes, and ADE20K, PixCon matches or improves a strong DINOv2-based UniMatch V2 baseline in a compute-matched one-switch protocol: it improves every Pascal-1/8 seed (a per-seed gain of about +0.2 mIoU) and its three-seed mean reaches 87.90, the published UniMatch V2-B figure. Because contamination is already rare under foundation-model teachers, our analysis indicates the $\rho_F=0$ guarantee acts chiefly as robustness as teachers weaken, while the accuracy gain comes from cleaner positive supervision, making clean-positive contrast a robust, low-cost default for foundation-model SSSS.

items.title: Researchers present STELLA, an efficient sensor-to-LLM translation framework for on-device human activity recognition achieving up to 11.83% F1 improvement and real-time inference on edge devices [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: STELLA: Efficient Sensor-to-LLM Translation for On-Device Human Activity Recognition
items.summary:
Researchers have developed STELLA, a new framework that enables efficient on-device human activity recognition (HAR) by translating sensor data into inputs for large language models (LLMs). STELLA uses a lightweight hierarchical tokenizer to compress multi-channel sensor data into compact tokens, which are then processed by a frozen pretrained LLM combined with natural-language prompts for accurate activity classification. This approach reduces the need for extensive LLM adaptation, supports on-device personalization, and maintains privacy by keeping all data and inference local to the device.

STELLA was tested across seven public HAR datasets and eight benchmark settings, achieving up to an 11.83% improvement in F1 score over previous methods. Personalization on the device further improved performance by up to 21.91% as user-specific data accumulated. The framework also outperformed other time-series tokenizers within the same LLM pipeline and demonstrated real-time inference capabilities on mobile and edge devices, highlighting its potential for practical, private, and personalized HAR applications on resource-constrained hardware.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03089v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: HAR is increasingly expected to run continuously on edge devices, yet recent LLM-based methods remain hard to deploy: raw sensor prompts are long, cloud inference adds latency and privacy risk, and fine-tuned LLM pipelines turn general-purpose models into task-specific classifiers. We present STELLA, an efficient sensor-to-LLM translation framework for on-device HAR that shifts the burden from LLM adaptation to sensor tokenization. A lightweight hierarchical tokenizer compresses an entire multi-channel inertial window into a fixed set of compact latent sensor tokens, which are projected into the embedding space of a frozen pretrained LLM and combined with a natural-language prompt for label scoring. This preserves activity-relevant temporal and cross-channel structure while keeping LLM-side computation predictable across sensor configurations. STELLA also supports on-device personalization, adapting only the lightweight tokenizer on small amounts of user-specific labelled data and augmenting inference with a local retrieval context, keeping the LLM, user data, and retrieval on device. Across seven public HAR datasets and eight benchmark settings, STELLA achieves new state-of-the-art performance, improving over prior methods by up to 11.83% F1; on-device personalization yields up to a further 21.91% F1 as user data accumulates after deployment. STELLA also outperforms representative time-series tokenizers under the same LLM pipeline and achieves real-time inference under practical mobile and edge budgets, showing that efficient sensor tokenization is a practical path toward accurate, private, and personalized LLM-based HAR on edge devices.

items.title: Researchers propose Proactive Thinking framework for large language models to pre-compute responses during conversational downtime, improving dialogue efficiency without performance loss [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Don't Wait to Reply: Towards Responsive yet Thoughtful Dialogue through Proactive Thinking
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced a Proactive Thinking framework for large language models (LLMs) that enables these models to pre-compute potential responses during conversational downtime, rather than waiting passively for user input. This approach aims to reduce latency and improve the fluidity of dialogue by allowing the model to anticipate and prepare future content, similar to how humans plan during natural pauses in conversation. The framework includes a training-free baseline that balances efficiency and quality through speculative continual thinking.

To test this method, the researchers adapted three benchmarks into time-aware environments that simulate real-time conversational flow. Their results show that proactive thinking enhances interaction efficiency without sacrificing performance, suggesting a shift toward more intelligent and anticipatory conversational AI systems that operate in real time.
