items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03093v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Thinking has emerged as a critical capability for Large Language Models (LLMs) tackling complex tasks. However, its reactive nature, where reasoning is passively triggered only upon receiving a user response, inevitably introduces latency that compromises conversational fluidity. This stands in sharp contrast to human dialogue, where speakers proactively anticipate and plan future content during natural pauses to ensure seamless interaction. To bridge this gap, we propose Proactive Thinking, a framework that empowers models to pre-compute potential response elements during conversational downtime instead of waiting idly for the next input. We then introduce a training-free baseline that can think ahead by anticipating future states, balancing efficiency and quality through speculative continual thinking. To evaluate this approach in practice, we adapt three benchmarks of varying complexity into time-aware environments that simulate real-time conversational flow. We demonstrate that proactive thinking effectively improves interaction efficiency without compromising performance. Ultimately, this work advocates for a fundamental shift toward more intelligent, anticipatory, and real-time conversational AI.

items.title: Researchers propose Adaptive Credit Policy Optimization (ACPO) using fine-grained surrogate entropy for token-level credit assignment in reinforcement learning, improving performance on reasoning and coding benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: ACPO: Adaptive Credit Policy Optimization via Fine-Grained Surrogate Entropy
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Adaptive Credit Policy Optimization (ACPO), a new framework for token-level credit assignment in reinforcement learning (RL) aimed at improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). ACPO uses a fine-grained surrogate entropy to modulate policy updates, focusing on uncertain decisions in successful outcomes and overconfident tokens in failures, addressing challenges posed by sparse outcome rewards and limitations of existing methods.

The approach provides deterministic entropy bounds and maintains alignment with policy-gradient directions under certain conditions. Experimental results on mathematical reasoning and coding benchmarks, including AIME 2025 and HumanEvalPro, demonstrate that ACPO consistently outperforms established RL baselines such as DAPO, GTPO, and SAPO, highlighting its potential to enhance token-level learning in complex tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03126v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has substantially improved the reasoning ability of large language models (LLMs), but sparse outcome rewards still make token-level credit assignment difficult. Existing scalable RL methods typically assign trajectory-level rewards uniformly across tokens, while recent entropy-aware approaches either rely on coarse detached heuristics or directly optimize true entropy, which can introduce non-local gradient components misaligned with sampled-token policy updates. We propose Adaptive Credit Policy Optimization (ACPO), a token-level credit assignment framework based on a mode-local surrogate entropy. ACPO asymmetrically modulates policy updates by emphasizing uncertain decisions in successful rollouts and overconfident tokens in failed rollouts. We show that the surrogate admits deterministic entropy bounds and, under modal alignment and proximal updates, preserves the policy-gradient direction to leading order. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and coding benchmarks, including AIME 2025 and HumanEvalPro, show that ACPO consistently improves over strong RL baselines such as DAPO, GTPO, and SAPO.

items.title: Researchers introduce CuBAS, a curvature-based adaptive sampling method for supervised classification that improves training set informativeness using geometric complexity across 60+ benchmark datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: CuBAS: Information Geometric Curvature-Based Adaptive Sampling for Supervised Classification
items.summary:
Researchers have developed CuBAS (Curvature-Based Adaptive Sampling), a novel method for supervised classification that enhances the informativeness of training sets by leveraging the geometric complexity of data distributions. CuBAS models labeled datasets as statistical manifolds and uses local curvature, derived from Fisher information, to identify regions of varying complexity. This approach partitions data into low-curvature clusters and high-curvature decision boundaries, enabling the selection of compact, highly informative training subsets.

The method constructs a k-nearest-neighbor graph and computes curvature scores using the Potts Markov random field model, allowing efficient and interpretable sampling. Evaluations on over 60 benchmark datasets show that CuBAS consistently outperforms random and uncertainty-based sampling strategies across different labeling budgets and classifier types. CuBAS is computationally efficient and grounded in differential geometry, offering a theoretically sound and practical tool for improving supervised learning.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03145v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The informativeness of a training set is as consequential as its size, yet most sampling strategies remain agnostic to the intrinsic geometry of the data distribution. We introduce CuBAS (Curvature-Based Adaptive Sampling), an information-geometric framework for adaptive data selection in supervised classification, grounded in the q-state Potts Markov random field (MRF) model. The central insight is that a labeled dataset can be viewed as a statistical manifold, on which local curvature, estimated via the ratio of second to first-order observed Fisher information, faithfully encodes the geometric complexity of the data distribution. We construct a k-nearest-neighbor graph over the labeled data and derive a closed-form curvature score at each vertex from the Potts sufficient statistics. This curvature signal partitions the graph into two complementary regimes: low-curvature regions, corresponding to smooth, homogeneous clusters, and high-curvature regions, concentrated around decision boundaries that are disproportionately informative for classification. By selecting nodes from both regimes, CuBAS constructs compact yet maximally informative training subsets. Empirical evaluation across more than 60 benchmark datasets demonstrates consistent and statistically significant improvements over random sampling and uncertainty-based baselines, across a wide range of labeling budgets and classifier architectures. CuBAS is computationally efficient (linear in the number of k-NN graph edges), theoretically grounded in the differential geometry of statistical manifolds, and interpretable in terms of the local shape operator of the data manifold.

items.title: Researchers propose Threshold Gating as a universal primitive for neural network nonlinearity, demonstrating equivalence to standard activations and enabling efficient training and hardware implementation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Rethinking Neural Nonlinearity as Gating
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Threshold Gating (TG) as a universal primitive for neural network nonlinearity, demonstrating that common activation functions like ReLU, Sigmoid, and Softmax can be represented as instances of TG. This approach preserves model performance across various architectures, including CNNs, transformers, and recurrent networks, without requiring retraining. TG also supports training from scratch, offering improvements in model compression, performance, and training efficiency.

The study further proposes a 'Minimal Branch Theorem' linking the number of TG branches to neural network trainability. Additionally, TG facilitates a unified hardware implementation for analog in-memory systems, potentially reducing power consumption and chip area by addressing bottlenecks associated with analog-to-digital and digital-to-analog converters.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03148v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Activation functions are considered an essential primitive for neural nonlinearity, i.e., they enable neural networks to serve as universal approximators. In this paper, we show that this nonlinearity can also be achieved by input-conditioned threshold gating through branches as a universal primitive. We demonstrate that standard activations -- whether piecewise-linear (ReLU, PReLU, Hardtanh) or smooth (SiLU, Sigmoid, Tanh, GELU) -- are in fact instances of a single Threshold Gating (TG) primitive. For softmax, we show that it admits an exact TG conversion via its equivalent per-element Sigmoid form. We then validate these equivalences by converting pretrained networks across CNNs, transformer-based models, and recurrent architectures, preserving model performance without requiring retraining. Threshold Gating also enables training from scratch that goes beyond replacing existing activations, enabling gains in model compression, performance, and shorter training. We also propose a 'Minimal Branch Theorem' which relates the minimum number of required branches in our primitive to the trainability of general deep neural networks. In terms of hardware implementation, TG maps to a unified implementation in the case of analog in-memory systems, addressing the bottleneck of analog-to-digital and digital-to-analog converters (ADC/DAC) that is known to significantly impact power consumption and on-chip area.

items.title: Researchers propose DMKGC, a conditional diffusion-guided framework for multi-domain knowledge graph completion, improving tail entity prediction by 4.3% MRR across 14 KGs and 3 benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Conditional Diffusion Guided Knowledge Transfer for Multi-Domain Knowledge Graph Completion
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced DMKGC, a novel conditional diffusion-guided framework designed to enhance multi-domain knowledge graph completion (MKGC). This approach improves the prediction of missing triples in a target knowledge graph by transferring knowledge from multiple support graphs without compromising domain-specific information. DMKGC treats each knowledge graph as a partial view of an entity's full information and generates domain-general embeddings through diffusion models conditioned on support graphs, achieving a 4.3% average improvement in mean reciprocal rank (MRR) for tail entity prediction across 14 knowledge graphs and three benchmarks.

The framework initializes domain-agnostic entity embeddings and encodes them within individual graphs before fusing equivalent entities from support graphs to guide the diffusion process. This method ensures unbiased generation of embeddings while preserving domain-specific characteristics, addressing limitations of previous approaches that enforced strict consistency constraints and risked losing contextual information. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DMKGC maintains performance gains even in low-resource data scenarios, highlighting its effectiveness in knowledge transfer across diverse domains.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03154v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-domain knowledge graph completion (MKGC) aims to improve missing triple prediction in a target KG by transferring knowledge from other support KGs. Existing methods typically enforce consistency constraints on equivalent entities across KGs to transfer knowledge, which risks suppressing domain-specific contextual information of entities. This design can also compromise entity representation information from all KG domains, impeding performance improvements, especially in low-resource data scenarios. To address this, we pioneer a generation-based paradigm for MKGC and propose DMKGC, a conditional diffusion-guided knowledge transfer framework. Our key insight is to treat each KG as a partial view of the entity entire information, and generate informative domain-general entity embeddings through diffusion models conditioned on support KGs. Particularly, we first initialize domain-agnostic entity embeddings as prior entity embeddings, and then encode them within individual KGs. Afterward, we fuse equivalent entities from support KGs as the conditional diffusion generation guidance. We leverage the prior entity embeddings as the proxy generation objective, which ensures this conditional generation to be unbiased towards any conditioned KGs. Simultaneously, we also train the generated embeddings to be predictive across KGs, thus preserving domain-specific information. Extensive experiments on 14 KGs in 3 benchmarks demonstrate a 4.3\% average MRR improvement in tail entity prediction over state-of-the-art methods, with sustained gains in low-resource data settings.

items.title: Study compares algorithm specification formats for language models implementing machine learning tasks, finding LaTeX pseudocode most effective under core information settings [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Which Algorithm Specification Formats Help Language Models Implement Machine Learning Algorithms?
items.summary:
A study published on arXiv investigates how different algorithm specification formats affect the accuracy of large language models (LLMs) when implementing machine learning algorithms. The research compares formats including ordinary prose, LaTeX pseudocode, Markdown, YAML, JSON, and Python code stubs across multiple tasks and models, analyzing 4,020 generated implementations. The findings reveal that LaTeX algorithm-style pseudocode yields the highest accuracy under core information conditions, while YAML and prose formats also perform well; code stubs do not consistently improve correctness despite defining function signatures.

The study evaluates critical implementation details such as tie-breaking, array shapes, numerical rules, return structures, and handling of invalid inputs. Under complete information settings, some models like GPT-5.4 mini show no significant differences between formats, whereas others still do. The results suggest that authors should explicitly specify interfaces, computation steps, numerical rules, and boundary-case behaviors rather than relying on the format alone to convey these details.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03158v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to implement algorithms from research manuscripts, but papers often leave implementation choices implicit. This study examines how the written format of an algorithm specification affects first-pass LLM implementation accuracy. We compare ordinary prose, LaTeX algorithm-style pseudocode, PDF-like extracted pseudocode, Markdown fields, YAML-like specifications, JSON-like specifications, and Python code stubs across five machine learning tasks, three models, and four experimental settings, yielding 4,020 generated implementations. Hidden tests evaluate details that often determine correctness, including tie-breaking, array shapes, numerical rules, return structures, and invalid-input behavior. Under the core-information setting, LaTeX algorithm-style pseudocode has the largest average format effect, with YAML-like specifications and ordinary prose close behind. Under complete information, GPT-5.4 mini shows no format differences in the matched comparisons, whereas Gemma 3 4B and Llama 3.2 3B still do. Code stubs do not consistently improve correctness despite specifying the function signature. The results support a writing recommendation: authors should state the interface, computation steps, numerical rules, and boundary-case behavior explicitly, instead of relying on a particular surface format to carry those details.

items.title: Study examines GPT-5.2 Spanish-Chinese journalistic translation quality under 48 prompt conditions, finding translation theory-driven prompts reduce awkward style errors but prompt language has minimal impact [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Role of Prompt Language and Translation-Theory-Driven Prompts in Large Language Models: A Case Study on Spanish-Chinese Journalistic Translation
items.summary:
A study investigated the impact of prompt language and translation theory-driven prompt design on the quality of Spanish-Chinese journalistic translations produced by GPT-5.2. Using a parallel corpus of four editorials from El Pais, translations were generated under 48 different conditions varying prompt types and languages. Evaluation through automated metrics and human assessment revealed that while automated measures favored a baseline prompt, human evaluators preferred a brief-oriented prompt, highlighting differences in evaluation methods. The study found that prompts informed by translation theory helped reduce awkward style errors, though unidiomatic expressions remained common, and the language of the prompt had little effect on translation quality.

These findings suggest that incorporating translation theory into prompt design can enhance translation quality in expert evaluations, particularly for journalistic texts. However, the study notes that the educational benefits of such prompts for language learners are still uncertain and require further research involving user-based studies to validate their effectiveness.

A parallel corpus of four editorials from El Pais was translated under 48 experimental conditions (4 prompt types, 3 prompt languages, and 4 articles). Translation quality was assessed using BLEU and BERTScore-F1 for automated evaluation, alongside human evaluation based on the Multidimensional Quality Metrics (MQM) framework. Automated metrics identified the baseline prompt (BASE) as the best-performing condition, whereas human evaluation ranked the brief-oriented prompt (BRIEF) highest (MQM: 8.66 vs. 7.84), a reversal likely attributable to the single-reference constraint inherent in automated measures. Sub-error type analysis revealed that translation theory-driven prompts selectively reduced Awkward style errors, while Unidiomatic style errors persisted across conditions. Prompt language had a negligible impact under both evaluation paradigms. These results indicate that translation theory-driven prompts can yield measurable quality gains under expert evaluation of journalistic translations, although their pedagogical implications for language learners remain suggestive and require validation through user-based studies.

Using a parallel corpus of four editorials from El Pais, translations were generated under 48 different conditions varying prompt types and languages. Evaluation through automated metrics and human assessment revealed that while automated measures favored a baseline prompt, human evaluators preferred a brief-oriented prompt, highlighting differences in evaluation methods. The study found that prompts informed by translation theory helped reduce awkward style errors, though unidiomatic expressions remained common, and the language of the prompt had little effect on translation quality.

These findings suggest that incorporating translation theory into prompt design can enhance translation quality in expert evaluations, particularly for journalistic texts. However, the study notes that the educational benefits of such prompts for language learners are still uncertain and require further research involving user-based studies to validate their effectiveness.

items.title: Researchers analyze decentralised federated learning over temporal networks, finding structural and temporal heterogeneities slow convergence compared to typical experimental scenarios [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Decentralised Federated Learning over Temporal Networks: The Role of Heterogeneities
items.summary:
Researchers have examined decentralised federated learning, a peer-to-peer approach for on-device machine learning model training that enhances privacy and communication efficiency without a single point of failure. Their study reveals that structural and temporal heterogeneities in communication networks significantly slow the convergence of the learning process compared to typical experimental setups, which often overlook these factors. The learning dynamics correspond to a lazy random-walk diffusion on temporal networks, highlighting the impact of real-world network irregularities on training speed.

By analyzing real-world temporal networks, the researchers found that these inhomogeneities commonly cause a marked slowdown in diffusion and thus in the convergence of the federated learning process. This insight challenges the optimistic convergence rates reported in many experimental scenarios and underscores the need to consider network heterogeneity for more accurate assessments of decentralised federated learning performance.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03171v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Decentralised federated learning, based on peer-to-peer communication, is increasingly proposed for on-device training of machine learning models, promising a privacy-preserving, communication-efficient training process with no risk of single-point failure. However, the role of structural and temporal inhomogeneities in such fully decentralised settings remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate their effects when model parameters are locally averaged during aggregation. We show that the decentralised federated learning process is governed, both in the early phase and the late, stationary limit, by the same dynamics as a lazy random-walk diffusion process on temporal networks. Based on this mapping, we demonstrate that the typical experimental scenario used in decentralised federated learning leads to unrealistically rapid convergence because of ignoring the temporal and structural inhomogeneities inherent in the communication network. We analyse real-world temporal networks and find that inhomogeneities most often dramatically slow down diffusion, hence the convergence process.

items.title: Researchers introduce CRRL, a causality-based reinforcement learning framework that trains autonomous system policies to collaborate with rule-based recovery, improving navigation and reducing stalled states in driving scenarios [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: CRRL: A Causality-Based Reinforcement Learning Framework for Autonomous System Recovery
items.summary:
Researchers have developed CRRL, a causality-based reinforcement learning framework designed to improve autonomous system recovery by training policies that effectively collaborate with rule-based recovery mechanisms. This approach addresses the limitations of traditional reinforcement learning, which often stalls in failure states and struggles to generalize to new scenarios, by incorporating causal relations from driving logs to help the system anticipate and respond to stalled states. CRRL integrates sensor data collection, causal model construction, and hybrid policy training to enhance navigation performance and reduce immobilization during driving tasks.

Evaluated through a comprehensive ablation study across multiple driving scenarios, CRRL demonstrated significant improvements in reward, distance traveled, and velocity compared to conventional methods. Notably, in roundabout navigation tests, nearly half of the episodes required no recovery intervention, indicating the framework's effectiveness in producing robust policies that cooperate seamlessly with rule-based safety components. These findings suggest that causal-guided training can enhance the reliability and adaptability of autonomous driving systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03177v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Traditional reinforcement learning (RL) for recovery in autonomous systems lacks causal understanding and generalizes poorly to novel failure scenarios. RL policies often stall in failure states, spending up to 70% of an episode immobilized. Rule-based recovery alone is inadequate, and adding heuristic recovery to a pretrained PPO policy worsens rewards because policies cannot coordinate well with unanticipated interventions. The issue is not missing recovery mechanisms but a lack of policies trained to collaborate with them. We introduce CRRL, a causal-guided RL framework that trains policies to work effectively with rule-based recovery. The recovery detects stalled states and assists the agent. Causal relations from driving logs shape the training signal, teaching the policy to anticipate stalls and adjust actions in recovery contexts. The framework follows MAPE-K, with sensor collection, causal model construction, and hybrid RL policy training corresponding to Monitor, Analyze, and Plan/Execute, respectively. We evaluate CRRL through a four-condition ablation study across three driving scenarios, with 20 episodes per condition. We find that causal training significantly improves reward, distance, and velocity. Moreover, 9 of 20 roundabout episodes required zero recovery intervention, confirming navigation competence. These results show that causal-guided training produces effective RL policies that cooperate with rule-based safety components.

items.title: Researchers develop ParMaxFEM, a parallelized C++ implementation of MaxFEM for scalable maximal frequent episode mining integrated into Desbordante, achieving up to 35× speedup on 8 cores
items.originalTitle: Scalable Maximal Frequent Episode Mining with Desbordante
items.summary:
Researchers have developed ParMaxFEM, a parallelized C++ implementation of the MaxFEM algorithm for maximal frequent episode mining, integrated into the open-source data profiler Desbordante. This new approach addresses the computational challenges of mining frequently appearing subsequences by improving performance and scalability, achieving up to an 8× speedup over the original SPMF implementation and up to 35× speedup using 8-core parallelization.

ParMaxFEM enhances the original MaxFEM by applying efficient pruning techniques and parallel processing, enabling faster discovery of maximal frequent episodes in event sequences. The integration with Desbordante allows users to treat patterns as first-class entities and supports custom program development for pattern discovery and validation, making the tool more accessible and versatile for data analysis tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03188v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Episode mining aims to extract subsequences of events that possess certain distinctive properties and constitute facts valuable to the user. Maximal frequent episode mining concentrates on discovery of frequently-appearing subsequences, which are not included into any other larger frequent subsequence. The state-of-the-art for this problem is the MaxFEM algorithm which enumerates possible subsequences, while applying various pruning techniques to accelerate the search. However, this is a computationally-intensive problem: reducing the minimum number of required subsequence occurrences or increasing the length of the subsequence both substantially raise running time, which limits practical use of MaxFEM. In this paper we describe our efforts in designing a high-performing algorithm for this problem. For this we: 1) develop an efficient C++ implementation of MaxFEM, and 2) devise an efficient technique to parallelizing it. As the result, we propose an improved parallel MaxFEM variant, which we call ParMaxFEM. Additionally, we integrate the improved algorithm into Desbordante - a high-performance, open-source data profiler with deep Python integration that treats patterns as first-class entities and allows users to develop their custom programs that can include discovery and validation of patterns. To evaluate our approach we compare both C++ implementations with the original SPMF implementation. Experiments demonstrated that our reimplemented version provides up to $8\times$ speedup over the SPMF baseline, while our parallelization technique provides up to $35\times$ improvement overall (on 8 cores).

items.title: Researchers propose a Bayesian framework using conditional variational autoencoders to evaluate scenario compatibility and structural uncertainty in generative population synthesis for transportation planning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A Bayesian Framework for Evaluating Scenario Compatibility in Generative Population Synthesis
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a Bayesian framework using conditional variational autoencoders to assess the compatibility of scenario targets with generative population synthesis models in transportation planning. This approach quantifies how well future aggregate population assumptions align with the structural patterns learned by generative models, addressing uncertainties that arise when imposing scenario constraints. The framework uses an ensemble of population realizations and Bayesian updating to measure scenario feasibility and the impact on structural uncertainty.

The method involves training a population-aware conditional variational autoencoder to capture plausible population structures while maintaining aggregate accuracy. Scenario targets are incorporated as probabilistic evidence, and their compatibility is evaluated through effective sample size metrics that reflect the concentration of posterior distributions. Experiments show that scenario effects depend on both the magnitude of targets and their alignment with the model's learned structure, revealing potential failures when targets fall outside the model's support.

This probabilistic diagnostic tool offers transportation planners a way to evaluate the feasibility and structural consistency of scenarios before proceeding with projections and planning, potentially improving the reliability of scenario-based analyses in transportation systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03190v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scenario-based transportation analysis specifies future assumptions through aggregate population targets, whereas generative population synthesis models produce detailed individual-level realizations. When scenario targets are imposed on generative models, current practice relies on deterministic marginal calibration, implicitly assuming that the targets are compatible with the model's learned structural support. However, whether scenario-level constraints lie within the generative support--and how strongly they distort structural uncertainty--remains largely unexamined. We propose an ensemble-based Bayesian updating framework to quantify scenario compatibility in conditional population synthesis. A population-aware conditional variational autoencoder is developed to learn a distribution over plausible population structures while preserving aggregate fidelity. An ensemble of realizations sampled from the learned prior provides an empirical approximation of structural uncertainty. Scenario targets are treated as probabilistic evidence over aggregate statistics, and posterior weights are obtained through Bayesian updating across the ensemble. Scenario compatibility is quantified using effective sample size (ESS), which measures posterior concentration and the compression of structural uncertainty induced by conditioning. Experiments demonstrate that scenario impact depends not only on target magnitude but also on alignment with the learned joint structure, and reveal structural failure modes when targets fall outside prior ensemble support. The proposed framework provides a probabilistic diagnostic model for evaluating scenario feasibility and structural consistency before downstream projection and transportation planning.

items.title: Researchers develop a vision-language agent for self-specializing calibration of superconducting transmon chips using a physics-grounded simulation environment and gradient-free online adaptation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Self-Specializing Vision-Language Transmon Chip Calibration in a Physics-Grounded Environment
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a vision-language agent designed to autonomously calibrate superconducting transmon chips by integrating a physics-grounded simulation environment with gradient-free online adaptation. This agent sequentially selects experiments, interprets ambiguous data, and updates its calibration strategy without weight updates, effectively managing noise, drift, and limited experimental budgets. The approach includes a realistic simulation of chip behavior, an agent that processes visual and textual information to maintain calibration, and an adaptation mechanism that refines performance based on past anomalies.

Testing on challenging chips demonstrated significant improvements in gate fidelity and reduced variance, with the agent successfully diagnosing hardware faults without direct access to ground truth. The system's scoring and reward mechanisms are transferable to real hardware, indicating potential for practical deployment in quantum device calibration.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03193v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Calibrating a superconducting transmon chip is a sequential decision problem under noise, drift, and a finite budget: an expert must choose experiments, read ambiguous plots, judge fit quality, and revise stale beliefs as the chip drifts. We study whether a vision-language agent can close this loop and specialize itself to one physical device without weight updates, via three co-designed artifacts. The first is a physics-grounded simulation environment for transmon chips: calibration observables derive from circuit-quantized parameters via scqubits, with realistic flux-line distortion, wall-time-scaled and mid-scan drift, and gate leakage, concerns a toy simulator would omit; each tool call advances a modeled clock so drift accrues by wall time, not call count. The second is a vision-language agent that runs the loop end to end, calling tools, reading plots, maintaining a structured notebook, and submitting parameters without hidden truth, scored against hidden parameters and gate fidelities measured on the device. The third is gradient-free online adaptation: a reflector reads truth-free anomaly signatures from past attempts and grows a small, human-readable device note appended to the prompt, admitted by a paired-snapshot accept gate that isolates strategy improvement from drift. On a hard-tier chip under budget pressure, six iterations raised the worst-case CZ fidelity from 0.678 to 0.787 and cut its variance, reproducing at four-qubit scale; a single accepted note raised CZ fidelity from 0.678 to 0.913 on its paired snapshot. A planted-fault study confirms the note is causal, diagnosing a hardware fault truth-free, its principal value raising the failure floor and cutting variance. The agent, scoring, and reward transfer to real hardware via a measurement-backend swap; only the accept gate is a simulation affordance, reducing to a held-out-slice or repeat-and-average form.

items.originalTitle: OpenGlass: A Sensing-Computing Split Architecture for Local MLLM-Driven Real-Time Visual Assistance
items.summary:
OpenGlass is an open-source system designed to provide real-time visual assistance with a focus on privacy and low latency, primarily benefiting blind and low-vision users. It uses a split architecture where an ESP32-based unit on wearable glasses captures visual data, while a nearby consumer device performs local multimodal large language model (MLLM) inference and speech output. This approach minimizes reliance on cloud services, keeping sensitive visual data on user-controlled devices and reducing network delays.

The system achieves median user-to-audio response times under two seconds in most trials, supporting tasks such as obstacle awareness, sign and object queries, and image quality checks. OpenGlass is intended as a reference platform rather than a certified navigation aid, and its developers have released the source code, hardware instructions, prompts, evaluation data, and logs to encourage further research and development in privacy-focused assistive technologies.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03213v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present OpenGlass, an open-source, privacy-oriented, local-first system for low-latency multimodal visual assistance, with a primary focus on blind and low-vision users. We evaluate response quality, query-ready-to-audio latency, safety-aware abstention, and auditable logs. Under real ESP32 Wi-Fi capture, OpenGlass reaches 993 ms median user-to-audio latency with resized payloads and 1625 ms with raw 1280 x 720 payloads; 97.5% and 93.3% of trials fall below 2 s, respectively. OpenGlass is a user-initiated visual-assistance reference platform for obstacle/hazard awareness, sign/object queries, and image-quality self-checking, rather than a certified navigation aid. We release source code, hardware instructions, prompts, evaluation data, and logs.

items.title: Researchers propose unbiased alignment methods for large language models using Unbiased Reward Model and Direct Preference Optimization losses to handle noisy human preference data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Unbiased Alignment for Large Language Models with Noisy Preferences
items.summary:
Researchers have developed new methods to improve the alignment of large language models with human preferences by addressing the issue of noisy data in preference datasets. They introduced the Unbiased Reward Model (URM) loss and the Unbiased Direct Preference Optimization (UDPO) loss, which mathematically correct distortions caused by noise, enabling unbiased training without the need for clean ground-truth data. These approaches have been theoretically validated for noise tolerance and compatibility, and experimental results show they outperform existing state-of-the-art methods across various datasets.

The proposed framework offers a robust solution to the challenges posed by real-world noisy preference data, which commonly affects reinforcement learning from human feedback and direct preference optimization techniques. By providing rigorous theoretical analysis and practical code availability, this work advances the reliability and effectiveness of aligning language models with human values and preferences.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03248v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The alignment of large language models with human preferences is commonly achieved through Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback or Direct Preference Optimization. However, these methods are vulnerable to the significant noise prevalent in real-world preference datasets. To address this critical issue, we present a theoretical framework for unbiased alignment, introducing the Unbiased Reward Model (URM) loss and the Unbiased Direct Preference Optimization (UDPO) loss. By mathematically correcting the distortion induced by preference noise, our novel objectives enable unbiased model training directly from noisy datasets, without requiring clean ground-truth supervision. We provide rigorous theoretical analyses demonstrating that our methods are noise-tolerant, parameter downward compatible, and classification-calibrated. Comprehensive experiments across diverse datasets demonstrate that our approaches outperform state-of-the-art baselines. Code available at: https://github.com/cswjl/unbiased-alignment.

items.title: Researchers release WorldTensor, a harmonised global dataset integrating environmental and socioeconomic data on a 0.25° grid for Earth system foundation model training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A harmonised dataset for Earth system foundation models
items.summary:
Researchers have developed WorldTensor, a harmonised global dataset that integrates hundreds of environmental and socioeconomic variables onto a standardized 0.25° spatial grid with an annual temporal framework. This dataset combines diverse data sources including climate, land, ocean, cryosphere, infrastructure, hazards, and socioeconomic indicators, addressing the lack of unified training resources for Earth system foundation models that consider both physical and human systems.

WorldTensor was created by regridding inputs from various resolutions and projections, converting point and vector data into gridded fields, and aligning temporal coverages from daily to multiyear observations. The dataset is distributed as NetCDF files with standardized metadata, providing a reproducible resource designed to support machine learning workflows for training and evaluating models that capture coupled dynamics across environmental and human systems at a planetary scale.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03298v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Foundation models for Earth systems have so far been trained primarily on physical climate and weather data, with limited representation of the human systems that both drive and respond to environmental change. The lack of a unified global training resource that combines climate, land, ocean, cryosphere, infrastructure, hazards, and socioeconomic data on a common grid hinders progress toward truly multimodal Earth system foundation models. We present WorldTensor, a harmonised global dataset that aligns hundreds of environmental and socioeconomic variables to a standardised 0.25$^\circ$ spatial grid and annual temporal framework. WorldTensor integrates reanalysis products, remote sensing, emissions inventories, land use reconstructions, hydrological observations, infrastructure and hazard datasets, and socioeconomic indicators within a single representation designed for machine learning workflows. To build the dataset, we regridded inputs across heterogeneous native resolutions and projections, rasterised point and vector datasets into spatially meaningful gridded fields, and reconciled temporal coverages ranging from daily observations to sparse multiyear socioeconomic snapshots. All outputs are distributed as NetCDF files with standardised coordinates, variable metadata, and a common CF metadata convention. WorldTensor provides a reproducible resource for training and evaluating foundation models that learn coupled dynamics across environmental and human systems at planetary scale.

items.title: Researchers present an automated pipeline using DeepSeek V3 to extract structured legal reasoning and control citation hallucinations in 330,000 Italian tax-court judgments [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: From Judgments to Issues: Structured Extraction of Legal Reasoning with Citation-Hallucination Control
items.summary:
Researchers have developed an automated pipeline that breaks down approximately 330,000 Italian tax-court judgments into individual legal issues and extracts structured XML representations based on the IRAC framework and legal syllogism. This system uses the DeepSeek V3 model to efficiently process the large corpus while incorporating a hallucination-detection filter to verify legal citations against a dedicated parser, ensuring accuracy in referencing.

The pipeline was validated on 50 judgments annotated by tax law experts, demonstrating strong agreement between the model and human annotators in issue extraction and citation accuracy. This approach represents the first expert-validated, issue-level structured extraction system with hallucination control for Italian tax-court decisions, enabling applications such as issue-level retrieval, citation-network analysis, and the creation of extensive datasets for legal reasoning research.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03325v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present an automated pipeline that decomposes Italian tax-court judgments into individual legal issues and extracts, for each issue, a structured XML representation grounded in the IRAC framework and the legal syllogism. The pipeline targets a corpus of approximately $330{,}000$ first- and second-instance decisions of the Italian tax courts and is built around a capable yet cost-efficient general-purpose model (DeepSeek V3), a choice driven by the need to process several hundred thousand documents at a sustainable cost. To address the well-documented unreliability of large language models on legal citations, we couple the extraction step with an automatic hallucination-detection filter that compares the references produced by the model with those identified in the judgment text by a dedicated parser (Linkoln), normalised to standard identifiers (URN-NIR, ECLI, CELEX). We validate the pipeline on $50$ judgments annotated by two PhDs in tax law, computing inter-annotator agreement and LLM-vs-expert agreement on both issue extraction and legal citations, together with a stand-alone evaluation of the hallucination filter. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first issue-level, expert-validated structured extraction pipeline with hallucination control for Italian tax-court decisions, and it provides a concrete starting point for downstream applications such as issue-level retrieval, citation-network analysis, and the construction of large-scale datasets of legal reasoning.

items.title: Researchers present SPORK, a training-free controller that accelerates agentic LLM inference by speculatively forking tool calls, reducing Qwen3-32B's GAIA P95 latency by 18% without accuracy loss [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SPORK: Self-Speculative Forking to Accelerate Agentic LLM Inference
items.summary:
Researchers have developed SPORK, a training-free controller designed to accelerate inference in agentic large language models (LLMs) by speculatively forking tool calls. This approach reduces the latency of Qwen3-32B's GAIA P95 by 18% without compromising accuracy. SPORK works by predicting upcoming tool calls early in the generation process, allowing tool execution to overlap with ongoing reasoning, thereby minimizing idle GPU time.

SPORK leverages the model itself as a predictor, achieving high accuracy in forecasting tool usage across multiple benchmarks. It incorporates a cost model and mechanisms such as prefix-cache forks, confidence gates, and partial-token acceptance to optimize speculation and handle mispredictions gracefully. The system falls back to serial execution if speculation fails, ensuring correctness is maintained.

The method is effective across various model sizes and architectures, including dense and mixture-of-experts models, and maintains task accuracy within one percentage point of baseline performance. SPORK operates as a lightweight controller over standard completion APIs without requiring retraining or auxiliary models, making it suitable for immediate deployment. The project is open source and available for use and further development.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03333v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLM agents are becoming a common interface for research, coding, and question answering, yet their Thought-Action-Observation loop is often serial: the model reasons, emits a tool call, then idles the GPU until the result returns. This wait consumes 16-37% of wall time in our workloads and 35-61% in prior reports. Speculative tool execution can hide this wait, but existing systems need auxiliary predictors, historical traces, or static workflow graphs, leaving a gap for training-free, day-one deployment. We observe that the model can be its own predictor: a probe forked at the start of generation predicts Qwen3-32B's upcoming tool name with 74.6-99.6% accuracy across five benchmarks. We present SPORK (Self-sPeculative fORKing), a training-free controller that dispatches the speculated tool call early, overlapping its execution with the remaining chain-of-thought decode. A cost model captures when speculation breaks even, and each component improves one of its terms: a prefix-cache fork cuts probe cost, a confidence gate filters mispredictions, and partial-token accept turns rejected probes into speculative-decoding drafts. On acceptance, the tool result is ready when reasoning ends; on rejection, SPORK falls back to serial execution with no correctness penalty. On real-tool benchmarks, SPORK cuts Qwen3-32B's GAIA P95 by 18% (131.9 to 108.1 s); the mechanism holds across model sizes from 4B to 32B and across dense and mixture-of-experts models, with task accuracy within 1 pp of baseline or better wherever measured. SPORK deploys as a thin controller over standard completion APIs (no retraining, no auxiliary models, no offline traces) and is orthogonal to token-level speculative decoding. SPORK is open source at https://github.com/baihuajun24/spork.

items.title: Researchers present FedAvg algorithm results for Human Activity Recognition, analyzing trade-offs between personalized and generalized accuracy under varying client data conditions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: FedAvg for HAR: Exploring the Tradeoff Between Personalized and Generalization Accuracy
items.summary:
Researchers have evaluated the FedAvg algorithm within the Human Activity Recognition (HAR) domain to explore the balance between personalized and generalized model accuracy in federated learning. Their study compares centralized, local, and federated learning approaches, including scenarios simulating changes in client data distribution. The results indicate that while FedAvg generally offers improved personalization alongside strong generalization compared to traditional centralized learning, this advantage diminishes under challenging conditions such as varying class distributions across clients.

The research involved designing multiple testing scenarios to assess performance trade-offs, highlighting the complexities of maintaining both personalization and generalization in federated learning environments. These findings underscore the need for careful consideration of client data variability when deploying federated learning models in real-world applications.

items.title: Researchers propose PedestrianDiffusion, a multimodal generative denoising framework for dense 6D inertial navigation state estimation with state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: PedestrianDiffusion: Multimodal Generative Denoising and Dense State Estimation for Inertial Navigation
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced PedestrianDiffusion, a novel multimodal generative framework designed to improve dense 6D inertial navigation state estimation. This approach addresses the limitations of consumer-grade inertial navigation caused by noise in Micro-Electro-Mechanical Systems (MEMS) by reformulating state estimation as a continuous conditional denoising process in the frequency domain. The method incorporates a zero-shot semantic conditioning mechanism using vision-language embeddings to adapt to diverse sensor noise profiles and employs a single-step deterministic solver to enable efficient asynchronous batch trajectory refinement on edge devices.

Extensive testing on multiple benchmarks, including OxIOD, RIDI, RoNIN, and TLIO, demonstrates that PedestrianDiffusion achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and robustness against impulse disturbances and kinematic drift. This work offers a comprehensive algorithmic foundation for the development of next-generation Neural Inertial Measurement Units (N-IMUs), potentially advancing the performance and reliability of inertial navigation systems in consumer applications.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03349v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The accuracy of consumer-grade inertial navigation is bottlenecked by the stochastic noise of Micro-Electro-Mechanical Systems (MEMS). Traditional deterministic neural architectures often succumb to ``estimation jittering,'' sacrificing high-frequency kinematic fidelity for numerical stability. We propose PedestrianDiffusion, a multimodal spectral-domain generative framework reformulating dense 6D state estimation as a continuous conditional denoising process. By operating in the frequency domain, our formulation bounds the spectral covariance, acting as a mathematical preconditioner to stabilize the reverse diffusion trajectory. Furthermore, we introduce a zero-shot semantic conditioning mechanism leveraging vision-language embeddings as categorical priors to generalize across heterogeneous sensor noise profiles. To address the computational intractability of generative tracking, we deploy a single-step deterministic probability flow ODE solver ($T=1$). This yields high-capacity asynchronous batch trajectory refinement, establishing the viability of generative architectures for asynchronous batch trajectory refinement on edge hardware. Extensive evaluations on the OxIOD, RIDI, RoNIN, and TLIO benchmarks demonstrate that PedestrianDiffusion achieves state-of-the-art performance, exhibiting unprecedented robustness to impulse perturbations and coupled 6D kinematic drift. This work provides a rigorous algorithmic blueprint for next-generation Neural Inertial Measurement Units (N-IMUs).

items.title: Researchers propose spectral shape-based metrics to manage and quantify large language models using weight empirical spectral density, enabling lineage tracking and performance analysis across diverse open-source LLMs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Spectral Signatures of Large Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced spectral shape-based metrics to manage and quantify large language models (LLMs) by analyzing the empirical spectral density of model weights. This approach, grounded in Heavy-Tailed Self-Regularization theory, provides a compact spectral signature that captures intrinsic properties of pretrained models and remains stable after training, facilitating model-level analysis without relying on task-specific benchmarks. The method is data-free, computationally efficient, and scale-invariant, making it suitable for large-scale evaluation across diverse LLM architectures and training procedures.

The team compiled a comprehensive corpus of major open-source LLM families to benchmark spectral and non-spectral metrics across various models and downstream tasks. Their findings demonstrate that the spectral signature can effectively track model lineage, cluster similar models without supervision, and serve as a proxy for assessing model performance. This metric offers a practical tool for organizing, comparing, and analyzing extensive collections of LLMs, addressing challenges in model management, licensing, and evaluation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03377v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapidly growing repository of publicly available large language models (LLMs) presents significant challenges for systematic management and quantification at scale, such as model lineage tracing, licensing, and evaluation. However, task-specific benchmarks are insufficient for this setting, as LLMs differ widely in architectures, scales, and training procedures. To address this challenge, we adopt spectral shape-based metrics for managing and quantifying LLMs based on Heavy-Tailed Self-Regularization theory. Our approach uses the shape information of the weight empirical spectral density as a compact spectral signature of each model. This signature captures intrinsic properties of pretrained models and remains robust during post-training, making it suitable for model-level analysis. In addition, this metric is data-free, computationally-efficient, and scale-invariant, enabling large-scale analysis in practice. Moreover, we curate a large and diverse model corpus consisting of major open-source LLM families, and use it to systematically benchmark spectral and non-spectral metrics across models and downstream tasks. We show that our spectral signature supports the tracking of the model lineage, the unsupervised clustering of similar models, and the quantification of the model performance. Overall, the proposed spectral signature provides a meaningful proxy for broad performance trends across LLMs, enabling efficient organization, comparison, and analysis of large model collections.

items.title: Researchers introduce Amortised Sequential Information Gathering to fine-tune LLMs with Bayesian Experimental Design, doubling 7B model success on 20 Questions and cutting inference cost 25x [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Amortising Bayesian Experimental Design for Sequential Information Gathering in LLMs
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Amortised Sequential Information Gathering (ASIG), a fine-tuning method that integrates Bayesian Experimental Design into large language model (LLM) policies to improve sequential information gathering. Tested on the 20 Questions task, ASIG more than doubled the success rate of a 7-billion-parameter model while reducing inference costs by over 25 times compared to a leading baseline. The approach also enhanced performance on MediQ, a medical diagnosis benchmark not seen during training, indicating its ability to generalize to new domains.

ASIG achieves these improvements by extending Group Relative Policy Optimisation with an Expected Information Gain reward, enabling LLMs to gather information more effectively across multi-turn interactions. This method offers a computationally efficient way to fine-tune LLMs for sequential decision-making tasks, demonstrating promising transferability and practical benefits in information-seeking applications.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03426v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit strong reasoning and world-knowledge capabilities, yet often struggle to gather information effectively across the multi-turn interactions required in sequential decision-making settings. We introduce Amortised Sequential Information Gathering (ASIG), a fine-tuning approach that amortises Bayesian Experimental Design (BED) into LLM policies via a multi-turn extension of Group Relative Policy Optimisation with an Expected Information Gain reward. Applied to MediQ, a medical diagnosis benchmark unseen during training, ASIG improves information-seeking performance at the 7B scale, suggesting that the learned strategies can transfer out of distribution. Our findings show that amortising BED into LLM policies provides an effective and computationally efficient approach to sequential information gathering.

items.title: Researchers introduce Agentic Test-Time Training to reduce performance drift in LLM agents during long episodes, improving success rates by up to 5 points on ALFWorld and SWE-bench Lite [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: No Time Like the Present: Agentic Test-Time Training for LLM Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Agentic Test-Time Training (aTTT), a method designed to reduce performance degradation in large language model (LLM) agents during extended task episodes. LLM agents often struggle over long interactions by revisiting states, repeating failed actions, and losing effective strategies. aTTT addresses this by continuously adapting model weights with a token-level reweighting technique that downplays repeated tokens from prior updates while fully weighting novel tokens, thereby mitigating drift caused by repetitive training data.

The team implemented a concurrent serving system using vLLM's runtime LoRA API to enable live updates with minimal overhead. Testing on benchmarks like ALFWorld and SWE-bench Lite showed that aTTT improved success rates by up to 5 points, particularly preserving existing task competence over long trajectories rather than teaching new skills. This approach offers a promising way to maintain LLM agent performance in complex, multi-turn environments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03441v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents often degrade over long episodes: as trajectories grow, they revisit explored states, repeat failed actions, and lose strategies that previously worked. Test-time training (TTT) offers a way to adapt model weights to the evolving task state, but existing LLM TTT methods largely adapt once to a fixed input. We study continuous TTT in multi-turn agent episodes, where each update changes the policy that generates later training text. This creates a self-training loop that helps when new trajectory information appears, but can amplify drift when the agent gets stuck and repeatedly trains on similar text. We find that update-text repetition distinguishes these regimes and introduce Agentic Test-Time Training (aTTT), a token-level reweighting method that downweights the loss on tokens appearing in repeated $n$-grams from prior updates while leaving novel tokens fully weighted. To run such updates inside live episodes, we build a concurrent serving system using vLLM's runtime LoRA API, limiting overhead to 1.9$\times$ the no-TTT cost. aTTT improves success by up to 5.0 points on ALFWorld and 4.9 points on SWE-bench Lite. The gains concentrate where models already have task competence but drift over long trajectories, suggesting that aTTT mainly preserves existing competence rather than teaching new abilities.

items.title: Researchers introduce TRIAGE, a stage-aware instrumentation framework for evaluating automated knowledge graphs in document-grounded graph retrieval-augmented generation with interpretable metrics across extraction, validation, and usage stages [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: TRIAGE: Trustworthy Retrieval Instrumentation And Graph Evaluation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed TRIAGE, a stage-aware instrumentation framework designed to evaluate automated knowledge graphs used in document-grounded graph retrieval-augmented generation (Graph-RAG). TRIAGE provides interpretable metrics across three key stages—knowledge graph implementation, expert validation, and usage—to assess the trustworthiness and query cost of the underlying graph. This framework enables precise localization of failures within the extraction, graph construction, or retrieval phases, improving diagnostic accuracy beyond simply identifying incorrect final answers.

The framework attaches specific metrics such as triple confidence, source coverage, and schema checks during implementation; structural quality assessments during expert validation; and retrieval coverage, faithfulness, and cost during usage. Most metrics operate without requiring gold-standard annotations, which are only used for offline calibration when references are available. TRIAGE forms a diagnostic chain that identifies the earliest stage where a failure occurs, guiding targeted remediation efforts.

As a theoretical framework, TRIAGE includes a proof of concept and a reproducible evaluation protocol, offering a systematic approach to improve the reliability and interpretability of automatically constructed knowledge graphs in AI-driven retrieval systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03447v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Knowledge graphs (KGs) that underpin Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Graph-RAG) are increasingly built automatically by LLM-driven extraction rather than curated by experts. Proper evaluation would require instrumenting all pertinent stages: extraction, graph construction, and inference, coherently enough to localize failures, so that a failure at one stage is not discovered as a wrong answer at the end. We introduce TRIAGE, a stage-aware instrumentation framework for automated, document-grounded graph-RAG that asks not only whether the underlying graph can be trusted but at what cost it can be queried. TRIAGE attaches stage-specific, independently interpretable metrics to three stages: the KG Implementation (triple confidence, source coverage, and schema and canonicalization checks), the KG Validation by expert (graph-level structural quality, with correctness and completeness computed only as offline calibration when a reference is available), and the KG Usage (retrieval coverage, faithfulness, and retrieval cost); the deployed metrics need no gold annotations, the gold-requiring ones serving only as offline calibration. At usage time these metrics form a diagnostic chain of necessary conditions whose first broken link localizes the failure, and the diagnosis maps to the stage levers that can remedy it: extraction, graph and schema, or retrieval. TRIAGE is a theoretical framework with a proof of concept and a reproducible evaluation protocol.

items.title: Researchers propose SkillOpt-Lite, a minimal pipeline for autonomous agent skill optimization that accelerates convergence and outperforms prior methods, integrated into VSCode Copilot for one-line skill evolution [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SkillOpt-Lite: Better and Faster Agent Self-evolution via One Line of Vibe
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced SkillOpt-Lite, a streamlined pipeline for optimizing autonomous agent skills that simplifies existing complex methods while ensuring theoretical and empirical rigor. This approach formalizes skill optimization through Zeroth-Order optimization and incorporates principles such as file-system-based trajectory exploration, consensus attribute mining, and independent validation gating to enhance convergence and generalization. SkillOpt-Lite demonstrates improved performance, notably boosting LiveMath scores on GPT-5.5 and GPT-5.4-nano models, with the latter surpassing standard GPT-5.4 optimized by previous methods.

The framework has been integrated into production coding tools like VSCode Copilot, allowing developers to evolve agent skills with minimal effort through a single line of code. By treating all agent components as editable code, SkillOpt-Lite naturally extends to full harness optimization, further improving accuracy on benchmarks such as SpreadsheetBench. The researchers have made the code publicly available to support further development and adoption.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03451v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: While skill optimization for autonomous agents has gained traction, existing methods rely on complex pipelines. This leaves a fundamental question unaddressed: What constitutes a minimal viable pipeline for skill optimization, where every component is justified by theory or empirical necessity? We formalize skill optimization via Zeroth-Order (ZO) optimization, mapping classical counterparts (central difference, trust regions) to recent literature. Noting that unlike blind numerical perturbations in classical ZO, skill trajectories serve as interpretable debugging feedback. Grounded in Claude Code philosophy and PAC learning, we establish three principles for convergence and generalization: file-system-based trajectory exploration, consensus attribute mining, and independent validation gating. Eliminating redundancies, we propose SkillOpt-Lite. It accelerates convergence and outperforms full SkillOpt: improving LiveMath by +8.8 points on GPT-5.5 and +25.4 points on GPT-5.4-nano, allowing the nano model to surpass standard GPT-5.4 optimized by SkillOpt. Finally, we integrate our framework into production coding agents like VSCode Copilot, enabling developers to evolve agent skills via one line of vibe. Because our framework treats all agent components simply as standard editable code, this minimal pipeline naturally generalizes to full harness optimization (HarnessOpt). On SpreadsheetBench, HarnessOpt enables GPT-5.4-nano to achieve 0.7758 accuracy, outperforming the larger GPT-5.5 running standard pipelines (0.7620). Code is available at https://github.com/EvolvingLMMs-Lab/SkillOpt-Lite.

items.title: Researchers propose Best-of-Better-N, an in-context learning framework that improves response alignment by retrieving and restyling high-reward examples for large language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Best-of-Better-$N$: Generating Pre-Aligned Responses with In-Context Learning
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Best-of-Better-N (BoBN), an in-context learning framework designed to enhance response alignment in large language models by retrieving and restyling high-reward examples relevant to the input query. This method addresses limitations of existing inference-time alignment techniques, such as Best-of-N, which struggle when the reference model assigns low probability to high-quality responses. BoBN uses a restyling step where retrieved responses are rewritten to match the target task's format and style, effectively shifting the model's output distribution toward higher-reward responses.

The team analytically demonstrates how in-context learning with BoBN provably improves alignment on target tasks. They evaluated the approach on safety alignment and mathematical reasoning benchmarks across multiple reference language models, finding that BoBN achieves better performance with a fixed number of responses and requires fewer samples to reach target performance levels. This advancement offers a promising alternative to training-based alignment methods by improving the quality and relevance of generated outputs through retrieval and restyling.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03453v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Inference-time alignment methods, such as Best-of-$N$, offer a flexible alternative to training-based alignment by using reward models to select high-quality responses generated by a reference LLM. However, the efficacy of these methods is inherently limited by the response quality: if the reference LLM assigns negligible probability to high-reward responses, no selection strategy will succeed in finding aligned outputs. In this work, we propose Best-of-Better-$N$ (BoBN), an in context learning-based generation framework to address this challenge. Our method utilizes retrieval from high-reward examples relevant to the input query and task. Crucially, we introduce a restyling step where retrieved responses are rewritten by the reference LLM to align with the target task's format and style. These restyled examples are used in-context to shift the sampling distribution toward the high-reward region. We analytically characterize how in-context learning shifts the output distribution of pretrained transformers toward the high-reward region, resulting in provable benefits on the target task. We then evaluate BoBN on safety alignment and mathematical reasoning benchmarks across several reference LLMs. BoBN's higher-quality responses enable better performance to be achieved when the number of responses $N$ is fixed, and smaller $N$ required to achieve a target performance.

items.title: Researchers propose a comprehensive benchmarking framework for mutual information estimation using copula-theoretic tests and evaluate non-parametric, discriminative, and generative estimators on complex data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Towards Diverse and Comprehensive Benchmarks for Mutual Information Estimation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a comprehensive benchmarking framework for mutual information (MI) estimation, addressing limitations of existing benchmarks that focus on simplified, low-dimensional data. Their approach uses a unified copula-theoretic perspective and introduces two families of tests that vary MI, dimensionality, and marginal complexity with synthetic and real-world data. They evaluated non-parametric, discriminative, and generative MI estimators, finding that no single method consistently outperforms others across all scenarios.

The framework includes a copula-first family of tests that systematically adjusts ground-truth MI and data complexity, and a marginals-first family that integrates real image data with controlled dependency structures. This extensive evaluation revealed fundamental challenges in MI estimation and led to the proposal of new tests targeting these limitations. The researchers have made their benchmarking code openly available to support further study and development in this area.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03487v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mutual information (MI) estimation is a central problem in machine learning and statistics; however, existing benchmarks typically evaluate estimators on simplified, low-dimensional distributions, leaving their performance on complex, realistic data largely unexplored. We address this gap with a comprehensive benchmarking framework grounded in a unified copula-theoretic perspective that subsumes existing benchmarks as special cases. Within this framework, we propose two complementary families of tests: a copula-first family that systematically varies ground-truth MI, dimensionality, and marginal complexity using synthetic and flow-based transformations; and a marginals-first family that couples real-world image data with controlled dependency structures, extending the classic same-class-pairing paradigm. We use this suite to extensively evaluate three classes of estimators: non-parametric, discriminative, and generative. Contrary to prevailing assumptions, our results indicate that there is no universal winner: each category can systematically outperform all other estimators under specific setups. By analyzing these cases, we identify fundamental estimation barriers and propose new tests that more effectively stress these specific limitations. We share the open source code at https://github.com/VanessB/mutinfo.

items.title: Researchers introduce PULS, a semantic world-model pipeline with KSD Bridge and Anticipatory State Predictor, achieving high video anomaly anticipation accuracy and zero-shot transfer on UCF-Crime and XD-Violence datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Latent Clarity: Bridging World-Model Kinematics to Semantic Manifolds for Video Anomaly Anticipation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed PULS (Predictive Unified Latent Space), a semantic world-model pipeline designed for continuous video anomaly anticipation. PULS integrates two key components: the KSD Bridge, which translates physical motion data into a semantic embedding space, and the Anticipatory State Predictor (ASP), which refines predicted future states. This approach achieves high accuracy in detecting anomalies on the UCF-Crime dataset and demonstrates strong zero-shot transfer performance on the out-of-distribution XD-Violence dataset without relying on traditional Multiple Instance Learning methods.

The KSD Bridge maps physical tensors into a text-aligned semantic space, enabling chunk-level anomaly detection with AUROC scores of 0.8994 for UCF-Crime and 0.8162 for XD-Violence. The researchers propose the Latent Clarity Hypothesis, suggesting that anticipated future representations are more semantically distinct than observed data due to the model's ability to filter out noise while preserving motion information. The ASP enhances these future representations, significantly improving zero-shot video question answering accuracy compared to baselines.

This work separates anticipation from observation by showing that predicted future states occupy distinct semantic subspaces, validated through a novel Triple-Track Lead-Time protocol. The findings indicate that Newtonian-invariant kinematic representations generalize well across datasets, highlighting the potential of PULS for robust, anticipatory video anomaly detection in diverse environments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03558v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Continuous video anomaly detection is dominated by reactive Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) that collapses spatiotemporal features into scalar scores. We introduce PULS (Predictive Unified Latent Space), a continuous semantic world-model pipeline comprising two modules: a 490M-parameter KSD Bridge (Kinematic-to-Semantic Distillation) and a 16.8M-parameter Anticipatory State Predictor (ASP). The KSD Bridge maps V-JEPA 2 physical tensors into the 2048-d Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B text-aligned hypersphere, trained on a subset of UCF-Crime. This translation alone yields a chunk-level AUROC of 0.8994 for UCF-Crime and 0.8162 for out-of-distribution XD-Violence without MIL or hierarchical fusion. We introduce and validate the Latent Clarity Hypothesis: because JEPA's temporal predictor discards aleatoric pixel noise while preserving kinematics, anticipated future representations are more semantically separable than observed presents. The ASP sharpens these anticipated future latents, achieving 44.5% mean 14-way zero-shot VQA accuracy (exceeding observation baseline by +9.6 pp). Applying the ASP to Observation Tensors collapses accuracy to 7.3% (random chance), proving Anticipation and Observation occupy distinct sub-manifolds. A Triple-Track Lead-Time protocol with an L1-surprise gate yields a peak +8.9 pp anticipatory advantage at T-0.5s (p < 0.001, N = 1,000 permutation), separating physical anticipation from static scene priors. Zero-shot transfer to XD-Violence confirms that Newtonian-invariant kinematic representations generalize out-of-distribution.

items.title: Researchers propose knowledge distillation framework focusing on teacher representation equivalence classes rather than absolute features, validated on Qwen2.5 and Llama-3.1 models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Teacher Supervision over Representation Equivalence Classes
items.summary:
Researchers have proposed a new framework for knowledge distillation that focuses on teaching a student model the equivalence class of a teacher's representation rather than its absolute features. This approach addresses the issue that pretrained representations are only identifiable up to orthogonal and isotropic scaling transformations, making absolute feature matching ill-posed. The framework unifies various distillation methods by targeting class invariants such as Gram structure and principal subspaces, and it has been validated on the Qwen2.5 and Llama-3.1 models.

The study includes a restoration experiment showing that while a corrupted model's representation can be nearly recovered, its capability cannot, highlighting that output-function (logit) matching is crucial for restoring capability. Additionally, a grafting experiment demonstrated that overlap in representation boundaries predicts successful transplantation of model components, though it is not sufficient on its own. These findings emphasize the importance of aligning output functions over hidden features for effective knowledge transfer.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03572v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Knowledge distillation is usually framed as a choice of what to match in the teacher - its logits, hidden features, or sample relations - which presupposes that the teacher's representation has absolute coordinates to match. It does not: a pretrained representation is identifiable only up to an orthogonal-and-isotropic-scaling equivalence class, so a student should learn the teacher's equivalence class, not its features. The organizing fact is that capability is the teacher's output function, a class invariant that factors through the quotient by the class action, so an objective recovers capability exactly when it is defined there. This makes absolute feature matching ill-posed, and admissible supervision a matter of targeting class invariants (Gram structure, CKA, principal subspaces) or aligning coordinates first, unifying feature matching, relational distillation, alignment, and grafting in one geometric account. Recovery is confined to the corpus-covered region, and a graft study confirms that boundary overlap predicts transplant success but is necessary, not sufficient.
