Based on PMD, we further instantiate PMDRouter, which scores each LoRA by its response magnitude from a single base-model prefill. Experiments on PMD-Bench show that PMDRouter achieves the strongest internal-signal performance across multiple zero-shot routing settings. These results demonstrate the feasibility of zero-shot LoRA routing and suggest that PMD can serve as a general framework for improving zero-shot routing methods. items.title: Researchers propose mask-based self-supervised task with transformers to improve sample efficiency in vision-based deep reinforcement learning, outperforming state-of-the-art methods on control benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Mask-based Predictive Representations for Reinforcement Learning
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced a mask-based self-supervised learning task combined with transformers to enhance sample efficiency in vision-based deep reinforcement learning. This approach uses mask prediction as an auxiliary task, enabling the model to leverage sequence and context information to predict masked inputs, thereby improving the agent's understanding and representation learning. The method reconstructs masked input sequences in latent space and, when integrated with reinforcement learning models, leads to better sample efficiency and outperforms current state-of-the-art methods on various continuous and discrete control benchmarks.

The proposed technique addresses the challenge of extracting effective states from high-dimensional image inputs with limited samples, a common issue in vision-based reinforcement learning. By focusing on non-reconstruction mask prediction rather than traditional reconstruction tasks, the model strengthens task comprehension and representation quality. This advancement demonstrates significant improvements in learning efficiency across multiple control tasks, suggesting a promising direction for future reinforcement learning research.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04153v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-based deep reinforcement learning involves dealing with high-dimensional inputs of image information. It is crucial to abstract effective states from high-dimensional image inputs and limited samples for sample-efficient reinforcement learning. To address this challenge, inspired by fields such as natural language processing and computer vision, we propose a self-supervised task based on mask prediction as an auxiliary task for reinforcement learning. This non-reconstruction method uses the sequence information collected by the agent from the environment and the context information in the sequence to predict the masked information, thereby strengthening the agent's understanding of the task and learning effective representations. Combined with transformers, we find that the model reconstructs the masked input sequence in the latent space. By feeding the compressed representations learned by this method into reinforcement learning models, we observe an improvement in the sample efficiency of reinforcement learning. Moreover, the model outperforms state-of-the-art sample-efficient reinforcement learning methods on multiple continuous and discrete control benchmarks.

items.title: Researchers propose hierarchical multi-to-single-modal knowledge distillation for efficient plasma disruption prediction on EAST dataset, preserving multimodal advantages while reducing inference cost [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Hierarchical Multi-to-Single-Modal Knowledge Distillation for Disruption Prediction in EAST
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a hierarchical multi-to-single-modal knowledge distillation framework to improve plasma disruption prediction in tokamak reactors using the EAST dataset. This approach trains a multimodal teacher model with both time-series diagnostic signals and visible images to capture disruption precursors, then transfers this knowledge to a time-series-only student model for inference, significantly reducing computational costs while maintaining predictive accuracy.

The framework employs Transformer-based encoders and a prototype-guided spatiotemporal hypergraph module during training, with knowledge distilled at graph-structure, representation, and decision levels. Tested on 640 discharges from the EAST dataset, the method preserves the advantages of multimodal learning and offers an efficient solution for disruption prediction. The researchers plan to release the source code publicly to support further development in this area.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04241v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Plasma disruption is a critical threat to tokamak safety. Existing data-driven predictors mainly rely on time-series diagnostic signals, while visible images provide complementary spatial cues including plasma deformation, local brightening, and radiation-structure evolution. Although the image modality improves the model's discriminative capability, it also substantially increases the computational cost during inference. To address this issue, we propose a hierarchical multi-to-single-modal knowledge distillation framework for disruption prediction on a synchronized EAST multimodal dataset. During training, visible images and time-series signals are used to train a multimodal teacher, which learns disruption precursor representations through Transformer-based encoders and a prototype-guided spatiotemporal hypergraph module. During inference, only the time-series student is retained, with multimodal knowledge transferred through graph-structure-level, representation-level, and decision-level distillation. On the 640-discharge EAST dataset, the results demonstrate that the proposed framework can preserve the discriminative advantages of multimodal learning while substantially reducing inference cost, and providing an effective route for efficient disruption prediction in EAST. The source code of this paper will be released on https://github.com/Event-AHU/OpenFusion.

items.title: Researchers introduce SensorGen, a large-scale study evaluating generative models for real-world sensor time series across 14 settings, 7 datasets, and 12 signal modalities [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Signal or Noise? Understanding Generative Models for Real-World Sensor Time Series
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced SensorGen, a comprehensive study evaluating generative models for real-world sensor time series data across 14 settings, 7 datasets, and 12 signal modalities. This study addresses the fragmented state of generative modeling for sensor data by systematically assessing models from five major families to understand their performance and limitations in practical scenarios.

SensorGen reveals that flow-matching models generally perform well across diverse settings, while specific signal properties influence model effectiveness, such as demographic covariates enhancing longitudinal data generation and time-frequency modeling benefiting high-frequency signals. The study also highlights that generated sensor signals have practical applications beyond visual realism, with improvements in generation quality and downstream task performance through scaling and synthetic data use.

By establishing a broader understanding of design choices, evaluation protocols, and failure modes, SensorGen provides valuable insights for advancing generative modeling techniques in continuous, high-dimensional, and noisy sensor time series data, which are common in many real-world systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04245v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative models have changed how machine learning represents complex data distributions, especially in language and vision, yet many real-world systems are observed instead as continuous, high-dimensional, and noisy sensor time series. Existing generative modeling of sensor data, however, remains fragmented across modalities, datasets, and task formulations, limiting a systematic understanding of when, how, and why generative models succeed or fail in real-world settings. To address this gap, we introduce SensorGen, a large-scale study of sensor-signal generation spanning 14 settings across 4 domains, 7 datasets, and 12 signal modalities. Leveraging SensorGen, we systematically evaluate generative models from five major families and uncover three key findings: (1) flow-matching models provide strong overall performance across most settings; (2) signal properties matter, with demographic covariates improving longitudinal generation and time-frequency modeling improving high-frequency signal generation; and (3) generated signals have practical utility beyond visual realism, with scaling improving generation quality and synthetic data improving downstream performance. Together, SensorGen establishes a broader understanding of design choices, evaluation protocols, and failure modes in real-world sensor data generation.

items.title: Researchers present FreshCache, a risk-constrained semantic caching system for open-web retrieval-augmented LLMs that models data freshness and reduces stale errors while saving up to 98% of search API calls [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Risk-Constrained Freshness-Aware Semantic Caching for Open-Web Retrieval-Augmented LLMs
items.summary:
Researchers have developed FreshCache, a semantic caching system designed for open-web retrieval-augmented large language models (LLMs) that accounts for data freshness to reduce stale errors while significantly cutting search API calls. FreshCache uses a three-tier approach that estimates the probability of cached results being outdated through a temporal inference model enhanced by a learned multilayer perceptron (MLP), allowing it to approve cache reuse only when the risk of staleness is within predefined error budgets. This method enables a gradual degradation of cache validity over time instead of a strict binary decision between stale cache hits and full retrieval.

The team introduced FreshCache-Bench, a benchmark dataset with over 8,000 queries across multiple freshness categories, validated against real web snapshots taken at intervals up to seven days. At a 24-hour evaluation, FreshCache with the MLP model achieved 97% savings in search API calls with a minimal stale error rate of 0.1%, outperforming existing methods such as SemanticTTL, vCache, and SCALM. Further analysis showed that only a small fraction of detected content changes actually impacted answer correctness, indicating a very low true stale error rate. The system's temporal risk gating and learned model contributed to significant reductions in stale errors compared to similarity-only caching approaches.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04281v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Semantic caching reduces the latency and cost of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) by serving cached answers to semantically similar queries, but most existing methods do not model the time-varying freshness of open-web evidence. We present FreshCache, a three-tier semantic cache that treats cache reuse as a risk-constrained temporal inference problem: before approving a cache hit, FreshCache estimates the probability that the cached result is stale using a fitted exponential decay model enhanced by a learned MLP, and approves reuse only when that probability falls below a per-tier error budget across answers (epsilon = 0.10), URL lists (epsilon = 0.20), and page content (epsilon = 0.35). This allows the system to degrade gracefully as entries age rather than forcing a binary choice between a stale hit and a full pipeline execution. We introduce FreshCache-Bench, a benchmark of 8,072 base queries across five freshness classes with ground truth staleness labels drawn from real web snapshots at 1, 12, 24 hours, and 7 days after a baseline crawl, expanded to 31,201 queries via paraphrase generation. At the 24-hour evaluation window, FreshCache_MLP achieves 97% search API savings at 0.1% hash-based stale error, and an LLM-judge evaluation on 396 confirmed change pairs shows that only 34.3% of detected content changes actually affect answer correctness, placing true answer-affecting stale error at approximately 0.034%. The rule-based FreshCache achieves 98% search savings at 3.3% stale error under a temporal holdout calibration, outperforming SemanticTTL (14.9% stale, 72% saved), vCache (7.2% stale, 47% saved), and SCALM (5.2% stale, 96% saved). Ablations show the temporal risk gate accounts for an 11.6 point reduction in stale error over similarity-only reuse, and the learned MLP reduces stale error a further 3.2 points over the rule-based model.

items.title: Researchers develop fixed-confidence best-arm identification algorithm for causal mediation analysis with sample-efficient, high-probability correctness guarantees, validated on large-scale advertising data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Fixed-Confidence Best-Arm Identification for Causal Mediation Analysis
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a fixed-confidence best-arm identification algorithm designed to maximize the expected natural direct potential outcome (NDPO) in causal mediation analysis. This approach isolates the effect of an intervention by excluding pathways through mediators that may be irrelevant or confounding. The algorithm, based on the Track-and-Stop framework and employing a cutting-set method, ensures sample-efficient identification with high-probability correctness guarantees, achieving both \(\delta\)-correctness and asymptotic optimality.

The team first established population-level identification of the expected NDPO within a causal bandit setting using observable interventional distributions. They then validated their method through empirical evaluations on a large-scale real-world advertising dataset (IPinYou), demonstrating its practical effectiveness in complex data environments.

items.title: Researchers present a unified membership inference framework for generative models across text-to-text, text-to-image, and image-to-text modalities with superior black-box attack performance [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: One Framework for All: Cross-Modal Membership Inference for Generative Models
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a unified membership inference framework that applies across multiple generative model modalities, including text-to-text, text-to-image, and image-to-text. This framework addresses privacy risks by determining whether specific data points were used in a model's training set, improving upon previous methods that were limited to individual model types. The approach leverages the observation that a generative model's output distribution can approximate its training data distribution, enabling membership inference through likelihood ratio testing in a shared embedding space.

The team conducted extensive experiments under strict black-box conditions, considering both partial-knowledge and zero-knowledge threat models, and evaluated the method against data used for fine-tuning and pre-training. Results show that this unified framework outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques, which are typically optimized for single model classes, demonstrating its broad applicability and enhanced effectiveness in protecting privacy across diverse generative models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04339v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large generative models across text-to-text, text-to-image, and image-to-text modalities have been shown to pose significant privacy risks. One fundamental threat is membership inference attacks (MIA), which aim to determine whether a given data point was used in a model's training set. Although prior work has investigated MIAs against these three classes of generative models, existing approaches treat them in isolation and are not cross-applicable, thereby limiting their real-world utility. To address this limitation, we present the first comprehensive study of a unified membership inference framework that applies across text-to-text, text-to-image, and image-to-text modalities. Our approach is grounded in a key modality-agnostic observation: the output distribution of a generative model can approximate its training data distribution. Leveraging this property, we model the distributions of model-generated outputs and auxiliary non-member samples in a shared embedding space, and perform membership inference via likelihood ratio testing. We conduct extensive experiments in a strict black-box setting under both partial-knowledge and zero-knowledge threat models, and evaluate membership inference against both fine-tuning and pre-training data. Experimental results demonstrate our approach's superior performance in comparison to existing state-of-the-art methods, which are typically optimized for a single model class.

items.title: Researchers propose Full-Stack FP4, a stable NVFP4 framework for 4-bit LLM pretraining addressing quantization noise in projections, optimizers, and attention with near-BF16 performance on 3B/64B-token models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Full-Stack FP4: Stable LLM Pretraining with Quantized Projections, Optimizers, and Attention
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Full-Stack FP4, a comprehensive framework for stable 4-bit large language model (LLM) pretraining that addresses quantization noise issues in transformer linear layers, optimizer states, and attention mechanisms. This approach employs module-specific precision strategies, including LoRA-SVD decomposition for linear projections, a robust AdamW second-moment transformation for optimizers, and a mixed-precision scheme for attention, achieving near-BF16 performance with only a 1.47% loss gap on 3 billion parameter models trained over 64 billion tokens.

The framework tackles unique numerical challenges such as error amplification in linear layers, fragility of optimizer second moments to low-precision denominators, and the need for strict forward-backward quantization consistency in attention computations. By integrating these solutions into a plug-and-play system, Full-Stack FP4 enables efficient and stable end-to-end NVFP4 pretraining, demonstrating significant improvements in stability and efficiency compared to previous methods.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04422v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent NVFP4 pretraining methods mainly target transformer linear layers, leaving optimizer states, optimizer arithmetic and attention underexplored in 4-bit pipelines. This critical gap blocks stable full-stack 4-bit pretraining, as the three core modules exhibit unique numerical failure patterns: linear layers hit hard quantization noise limits with dimension-propagated error amplification; AdamW second moments are heavy-tailed non-negative values fragile to low-precision denominators; attention carries error-prone computation paths demanding strict forward-backward quantization consistency. We propose Full-Stack FP4, the first complete NVFP4 pretraining framework resolving all three stability bottlenecks via module-wise precision strategies. For linear projections, LoRA-SVD lightweight decomposition suppresses quantization noise and breaks the direct-quantization error ceiling, shrinking the linear-only loss gap from 1.40% to 0.61%. For optimizers, we design AdamW second-moment transformation for robust NVFP4 storage and fully support native NVFP4 Newton-Schulz iterations for the Root (Muon) optimizer. For attention, a mixed-precision scheme quantizes Q/K/V and backward dS while guarding vulnerable paths in BF16, paired with unified tensor reuse to sustain forward-backward alignment. We further analyze fast error accumulation in naive low-bit matrix multiplication and the extreme sensitivity of PV / dOV^T attention branches. All modules are plug-and-play with cumulative stability and efficiency improvements. Our 3B/64B-token pretraining validates near-BF16 performance with merely 1.47% loss gap, verifying feasible stable end-to-end NVFP4 LLM pretraining.

items.title: Researchers introduce dOPSD, an on-policy self-distillation method for diffusion language models that improves math reasoning and code generation by deriving teacher privilege from the model's own decoding trajectory [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: dOPSD: On-Policy Self-Distillation for Diffusion Language Models
items.summary: Researchers have developed dOPSD, an on-policy self-distillation method for diffusion large language models (dLLMs) that enhances their reasoning abilities in math and code generation tasks. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on external ground-truth references, dOPSD derives the teacher model's privileged information from the student's own decoding trajectory, allowing the model to improve by evaluating its own intermediate outputs. This method outperforms existing supervised and on-policy baselines on benchmarks such as Dream and LLaDA.
items.description: Researchers have developed dOPSD, an on-policy self-distillation method for diffusion large language models (dLLMs) that enhances their reasoning abilities in math and code generation tasks. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04428v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) generate text by iteratively denoising a masked sequence, offering a parallel alternative to autoregressive models, but eliciting strong reasoning through post-training remains difficult: supervised fine-tuning is off-policy and suffers from exposure bias, while reinforcement learning gives only sparse, sequence-level rewards and is hard to apply without tractable sequence likelihoods. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) offers a promising alternative, using one model as both student and teacher to provide dense, token-level, on-policy supervision, but its effectiveness hinges on giving the teacher privileged information (PI) - typically an instance-specific ground-truth reference unavailable at inference - so the student ends up distilling a weak PI-free consensus policy that yields little improvement on dLLM reasoning. We introduce dOPSD, which instead derives the teacher's privilege directly from the student's own denoising trajectory, evaluating masked positions using later, more-decoded steps of that same trajectory rather than an external label, so the teacher's advantage emerges from the model's own decoding process; on Dream and LLaDA, dOPSD improves both in-domain math reasoning and out-of-domain code generation, outperforming supervised and on-policy baselines.

items.title: Researchers release evalci, a Python library for statistically rigorous comparison of language model evaluations with confidence intervals and significance tests [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: evalci: A Python Library for Statistically Rigorous Comparison of Language Model Evaluations
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced evalci, a Python library designed to provide statistically rigorous comparisons of language model evaluations by incorporating confidence intervals and significance tests. This tool addresses the common issue in language model benchmarking where differences in accuracy are reported without assessing whether these gaps could be due to sampling noise, potentially overstating the confidence in model comparisons. Evalci processes per-item results tables to generate publication-ready statistical claims, supporting adapters for popular evaluation frameworks and validating its routines against independent references.

The library includes features such as paired permutation tests, multiple-comparison corrections, and power analysis, all implemented using standard Python packages like numpy, scipy, and pandas. A case study using evalci re-examined the MMLU benchmark results of nine language models, revealing that several adjacent rank differences on the leaderboard were not statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Evalci is available for installation via PyPI and its source code is accessible on GitHub.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04429v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The dominant practice in language model evaluation is to report a single accuracy number per model and declare the higher one better, without testing whether the gap could plausibly be sampling noise. On benchmarks of a few thousand items, and under temperature sampling where a model can differ from itself run to run by more than the reported gap between models, this practice routinely overstates confidence in headline claims. The statistical machinery to fix this -- confidence intervals, paired significance tests, power analysis, clustered standard errors, multiple-comparison correction -- is well established, but no standard, pip-installable tool packages it in the shape an evaluation actually takes: a per-item results table. We present evalci, a pure-Python library (numpy/scipy/pandas only) that turns a per-item results table into a publication-ready claim -- e.g., "Model A beats Model B, $\Delta=3.1$ pts, 95% CI [1.2, 5.0], paired permutation $p=0.002$, $n=1{,}319$" -- in one function call, with adapters for lm-evaluation-harness and HELM output. Every routine is validated against an independent reference (statsmodels, or brute-force exact enumeration) rather than only against itself. As a case study, we re-analyze a public comparison of nine language models' MMLU accuracy and find that 3 of the 8 adjacent leaderboard-rank gaps are not statistically significant after correcting for the 36 pairwise comparisons the ranking implies. evalci is available at https://pypi.org/project/evalci/ (source: https://github.com/Shreyaskc/evalci, DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21201815)

items.title: Researchers establish statistical guarantees and applications for pairwise quantile regression with theoretical bounds and facial recognition error analysis [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: On Pairwise Quantile Regression -- Statistical Guarantees and Applications
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a statistical framework for pairwise quantile regression, extending traditional quantile regression to analyze similarity functions between pairs of independent observations, such as biometric data from pixelated ID photos. They provide theoretical guarantees for this approach by treating it as an empirical minimization problem using a pairwise pinball loss, and establish generalization bounds with conditions for fast learning rates. The methodology is supported by simulation experiments and is applied to analyze errors in facial recognition similarity scoring.

The study leverages advanced concentration results for U-processes to underpin the statistical learning problem and confirms the practical validity of the approach through empirical evidence. This work offers a novel tool for understanding conditional distributions in contexts where the response variable is a similarity measure, broadening the applicability of quantile regression techniques.

By applying this framework to facial recognition error analysis, the researchers demonstrate its potential to improve biometric system assessments, providing insights into error patterns and contributing to more reliable similarity scoring methods in biometric applications.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04431v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantile regression provides a powerful tool for summarizing the conditional distribution of a real valued random variable (r.v.) of interest $Y$ as a function of covariates $Z$ in cases where it shows a large dispersion with high probability, going beyond the situation where standard least square regression is informative/predictive. items.title: Researchers show covert trait propagation enables student models trained on noise to inherit teacher representations through geometric alignment in MLP distillation on MNIST [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Covert Trait Propagation Is Representation Alignment: Mechanistic Evidence from Hidden-Channel Distillation
items.summary:
Researchers have demonstrated that a student neural network model trained solely on uniform noise can still acquire its teacher model's digit-classification capabilities if both models share the same initialization. This phenomenon, studied in a multilayer perceptron (MLP) distillation setting on the MNIST dataset, is driven by a process called covert trait propagation (CTP), where geometric alignment between the student and teacher models enables the transfer of learned representations. Key experiments reveal that alignment of specific network projections is crucial for this transfer, and that the mechanism is not purely informational but depends on geometric factors within the network.

The study further explores how shared initialization creates a common coordinate system that facilitates alignment through gradient updates, and validates the mechanism through multiple experiments including the effects of freezing certain network components and analyzing multi-teacher ensembles. Extending this geometric perspective to instruction-tuned large language models (LLMs), the researchers identify similar alignment effects activated by training, while also noting that some commonly used metrics may introduce artifacts in interpreting these behaviors.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04432v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A student model trained on pure uniform noise can still inherit its teacher's digit-classification ability, provided the two share initialization. Previous work proves this transfer is guaranteed when the teacher's learning rate is small enough, but does not explain where in the network the channel lives or what sets its capacity. Working in an MLP distillation setting on MNIST, we show these channels are not purely informational: geometric alignment gates access to the information the channel carries. Shared initialization makes the output projection W_2 a common coordinate key, and KL gradients reshape the student's input projection W_0 until its hidden representations align with the teacher's. We call this covert trait propagation (CTP). Five experiments support this mechanism: channel closure tracks weight drift, not teacher accuracy; freezing W_0 destroys transfer while freezing W_2 leaves it intact; multi-teacher ensembles cancel out despite each teacher carrying comparable label information; and linear centered kernel alignment (CKA) tracks student accuracy at r=0.98 across a continuous initialization sweep. Applying the same geometric lens to cross-token behavioral entanglement (CTBE) in instruction-tuned LLMs, we find the effect appears to be activated by alignment training, acting on an inherited substrate, and that the standard log-ratio metric produces an apparent frequency bias that is largely a circularity artifact.

items.title: Wan-Streamer v0.2 raises interactive output resolution to 640x368 while preserving 200 ms model latency and 550 ms total remote interaction latency with multi-GPU architecture [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Wan-Streamer v0.2: Higher Resolution, Same Latency
items.summary:
Wan-Streamer v0.2 is an upgraded audio-visual interaction model that increases the interactive output resolution from 192x336 to 640x368 while maintaining a model-side latency of about 200 milliseconds at 25 frames per second. This enhancement allows for clearer visualization of agents' posture, gaze, hands, and surrounding scene elements during real-time conversations without increasing user-visible delay.

The system achieves this by retaining a single-GPU low-latency path for perception and language processing, while employing a multi-GPU architecture for the more demanding visual generation tasks. This design splits the high-resolution video sequence across multiple GPUs for efficient processing, preserving a compact interface between components and keeping total remote interaction latency around 550 milliseconds, including network communication time.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04443v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present Wan-Streamer v0.2, a latency-preserving upgrade of the native-streaming, end-to-end audio-visual interaction model. v0.2 keeps the v0.1 modeling formulation, but raises the interactive output stream from 192x336 to 640x368 while preserving approximately 200 ms model-side signal-to-signal latency at 25 FPS. The higher-resolution stream supports scene-grounded mid-shot agents whose posture, gaze, hands, nearby objects, and local scene layout remain legible during real-time conversation. To support the larger visual stream without adding user-visible delay, v0.2 keeps the thinker as a single-GPU low-latency path for streaming perception, the short language/state Transformer pass that builds the generation cache, and final decoding. The performer becomes a multi-GPU Ulysses-style context-parallel group for the expensive next-unit latent generation. Each performer rank writes incoming K/V into a pre-sharded local cache. The long high-resolution latent video sequence is split across ranks for denoising and gathered through Ulysses communication, while the much shorter audio latent sequence is generated without sequence sharding. In this split, the thinker's language/state computation reaches the performer only as K/V conditioning, so no separate language sequence has to be communicated inside the performer group. This concentrates additional hardware on visual generation while preserving the compact thinker-performer boundary, keeping total remote interaction latency at approximately 550 ms when a 350 ms bidirectional network budget is included.

items.title: Researchers develop deep learning surrogate model to accelerate ASTEC nuclear reactor severe accident simulations, predicting 80 variables up to 40 hours in under a minute [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: A Deep Learning-based surrogate model for Severe Accidents in nuclear reactors using ASTEC
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a deep learning surrogate model to significantly accelerate simulations of severe accidents in nuclear reactors using the ASTEC code. This model combines an AutoEncoder for dimensionality reduction and a Neural Ordinary Differential Equation for time-stepping, enabling the prediction of around 80 physical variables simultaneously. The surrogate model can simulate up to 40 hours of reactor accident scenarios in under a minute, compared to several days required by traditional methods, making it suitable for real-time applications such as operator training.

The surrogate model was trained on data generated by the ASTEC simulator for scenarios including station blackout and loss-of-coolant accidents. It maintains stable predictions over long time horizons and achieves a dimensionality reduction factor of over 300, allowing efficient computation on both CPUs and GPUs. This study represents the first exploration of deep learning surrogate modeling to approximate the complex, nonlinear physics involved in severe nuclear reactor accidents as modeled by ASTEC.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04450v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Integral codes like the Accident Source Term Evaluation Code (ASTEC) are powerful tools to study the physics of Severe Accidents (SAs) in nuclear reactors. Real time SA simulators can also be helpful in training operators of nuclear plants to react correctly to malfunctions. However, SA simulators can take up to several days per simulation, making their use infeasible for real time applications. In this work we show how to speed up a SA simulator with a fast, Deep Learning based (DL), surrogate model (SM). The SM is built as a combination of a dimensionality reduction stage, via an AutoEncoder, and a time-stepping stage, via a Neural Ordinary Differential Equation. The data on which the SM is trained are obtained from the ASTEC simulator, by sampling a set of operator actions for station blackout (SBO) and loss-of-coolant accidents (LOCA). The objective of the developed SM is to approximate multiple spatio-temporal fields for the thermal-hydraulic physics, core degradation, and fission product release modules in ASTEC's vessel domain. The SM predicts simultaneously around $80$ different physical variables (both scalar and fields), maintaining a stable autoregressive rollout up to $50$ thousand time steps. In addition, the AutoEncoder achieves a dimensionality reduction by a factor of over $300$, which allows the SM to predict up to $40$ hours of simulation in under a minute, both on CPU and GPU. This work is the first study of the capabilities and limits of DL based surrogate modeling in approximating the challenging, highly non-linear physics of ASTEC.

items.title: Researchers introduce operator-on-F as a complementary diagnostic to value-equivalence for evaluating latent world models in model-based reinforcement learning, showing strong correlation with planning return loss [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Operator-on-F complements value-equivalence: a planning-time diagnostic for latent world models
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced operator-on-F, a new diagnostic tool designed to complement traditional value-equivalence methods for evaluating latent world models in model-based reinforcement learning. This approach compares a model's k-step latent pushforward to the environment's on an observable subset, providing a more sensitive measure of planning-relevant errors that are often missed by reward and value prediction metrics. The study demonstrates that operator-on-F correlates strongly with planning return loss, outperforming conventional error measures in distinguishing model performance across different sizes and architectures.

In experiments involving a TD-MPC2 size sweep on the cheetah-run task, reward-prediction errors showed limited variation and weak correlation with return, while operator error varied widely and closely tracked declines in planning return. At larger model sizes, operator error increased significantly, coinciding with a collapse in planning return, despite reward-prediction error remaining within a narrow range. The operator diagnostic also effectively differentiated between architectures, highlighting its utility as a complementary evaluation tool rather than a replacement for existing methods.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04464v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: World-model evaluation for model-based reinforcement learning typically asks whether the learned model predicts reward and value well, which can leave planning-relevant errors in the model's latent rollouts unmeasured. We introduce a complementary diagnostic, operator-on-F, that compares a model's k-step latent pushforward to the environment's on an observable subset F, using the model's own predictor. On a TD-MPC2 size sweep over cheetah-run, reward-prediction error stays within [0.028, 0.091] for every model size - only about 3x variation - so an unnormalized reward-fit check has narrow resolution to distinguish them; the (unnormalized) Bellman residual and reward error themselves have weak relationships with return (Spearman -0.10 and -0.30). Operator error spans 0.28 to 2.62 over the same sizes. At 317M the operator error is 2.62 - an order of magnitude above the 0.28-0.36 cluster - and the planning return collapses to 0.9, while reward-prediction error (0.091) is the highest of the five but stays within the same small [0.028, 0.091] range as the rest of the sweep. The rank correlation between operator error and return loss is -0.90 (anchor-bootstrap 95% CI [-0.90, -0.70] at n=5 sizes; leave-one-out removal of any single size leaves it at -0.80 or stronger). The operator also returns informative, architecture-discriminating estimates in a cross-architecture comparison between TD-MPC2 and a pure-SSL latent world model. The operator diagnostic complements value-equivalence rather than replacing it.

items.title: Researchers propose stabilisation strategies for LLM-augmented cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning to address regime-dependent failures caused by dynamic reward weight updates [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Regime-Conditional Stabilisation of LLM-Augmented Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
items.summary:
Researchers have identified challenges in integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) with cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), specifically when dynamically updating LLM-generated reward weights during training. This practice violates the stationarity assumption of Potential-Based Reward Shaping (PBRS) and contaminates the experience replay buffer, leading to regime-dependent failures that vary based on the baseline system's competence. To address this, the team proposed two stabilization methods: a Phase-Based Freeze Schedule to maintain stationarity during training phases and Exponential Moving Average (EMA) smoothing to limit reward weight fluctuations.

The researchers tested these strategies across three cooperative environments using QMIX and an exploratory VDN extension, identifying three distinct regimes. In the augmentative regime, where the baseline performs moderately well, EMA improved success rates significantly, while naive dynamic updates caused performance collapse. In the essential regime, where the baseline fails, any shaping enabled task completion. In the supplementary regime, where the baseline is nearly optimal, stabilized shaping maintained performance without adding variance. These findings highlight the importance of maintaining reward-signal stationarity and suggest that understanding the regime can predict whether dynamic LLM shaping will be beneficial or detrimental.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04470v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a natural interface for translating human objectives into reward signals for cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), yet the training-time dynamics of this integration remain poorly understood. We show that dynamically updating LLM-generated reward weights during off-policy MARL violates the stationarity assumption of Potential-Based Reward Shaping (PBRS) and contaminates the experience replay buffer, whose stored transitions carry reward labels computed under stale shaping weights. We characterise the result as a regime-dependent failure whose severity depends on how competent the unshaped baseline already is. To control it we propose two stabilisation strategies: a Phase-Based Freeze Schedule that enforces strict stationarity within training phases, and Exponential Moving Average (EMA) smoothing that bounds per-episode weight drift. We evaluate across three cooperative environments and five random seeds with QMIX, complemented by an exploratory VDN extension, yielding a three-regime taxonomy. In the augmentative regime (Simple Spread), where the baseline is functional (74.4 %), EMA significantly improves success to 86.7 % ($+12.3$ pp, $p<0.01$) while naive dynamic updates collapse it to 15.2 %. In the supplementary regime (SMAC 3m), where the baseline is near-saturated (98.8 %), stabilised shaping preserves performance (99.9 %) while unstabilised shaping adds variance without gain. These findings establish reward-signal stationarity as a necessary design constraint and indicate that regime placement is a practical predictor of whether dynamic LLM shaping helps or harms.

outputCleanup.description:
Researchers have identified challenges in integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) with cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), specifically when dynamically updating LLM-generated reward weights during training. This practice violates the stationarity assumption of Potential-Based Reward Shaping (PBRS) and contaminates the experience replay buffer, leading to regime-dependent failures that vary based on the baseline system's competence. To address this, the team proposed two stabilization methods: a Phase-Based Freeze Schedule to maintain stationarity during training phases and Exponential Moving Average (EMA) smoothing to limit reward weight fluctuations.

The researchers tested these strategies across three cooperative environments using QMIX and an exploratory VDN extension, identifying three distinct regimes. In the augmentative regime, where the baseline performs moderately well, EMA improved success rates significantly, while naive dynamic updates caused performance collapse. In the essential regime, where the baseline fails, any shaping enabled task completion. In the supplementary regime, where the baseline is nearly optimal, stabilized shaping maintained performance without adding variance. These findings highlight the importance of maintaining reward-signal stationarity and suggest that understanding the regime can predict whether dynamic LLM shaping will be beneficial or detrimental.

items.title: Researchers propose PulmoSight-XAI, an explainable multi-view attention ensemble with gradient boosting meta-learning achieving state-of-the-art multi-label chest X-ray classification on 14 thoracic pathologies [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: PulmoSight-XAI: An Explainable Multi-View Attention Ensemble with Gradient Boosting Meta-Learning for Multi-Label Chest X-Ray Classification
items.summary:
Researchers have developed PulmoSight-XAI, an explainable multi-view ensemble framework that combines attention mechanisms and gradient boosting meta-learning to classify 14 thoracic pathologies from chest X-rays. The system independently analyzes frontal and lateral radiographs using multiple convolutional neural networks enhanced with multi-scale feature fusion and attention modules, addressing challenges like class imbalance and co-occurring diseases. Evaluated on a large dataset, it achieved state-of-the-art performance with high AUROC scores and demonstrated strong anatomical consistency through various explainability techniques.

The framework employs a novel hybrid loss function to handle class imbalance and integrates test-time augmentation predictions and uncertainty measures into hierarchical meta-learners, including XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost, followed by optimized stacking. This approach preserves fine-grained features and emphasizes pathology-specific information, providing a transparent and clinically practical tool for automated thoracic disease diagnosis.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04478v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Automated chest X-ray classification remains challenging due to severe class imbalance, co-occurring pathologies, and the loss of localized features in conventional architectures. To address these, we propose an explainable hierarchical multi-view ensemble framework for the robust classification of 14 thoracic pathologies. The framework employs view-specific training by independently modeling frontal and lateral radiographs using an ensemble of five complementary convolutional neural networks. Replacing global average pooling, a multi-scale feature fusion strategy augmented with Convolutional Block Attention Modules (CBAM) preserves fine-grained intermediate representations while emphasizing high-level pathology-specific semantic features. To mitigate positive-negative imbalance and varying inter-class difficulty, models are optimized using a novel hybrid objective combining Asymmetric Loss with Adaptive Focal Loss. Beyond simple probability averaging, the framework incorporates a hierarchical meta-learning strategy where test-time augmentation (TTA) predictions and cross-model uncertainty measures are integrated into Level-1 gradient-boosting meta-learners (XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost), followed by Level-2 stacking with optimized alpha blending. Evaluated on a large-scale CheXpert-style dataset, the framework achieves state-of-the-art macro-average AUROC scores of 0.9319 for frontal and 0.9154 for lateral radiographs. Furthermore, comprehensive explainability analysis using seven post-hoc attribution techniques demonstrates strong anatomical consistency and clinically meaningful decision localization. By integrating architectural diversity, multi-scale attention, hierarchical meta-learning, and rigorous explainability, the proposed framework provides a transparent, highly accurate, and clinically practical computer-aided diagnosis system for thoracic disease classification.

items.title: Researchers analyze encoder probing and decoder attribution methods for neural multi-attribute vehicle routing problem solvers using Hard-Mask and Recourse decoders, revealing differences in constraint representation and policy feasibility [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Two Black Boxes, One Solver: Encoder Probing and Decoder Attribution for Neural Multi-Attribute VRP under Hard-Mask and Recourse Decoders
items.summary:
Researchers have examined neural autoregressive solvers for the Multi-Attribute Vehicle Routing Problem (MAVRP), focusing on understanding how these models represent constraints and justify decisions at each step. They analyzed encoder representations using various probing techniques and evaluated decoder attribution methods through gradient-based approaches, assessing explanations for fidelity, stability, and actionability. Their study compared six model variants combining different encoders and decoders, revealing that graph inductive biases enhance representation and explanation quality, and that certain training regimes enable models to better handle infeasibility by producing useful counterfactuals.

The research highlights differences between encoder types, such as the Mixture-of-Experts encoder's distributed constraint representation, and contrasts two decoder approaches—Hard-Mask and Recourse—showing that Recourse-trained policies more effectively represent infeasibility and generate feasible alternatives. These insights provide a deeper understanding of how neural solvers process complex routing constraints and offer interpretable justifications, which is valuable for dispatchers who need to validate or compare routing decisions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04487v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural autoregressive solvers for the Multi-Attribute Vehicle Routing Problem (MAVRP) reach competitive cost but offer no per-step justification, a problem when dispatchers must validate, accept, or compare them. We open two complementary black boxes in one protocol. On the encoder side, linear probes, spontaneous-organization metrics, rank-based richness measures, and discovered-direction analyses with intervention validation characterize how the latent represents constraint families at the graph, node, and edge level. On the decoder side, three attribution methods (gradient, integrated gradients, DeepLIFT) feed three reading angles: abductive, contrastive against the best feasible alternative, and counterfactual (smallest input change that switches the action or restores feasibility). Explanations are scored on fidelity, concentration, stability, sanity, and actionability. Across six variants combining three encoders (Attention baseline, Unimp, UnimpMoe) with two decoders (Hard-Mask, Recourse), we find that graph inductive bias improves both representational predictability and decoder sanity, that the Mixture-of-Experts encoder represents constraints in a distributed rather than axis-aligned way, and that the Recourse training regime, not merely its softer mask, produces policies that represent infeasibility usefully, exposing make-feasible counterfactuals that Hard-Mask policies fail to produce even when fed infeasible alternatives externally.

items.title: Researchers find GPT-4 can learn the principled-versus-statistical distinction from language, while earlier models struggle despite sensitivity to statistical prevalence [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Failures and Successes to Learn a Core Conceptual Distinction from the Statistics of Language
items.summary:
Researchers have investigated whether language models can learn to distinguish between principled truths, which hold by category membership, and statistical truths, which hold due to frequency. While earlier models showed sensitivity to statistical prevalence, they struggled to represent this core conceptual distinction. The study found that GPT-4 is the first model to successfully learn the principled-versus-statistical distinction from language alone.

This finding suggests that advanced language models like GPT-4 may be capable of acquiring sophisticated causal and conceptual knowledge directly from linguistic input, potentially bootstrapping fundamental human-like conceptual distinctions through language experience. The research highlights a significant step forward in understanding how AI models process and internalize complex semantic concepts beyond mere statistical patterns.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04523v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generic statements like "tigers are striped" and "cars have radios" communicate information that is, in general, true. However, while the first statement is true in principle, the second is true only statistically. People are exquisitely sensitive to this principled-vs-statistical distinction. It has been argued that this ability to distinguish between something being true by virtue of it being a category member versus being true because of mere statistical regularity, is a general property of people's conceptual machinery and cannot itself be learned. We investigate whether the distinction between principled and statistical properties can be learned from language itself. If so, it raises the possibility that language experience can bootstrap core conceptual distinctions and that it is possible to learn sophisticated causal models directly from language. We find that language models are all sensitive to statistical prevalence, but struggle with representing the principled-vs-statistical distinction controlling for prevalence. Until GPT-4, which succeeds.

items.title: Researchers formalize concept representations and contextual transformations as shared geometric structures in large language models across six model families [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Language Models Represent and Transform Concepts with Shared Geometry
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a framework to understand how large language models represent and transform concepts using shared geometric structures. By modeling concepts as point-cloud manifolds and contextual transformations as vector fields, they analyzed six different language model families and found that context affects each concept uniquely. This variation in concept displacement is semantically organized and consistent across models, indicating a common underlying geometry in how concepts and their contextual changes are represented.

The study reveals that not only are concept representations shared among models, but the way context transforms these concepts follows a structured pattern linked to semantic properties like lexical concreteness and density. This shared geometric structure allows displacement patterns from one model to predict those in others, suggesting a richer and more organized representation of concepts and context in language models than previously recognized.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04525v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How concepts are represented in neural networks is a fundamental question in machine learning. The dominant view treats concept representations as stationary geometric objects. Yet concepts appear in context, and context transforms them. Drawing from neural population geometry, we formalize concept representations as point-cloud manifolds and contextual transformations as vector fields, and instantiate this framework in large language models. Across six model families of varying scales, we find that context moves each concept differently. The variance in these displacements is semantically organized, correlating with lexical concreteness and density. Importantly, both the concepts being transformed and this variance structure are shared across models: displacement structure transported from one model predicts held-out displacements in others significantly above chance. Together, these findings show that models share a common geometry not only in how concepts are represented, but more importantly in how context transforms them, a structure with richer organization than prior work has recognized.

items.title: Researchers propose Lyapunov-stabilised quantisation framework for fixed-point neural networks to prevent activation overflow and improve accuracy on MNIST with 4-16 bit precision [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Lyapunov-Guided Training for Hardware-Safe Neural Networks Under Fixed-Point Arithmetic
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a Lyapunov-stabilised quantisation framework to improve the reliability of low-precision neural networks using fixed-point arithmetic, which often suffers from activation overflow and accuracy loss due to two's-complement overflow wrapping. This approach monitors hidden-state energy with a layerwise Lyapunov function and applies a monotone projection to maintain bounded and stable state evolution, effectively preventing activation overflow during training and inference.

The method was tested on the MNIST dataset using a compact patch-based transformer with bit-widths ranging from 4 to 16 bits. Results showed that traditional quantisation-aware training without constraints led to high activation overflow rates and near-chance accuracy, while the proposed Lyapunov projection reduced overflow to below 0.012% and restored stable learning, achieving 86.55% accuracy at 12 bits. This demonstrates that Lyapunov-based control can serve as a hardware-aware stabilization mechanism for fixed-point neural networks, enhancing their performance on resource-constrained devices.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04531v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Low-precision neural networks are attractive for resource-constrained hardware, but fixed-point arithmetic introduces failure modes that are often hidden by idealised quantisation models. In particular, two's-complement overflow wrapping can corrupt hidden activations by changing both their magnitude and sign, leading to unstable numerical error propagation and severe accuracy degradation. This paper proposes a Lyapunov-stabilised quantisation framework for low-precision neural networks operating under hardware-style wrapping arithmetic. The hidden-state energy is monitored through a layerwise Lyapunov function, and a monotone projection is applied to enforce bounded and non-increasing state evolution across depth. The method is evaluated on MNIST using a compact patch-based transformer under post-training quantisation and quantisation-aware training with fixed-point bit-widths from 4 to 16 bits. Monte Carlo results show that unconstrained wrapped quantisation-aware training collapses to near-chance accuracy across 6-16 bits, with activation overflow rates exceeding 11%. In contrast, the proposed monotone Lyapunov projection suppresses activation overflow to below 0.012% and restores stable low-precision learning, achieving 86.55% accuracy at 12 bits. These results demonstrate that Lyapunov-based state control can act as a hardware-aware stabilisation mechanism for reliable fixed-point neural inference and training.

items.title: Researchers present CRISP, a spatiotemporal camera-radar backbone pretrained via forecasting-based world-model learning for autonomous driving, improving long-horizon point cloud forecasting and downstream tasks on nuScenes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: CRISP: A Spatiotemporal Camera-Radar Backbone for Driving via Forecasting-Based World-Model Pretraining
items.summary:
Researchers have developed CRISP, a spatiotemporal camera-radar backbone designed for autonomous driving that is pretrained using forecasting-based world-model learning. CRISP generates a unified bird's-eye-view representation by predicting future LiDAR point clouds from historical multi-view images and radar data, using LiDAR only during pretraining. This approach enhances long-horizon point cloud forecasting and improves performance on various downstream tasks such as 3D detection, tracking, mapping, motion forecasting, and planning, using only camera and radar inputs during deployment.

To optimize forecasting-based pretraining for camera-radar fusion, CRISP incorporates an enhanced radar encoder, radar-enhanced temporal self-attention, and multimodal feature rendering with modality innovation gating. These innovations enable the model to effectively integrate radar range and Doppler information with camera data, improving temporal propagation in the bird's-eye-view representation. Experiments on the nuScenes dataset demonstrate CRISP's effectiveness and suggest that predictive camera-radar pretraining offers a scalable solution for autonomous driving under practical sensor configurations.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04541v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Camera-radar (CR) fusion is a practical sensing configuration for autonomous driving, but existing models are typically trained with task-specific supervision, limiting reusable representation learning. items.title: Researchers present Auto, an AGI compiler that records and compiles LLM agent behavior into verified WebAssembly binaries, achieving 6.4x cost reduction and 96.9% parity on AUTO-BENCH benchmark [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Auto: The AGI Compiler
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Auto, an AGI compiler that records the behavior of large language model (LLM) agents and compiles deterministic parts into verified WebAssembly binaries. This approach reduces computational costs by 6.4 times while maintaining 96.9% accuracy on the AUTO-BENCH benchmark, which measures agent performance across various tasks. Auto uses a tiered runtime with calibrated guards to ensure correctness and recompiles behavior traces to avoid redundant computation.

Auto identifies deterministic segments of agent behavior and converts them into permanent, verified programs that run efficiently in a sandboxed environment. Testing on a 300-item task stream with distribution shifts demonstrated significant cost savings and near-parity performance compared to the original agent. The system also highlights challenges related to guard calibration and reference fidelity, which affect the reliability of compiled outputs. The project code is available on GitHub for further exploration.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04542v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Every LLM agent run re-derives its behavior token by token on a frontier model: brilliant, expensive, slow, and unbounded. We present Auto, a compiler that records live agent behavior, measures which parts are secretly deterministic, extracts them into verified programs or distilled specialists, and emits cognition binaries: WebAssembly artifacts whose manifests carry measured guarantees and whose declared capabilities are physically enforced by the sandbox. A tiered runtime executes compiled behavior behind conformally calibrated guards; guard trips deopt to the reference agent, and the captured trace recompiles back down, so nothing is figured out twice. We use "AGI compiler" in one narrow, testable sense: a system that autonomously converts novel experience into permanent, verified, near-free skill while measuring what it does not know. On AUTO-BENCH, a benchmark we introduce and pre-register, 87.1% of 560 recorded frontier-agent spans are witnessed-deterministic (three of the four censused task families measure 100.0%). On a 300-item stream with three scheduled distribution shifts, the closed loop compiles three artifact generations and drives marginal cost from 59 to 2 micro-dollars per item (6.4x end-to-end) at 96.9% parity on witnessed inputs with zero errors. The same stream also quantifies the failure modes: a loose guard silently mislabels 48.9% of compiled answers, and an unfaithful deopt reference causes the verification gate to refuse recompilation. Calibration and reference fidelity, not model capability, decide whether cheap stays correct. Code: https://github.com/RightNow-AI/auto

items.title: Researchers present Mask2Real-WM, a two-stage action-conditioned world model using segmentation masks to improve sim-to-real transfer for dexterous robotic manipulation with 23 degrees of freedom [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Mask2Real-WM: Segmentation Masks as a Sim-to-Real Bridge for Controllable Dexterous World Models
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Mask2Real-WM, a two-stage action-conditioned world model designed to improve sim-to-real transfer in dexterous robotic manipulation involving 23 degrees of freedom. The model separates pixel prediction into a dynamics model that forecasts future segmentation masks based on past masks and action sequences, and a rendering model that converts these masks into photorealistic RGB images using an advanced diffusion backbone. This approach reduces the simulation-to-reality gap by leveraging segmentation masks, allowing extensive pretraining on synthetic data followed by fine-tuning with limited real-world demonstrations.

Experiments on a dexterous pick-and-place task demonstrate that both mask conditioning and simulation pretraining are essential for precise control over each degree of freedom. Unlike monolithic models that capture general hand and end-effector movements, Mask2Real-WM reliably reflects fine-grained, per-joint action effects, highlighting its potential for enhancing robotic manipulation accuracy and control.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04546v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Action-conditioned world models allow robots to predict the future consequences of candidate actions without additional physical interaction, supporting policy evaluation, planning, and data augmentation. We present Mask2Real-WM, a two-stage action-conditioned world model for dexterous manipulation that decouples pixel prediction into a dynamics model and a rendering model. The dynamics model predicts future segmentation masks from past masks and 23-DoF action sequences. The rendering model maps the predicted masks to photorealistic RGB using a ControlNet-augmented Stable Video Diffusion backbone. The smaller sim-to-real gap in segmentation space enables the dynamics model to benefit from large-scale pretraining on over 50 h of synthetic simulation data, followed by fine-tuning on fewer than 2.5 h of real demonstrations. Experiments on a dexterous pick-and-place benchmark show that mask conditioning and simulation pretraining are both required for per-DoF action controllability across all 23 degrees of freedom. In contrast, monolithic baselines capture broad hand and end-effector trajectories but do not reliably reflect fine-grained, per-joint action effects.

items.title: Researchers propose PREDIKTOR, a multi-view framework aligning patient-specific gene regulatory networks and transcriptomic perturbation profiles to predict clinical drug response, outperforming baselines on TCGA and I-SPY2 trial data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Predicting Therapeutic Outcome via Aligning Patient-Specific Knowledge Graph and Gene-Level Perturbation Representations
items.summary:
Researchers have developed PREDIKTOR, a multi-view framework designed to predict patient-specific clinical drug responses by aligning personalized gene regulatory networks with simulated transcriptomic perturbation profiles. This approach integrates individualized gene networks derived from tumor expression data with drug-target information and uses a graph neural encoder alongside a pretrained gene-gene attention model to generate mechanistically informed embeddings. PREDIKTOR demonstrated superior performance compared to existing methods on TCGA datasets and showed effective zero-shot transfer to the I-SPY2 clinical trial data, improving prediction accuracy by 5.6% in AUROC.

The framework constructs patient-specific gene regulatory networks using DysRegNet and incorporates drug-target links from DrugBank to create a drug-centric embedding. Simultaneously, it simulates post-treatment transcriptomic profiles using a model pretrained on LINCS L1000 data. These two views are aligned in a shared latent space through a contrastive learning objective, enabling end-to-end classification of therapeutic response. The aligned embeddings also provide stable gene and pathway attributions that correspond to known biological mechanisms, enhancing interpretability and supporting precision oncology applications.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04557v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate prediction of patient-specific therapeutic response from pre-treatment transcriptomes is hindered by the scarcity of matched clinical response labels and post-treatment molecular profiles. Preclinical transfer-learning models can simulate drug-induced expression changes but are often hard to interpret and unstable, whereas knowledge-graph methods provide mechanistic context yet remain static and fail to capture drug-induced transcriptomic perturbation dynamics. We propose PREDIKTOR, a patient-centered multi-view framework that aligns a personalized network view with a transferable transcriptomic perturbation view to predict clinical drug response. For each patient, we construct an individualized gene regulatory network from tumor expression using DysRegNet and augment it with drug-target links from DrugBank; a graph neural encoder yields a drug-centric, mechanistically grounded embedding. In parallel, a frozen condition-specific gene-gene attention model pretrained on LINCS L1000 generates a simulated post-perturbation transcriptomic profile for the same patient-drug pair. We align the two views in a shared latent space via a CLIP-style contrastive objective with drug-context hard negatives, then concatenate the representations for end-to-end response classification. On TCGA, PREDIKTOR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines under patient-, drug-, and tissue-split evaluations, and transfers zero-shot to the I-SPY2 trial, improving AUROC by 5.6% over competing methods. The aligned embeddings yield stable gene and pathway attributions that recover known mechanisms, supporting actionable and interpretable precision oncology.

items.title: Researchers propose cost-efficient on-policy data augmentation using few teacher steps at learner-induced contexts to improve LLM agent post-training across HotpotQA, ALFWorld, and Terminal-Bench-Dev [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A Few Teacher Steps Go a Long Way: Cost-Efficient On-Policy Data Augmentation for Agent Post-Training
items.summary:
Researchers have proposed a cost-efficient method for on-policy data augmentation to improve the post-training of large language model (LLM) agents. Their approach focuses on using a few teacher-generated steps at learner-induced contexts rather than relying on full teacher demonstrations, which often create a mismatch between training and testing conditions. This method was tested across HotpotQA, ALFWorld, and Terminal-Bench-Dev, showing improved performance over traditional behavioral cloning at matched supervision budgets.

The study frames on-policy data construction as a budget-allocation problem, exploring how to best allocate teacher output among start-to-finish demonstrations, continuation length, outcome filtering, and coverage of learner-induced contexts. Results indicate that short teacher continuations at learner-induced contexts can match or outperform more heavily filtered or longer teacher outputs, suggesting a more efficient use of supervision resources for fine-tuning LLM agents.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04574v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For LLM agents, supervised fine-tuning is not only about teacher labels' quality, but also about which interaction contexts those labels condition on. Pure behavioral cloning uses full teacher demonstrations, creating a mismatch between teacher-induced contexts seen in training and student-induced contexts encountered at test time. Recent work addresses this mismatch by querying a teacher at contexts reached by the student, often with increasingly elaborate filtering of the teacher's continuations. We instead frame on-policy data construction as a budget-allocation problem: under matched supervision resources, should teacher output be spent on more start-to-finish demos, longer continuations, outcome filtering, or broader coverage of learner-induced contexts? We formalize this design space through the rollout policy, switch-time distribution, continuation horizon, filtering rules, and two complementary costs: teacher inference generated before filtering and teacher supervision retained for SFT. Across HotpotQA, ALFWorld, and Terminal-Bench-Dev, bounded unfiltered teacher continuations at learner-induced contexts improve over pure behavioral cloning at matched budgets. On HotpotQA and ALFWorld, where we run the full comparison, few-step continuations match or exceed success-filtered and critical-context-filtered alternatives. Our findings suggest that a few teacher steps, placed at learner-induced contexts, can be a more cost-efficient supervision allocation than longer or more heavily curated teacher completions.

items.title: Researchers propose SaMer, an object-aware token merging method that compresses image tokens by over 93% while preserving object evidence for improved vision-language retrieval on Flickr30K and MSCOCO [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Do All Visual Tokens Matter Equally? Object-Evidence Preserving Token Merging for Vision-Language Retrieval
items.summary:
Researchers have developed SaMer, an object-aware token merging method that significantly compresses image tokens by over 93% while maintaining critical object-level information for vision-language retrieval tasks. SaMer reduces storage requirements and improves retrieval accuracy on datasets like Flickr30K and MSCOCO by merging image tokens into representative centroids without losing important visual evidence needed for effective query matching.

The method uses object annotations during training to guide token merging and avoids mixing tokens from different objects, but it does not require bounding boxes or detectors during inference. By adapting only the shared projection layer and keeping vision and language backbones frozen, SaMer achieves a 16-fold reduction in storage and outperforms existing compression techniques. This approach highlights the importance of preserving object evidence in efficient multi-vector retrieval systems, enabling better phrase-level grounding and improved retrieval performance.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04605v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multi-vector vision-language retrieval preserves fine-grained visual evidence through maximum-similarity late interaction, but dense image-side tokens make storage and scoring expensive. Existing token compression methods reduce this cost, yet they can remove or collapse object- and region-level evidence that future query tokens may need to select. We propose SaMer, an object-aware token merging framework that compresses image-side post-projector tokens into $K$ representative centroids while preserving the original late-interaction interface. SaMer uses object annotations only during training as a merge prior to discourage cross-instance mixing, requires no ground-truth bounding boxes or detectors at inference time, and adapts only the shared projection layer with frozen vision and language backbones. With $K=64$, SaMer removes more than 93% of image-side tokens and reduces ColPali storage by $16.09\times$, while improving R@1 on Flickr30K and MSCOCO. These gains arise because object-aware merging preserves query-selectable object evidence that pruning or feature-only pooling can remove or collapse. SaMer also outperforms compression baselines and shows stronger phrase-level grounding, suggesting that efficient multi-vector retrieval depends not only on reducing token count, but on preserving the evidence future query tokens need to select.

items.title: Researchers propose Circadian Rhythm Score for depression screening and intervention, achieving 0.825 ROC-AUC on 15,233-person China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study dataset [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Machine Learning for Depression Screening and Intervention: an Original Circadian Rhythm Score-based Methodology
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a new Circadian Rhythm Score (CRS) to improve depression screening by integrating multiple daily behavioral indicators into a single, interpretable measure. Tested on data from 15,233 participants in the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study, the CRS-based framework achieved a robust screening performance with an ROC-AUC of 0.825. This approach not only enhances prediction accuracy but also identifies actionable behavioral thresholds for interventions, such as recommended exercise levels and optimal nap durations for sleep-deprived individuals.

The CRS compresses diverse behaviors like sleep, activity, and social interactions into a unified representation while preserving meaningful behavioral semantics. The researchers employed gradient-boosted trees and SHAP analysis to reveal complex relationships between circadian rhythms and depression risk. Additionally, the framework incorporates interaction modeling and counterfactual regression to estimate individualized and dose-dependent effects, supporting intervention-oriented decision-making under varying circadian contexts.

By combining supervised representation learning with interpretable modeling, this work offers a scalable and practical tool for depression screening and personalized intervention planning, potentially advancing healthcare data mining and mental health management.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04648v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Depression screening from large-scale behavioral data is challenged by fragmented circadian indicators, limited interpretability, and the lack of intervention-oriented analysis. Existing approaches typically analyze sleep, activity, and social behaviors in isolation, failing to capture their joint circadian structure. To address this limitation, we first propose the Circadian Rhythm Score (CRS), a composite index that compresses multi-domain daily behaviors into a unified representation of circadian rhythm. CRS is constructed to maximize discriminative power for depression screening while preserving behavioral semantics through non-negativity constraints. Empirical results demonstrate near-lossless compression, where a single CRS retains almost the full predictive capability compared with multiple raw behavioral indicators. Building upon CRS, we develop an interpretable depression screening framework based on gradient-boosted trees and SHAP analysis, revealing nonlinear and saturation-like associations between circadian rhythm and depression risk. Beyond risk prediction, we further integrate interaction modeling and counterfactual regression to estimate heterogeneous and dose-dependent behavioral effects, enabling intervention-oriented reasoning under different circadian contexts. Experiments on the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS, n=15,233), demonstrate robust screening performance (ROC-AUC=0.825) and identify actionable behavioral thresholds, including a minimum effective exercise dose of approximately 300 MET-min/week and an optimal restorative nap duration of approximately 65 minutes for sleep-deprived individuals. By bridging supervised representation learning and interpretable modeling, this work provides a scalable framework for depression screening and intervention-aware healthcare data mining.
