items.title: Researchers introduce ToolFailBench, a diagnostic benchmark analyzing tool-use failures in 19 large language models across 1,000 tasks in finance, medicine, law, cybersecurity, and real estate [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: ToolFailBench: Diagnosing Tool-Use Failures in LLM Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have developed ToolFailBench, a diagnostic benchmark designed to analyze tool-use failures in large language models (LLMs) across 1,000 tasks spanning finance, medicine, law, cybersecurity, and real estate. Unlike aggregate benchmark scores that can obscure specific failures, ToolFailBench identifies distinct failure modes such as skipping necessary tool calls, ignoring tool results, fabricating outputs, and unnecessary tool use. The benchmark evaluates 19 prominent LLMs, revealing that even the best models achieve only an 86.33% clean tool-use rate, indicating room for improvement in faithful tool utilization.

ToolFailBench differentiates between tasks that require tool use and control tasks that should be answered directly without tools, enabling a nuanced assessment of model behavior. The study found that models with similar overall accuracy often fail in different ways; for example, some models consistently avoid unnecessary tool calls, while others, like Llama-3.1 variants, tend to call tools indiscriminately. These findings suggest that evaluating LLMs should go beyond whether tools are called to also consider whether tool outputs are correctly used and whether tools are avoided when not needed.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04686v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tool calling is central to modern language model agents, but aggregate benchmark scores often hide where tool use fails. A model that never calls a needed tool and a model that calls the tool but ignores the result can look similar under final task accuracy. We introduce ToolFailBench, a diagnostic benchmark for measuring tool-use failures across 1,000 tasks in finance, medicine, law, cybersecurity, and real estate. Tool-required tasks return values the model wouldn't guess, forcing it to trust the tool while control tasks attach the same tools but should be answered directly. We label each trace with Tool-Skip, Result-Ignore, Output-Fabrication, and Unnecessary-Tool-Use, using a rule classifier and two LLM judges aggregated by majority vote. Across 19 headline models, the best reaches 86.33% Clean Tool-Use Rate, showing that faithful tool use is not saturated. More importantly, models with similar aggregate scores fail in different ways: most stay disciplined on no-tool controls, while Llama-3.1 models show an Always-Call pattern, and at the same parameter scale Llama-3.1-70B and Qwen2.5-72B differ by 89 percentage points on control-task accuracy. Tool-use evaluation should measure not only whether agents call tools, but whether they use tool outputs correctly and avoid tools when none is needed.

items.title: Researchers propose Reward-Swap Policy Optimization (RSPO) to improve multi-turn LLM agent training by combining dense process rewards with outcome rewards, showing consistent gains on WebShop and ALFWorld benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: RSPO: Reward-Swap Policy Optimization for Multi-Turn LLM Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Reward-Swap Policy Optimization (RSPO), a new method to enhance the training of large language models (LLMs) for multi-turn interactive tasks using reinforcement learning. RSPO addresses challenges in long-horizon tasks where sparse outcome rewards slow convergence and dense process rewards, while richer, may misalign with true outcomes. The approach combines dense process rewards with outcome rewards through a reward-swap mechanism, ensuring diverse trajectory sampling and alignment with true rewards to improve model performance.

The team tested RSPO on the WebShop and ALFWorld benchmarks, applying it to various reinforcement learning algorithms such as GRPO, PPO, and GiGPO. Results showed consistent performance improvements across different baselines and tasks, demonstrating RSPO's effectiveness in leveraging dense feedback without compromising alignment with final outcomes.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04713v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning holds significant potential for training large language models (LLMs) to handle multi-turn interactive tasks. However, in long-horizon, multi-turn tasks characterized by sparse outcome rewards, directly training with outcome rewards often results in slow convergence due to the sparsity of signals and the lack of fine-grained feedback. Furthermore, the model may fail to learn successful trajectories that are not sampled during training, thereby limiting its performance. Conversely, while employing customized dense process rewards provides richer signals and accelerates convergence, these surrogate rewards may exhibit potential misalignment with the ground-truth outcome rewards. This inconsistency can bias the training direction and ultimately degrade the model's final performance. In this work, we propose Reward-Swap Policy Optimization (RSPO), a method designed to leverage the rich information from dense process rewards to facilitate training with outcome rewards. By utilizing a reward-swap mechanism, RSPO ensures the diversity of sampled trajectories while guaranteeing consistency between the optimization objective and the true outcome rewards, thereby elevating the performance ceiling of the model. We conduct extensive experiments on two challenging agent benchmarks, WebShop and ALFWorld. By applying our method to various reinforcement learning algorithms, including GRPO, PPO, and GiGPO, we demonstrate that RSPO achieves consistent performance improvements across different baselines and benchmarks.

items.title: Researchers propose Wasserstein residuals method for learning gradient flows from population dynamics, introducing a simulation-free particle-based stitching approach with state-of-the-art trajectory inference performance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Wasserstein Residuals: Learning Gradient Flows from Population Dynamics
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced a new method called Wasserstein residuals for learning gradient flows from population dynamics, which models the evolution of distributions driven by an energy functional. Unlike traditional approaches based on the Jordan--Kinderlehrer--Otto (JKO) scheme that require costly optimal transport computations and are limited by time discretization, this method uses a residual approach with a non-negative loss function to enforce continuity equations, resulting in a single global objective. This framework unifies existing methods and leads to a novel particle-based technique called stitching, which is simulation-free and effective even with large gaps between observations.

The stitching method demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on trajectory inference benchmarks, offering a robust and efficient alternative for reconstructing population dynamics. The approach combines the residual loss with a data-fitting divergence, enabling flexible and accurate modeling of dynamic distributions without the computational overhead of solving optimal transport problems. The researchers have made their code publicly available to facilitate further exploration and application of this technique.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04738v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reconstructing population dynamics is a central problem in the physical and data sciences. Often, the dynamics are modeled as a Wasserstein gradient flow (WGF): a curve of distributions driven by an energy functional. Though there are multiple mathematical characterizations of a WGF, the dominant algorithmic approach relies on the Jordan--Kinderlehrer--Otto (JKO) scheme. JKO-based methods are inflexible to time discretisation and require solving costly optimal transport problems. We take a residual approach, enforcing the continuity equations via a non-negative loss function whose minimum is the WGF. Combined with a data-fitting divergence, this gives a single global objective. This perspective unifies several existing methods and leads to a new particle-based method, stitching, that is simulation-free and robust to large gaps between observations. We demonstrate that the stitching method achieves state-of-the-art performance across trajectory inference benchmarks. For code see github.com/BasisResearch/wasserstein-residuals.

Article Content: Classified under Statistics > Machine Learning; discusses a residual approach with a non-negative loss function and data-fitting divergence to learn gradient flows.

importance.development_summary: This research paper proposes a new residual approach to learning Wasserstein gradient flows for reconstructing population dynamics, improving flexibility and efficiency over existing JKO-based methods. The method introduces a single global objective and a particle-based stitching technique that is simulation-free and robust to large observation gaps. The approach achieves state-of-the-art results on trajectory inference benchmarks but remains at a research stage with no clear enterprise deployment path yet.
importance.recommended_action: Monitor for further validation and potential enterprise applicability.
importance.rationale: The development is a novel research contribution in modeling population dynamics with Wasserstein gradient flows, offering algorithmic improvements. The impact is informational, useful for awareness but not requiring immediate action.
